News.title: Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room
News.content:
A domestic violence victim has told BBC Breakfast how she was attacked in her hotel room after Travelodge reception staff gave a key to her abuser.

The woman, whom the BBC is calling Lucy, said she was "failed" by the chain and described it as one of the "most traumatic nights of my life" after the man kicked the door off its hinges.

She contacted the BBC after hearing about the sentencing of Kyran Smith, who sexually assaulted a woman in her bed at a Travelodge in Maidenhead in 2022.

Speaking about Lucy's case, Travelodge said that while incidents like this were "very rare", customer safety and security was, and remained, a priority with staff undergoing recent training.

Lucy said she was staying at the hotel in October 2025 for "a night away from the fear" following a period of abuse that left her "frightened and exhausted".

"He walked into the hotel and told the receptionist that his girlfriend was upstairs having a seizure. He asked what room I was in and what floor I was staying on," she said.

The receptionist handed him a key before directing him upstairs to Lucy's room, she said.

"I couldn't believe it. The one place I thought he could never get to, he had somehow reached. I felt sick with panic. My safe place disappeared in an instant," she added.

She said he physically attacked her and tried to grab her phone.

After Lucy convinced her attacker to leave, he returned, "banging, shouting and becoming more aggressive".

"I was absolutely terrified. I froze, hoping he would stop. Instead, he kicked the hotel room door off its hinges and forced his way back inside."

She said she ran downstairs "shaking, crying and begging for help", adding: "I thought someone would protect me."

Instead, Lucy was offered another room in the hotel.

News.title: Burnham brings forward ban on 'subscription traps' to ease cost of living
News.content:
Consumers will benefit from an end to so-called subscription traps and a crackdown on "pretend prices", Andy Burnham has said.

The prime minister is bringing forward a package of changes announced under his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, to make it easier to cancel subscriptions.

Burnham is also planning to outlaw shops using fake "was" prices, which he said trick shoppers into thinking they are getting better value on purchases.

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride branded the measures "reheated" and said the prime minister "has already run out of ideas".

The plans were announced under Sir Keir in April, but are being brought forward by Burnham's government in a bid to give families "room to breathe" amid the high cost of living.

Burnham, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, has promised a series of "everyday fixes" to help people with the cost of living.

He said: "I'm determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living."

The measures being brought forward are aimed at making it easier for consumers to cancel unwanted subscriptions and stopping people being rolled onto expensive contracts without their knowledge.

They were expected to come into force next spring, but Burnham's government has promised they will now be implemented by January 2027.

When they were announced in April, the government said the plans would save consumers Â£400m a year in total, or up to Â£170 per person.

On top of the already planned changes, Burnham is also vowing to end shops' use of "pretend prices". This will stop retailers using "was" prices, made-up discounts or misleading recommended retail prices (RRPs) to highlight deals.

The government will launch a consultation this autumn to decide how the new measures should be implemented.

Consumer group Which? said it has "repeatedly exposed businesses, including trusted household brands, ripping off customers with dodgy deals that aren't what they seem".

Its head of consumer rights policy, Sue Davies, welcomed the announcement and called for the government to bring the rules in "swiftly".

But Stride said: "The cost of living didn't become a problem last week, so you have to ask why it has taken Labour so long to enact legislation passed by the previous government."

The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumer Act, passed under the Conservatives in 2024, cracked down on hidden fees, fake reviews online and made it easier for customers to cancel subscriptions.

The announcement is Burnham's latest intervention aimed at easing the cost of living, following a Â£2 bus fare cap in England and a VAT cut on household electricity bills.

But he is likely to come under pressure to make more significant changes in the Budget, which will be delivered by Chancellor John Healey on 28 October.

But Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

News.title: China evacuates one million from homes as massive storm arrives
News.content:
Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall.

It packed maximum wind speeds of 150km/h (94mph) when it first slammed into Yuhuan in the Zhejiang province at 17:30 (09:30 GMT) before making a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later, meteorological authorities said.

The typhoon halted transportation across the region â 1,400 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone.

Chinese authorities had earlier issued their highest-level red alert for Dolphin, but by Monday morning they downgraded it to a tropical storm.

The storm is moving inland within China, and authorities are still warning of torrential rains, severe flooding and the risk of landslides through to Wednesday.

Heavy rain was forecast on Monday for the provinces of Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and the city of Shanghai.

News.title: Brief relief ahead of fifth heatwave - as more areas could move into drought
News.content:
Much of the country will feel some relief from the heat early in the week before temperatures spike again.

On Monday, the air will feel a little fresher compared to the weekend with maximum temperatures in northern areas of the UK around 18 to 24C.

Further south, while cooler than Sunday, it will still be a very warm day with temperatures between 22 to 27C.

By Tuesday, warmer air will start to move back in across the UK with the highest temperatures across central southern England, the Midlands and east Wales.

Yellow heat-health alerts remain in force for much of England until 21:00 BST on Tuesday, though they are likely to be extended or upgraded as the heatwave nears.

Highs are likely to be around 27 to 30C.

Wednesday will see temperatures widely across England and Wales head into the high twenties and low thirties.

The peak of the extreme heat is set to arrive on Thursday, with temperatures reaching 36C (97F) in south-east England, and up to 35C likely across central and eastern England.

This would mark the fourth consecutive month where 35C has been reached in the UK â a new record.

Many locations will exceed their heatwave threshold of 25 to 28C â dependent on location â for the first day.

Some of the warmth will spread further north into northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland with temperatures into the low to mid-20s Celsius.

As heat builds throughout the week, overnight temperatures will stay relatively high bringing some uncomfortable nights for sleeping.

Minimum temperatures may not go lower than 16 to 18C across England and Wales.

There's also a possibility of a 'tropical night' â where temperatures remain above 20C all night â in south-east England.

News.title: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules
News.content:
A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says will save them money.

From September, uniforms will be limited to three items with a school logo, like a blazer, jumper or sportswear â plus a tie for secondary schools.

Schools are already advised to keep these items to a minimum, meaning many are already within the rules, but about a quarter of schools will need to make changes by the time the law comes into effect.

The government says the changes will save some families "up to Â£50 per child", but schoolwear suppliers say they now face uncertainty in demand for this year's uniforms.

Co-op Academy Belle Vue, in Manchester, is planning to drop the number of its compulsory branded items from seven to three, plus a tie.

It estimates the average cost of the branded parts of the uniform last year was Â£101.94 with a pinafore, and Â£83.95 without â but this year it will cost families an average of Â£53.97.

Next year, when the school switches to a new supplier, it says it will fall further.

The school has decided to get rid of its branded blazer, the branded pinafore, branded shorts and PE jogging bottoms.

News.title: Risk of patient safety 'bonfire' with Health Bill changes, Lib Dems say
News.content:
The Liberal Democrats have urged Andy Burnham to stop the "bonfire of patient safety" as part of the government's plans to modernise the NHS.

Healthwatch England (HWE), an independent body which represents the views of patients at their local health and social care providers, is set to be scrapped under the NHS Modernisation Bill.

The Health Service Safety Investigation Bureau (HSSIB), which carries out patient safety investigations, is also being abolished.

The government says its changes will strip back bureaucracy and improve patient safety.

The Lib Dems warned it risks another Stafford Hospital scandal â where years of abuse and neglect led to hundreds of unnecessary patient deaths.

A Healthcare Commission report found the scandal â one of the biggest in NHS history â involved at least 400 more deaths than expected between 2005 and 2008.

Under the government proposals, Healthwatch's responsibilities will be transferred to integrated care boards (ICBs) and local authorities, meaning they would have to respond to feedback about their own services, rather than being challenged by an independent body.

Separately, HSSIB's functions will be transferred to the government-run Care Quality Commission (CQC), which the Lib Dems argue raises concerns there is no guarantee that staff who raise safety concerns are given anonymity.

Other measures include the abolition of NHS England in a bid to centralise the running of health and social care services under the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC).

The government says this will reduce bureaucracy and allow more resources to be delivered to frontline healthcare services.

News.title: Ocasio-Cortez freezing her eggs and says she hasn't ruled out presidential run
News.content:
New York Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has revealed she has decided to freeze her eggs and has shared her first steps in the process on social media.

The 36-year-old posted the clips on Sunday, hours before telling ABC News This Week she had not "ruled out the possibility" of running for president.

In the clips, Ocasio-Cortez shows herself taking an injection and talks through tips she has learnt, before answering questions about costs, clinical procedures, storage and how fertility care works under what she calls the US's "broken" medical system.

In an interview on ABC News she said she wanted to "normalise" conversations about the process.

She said it was important "especially in this political environment".

"This administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy," she said. "I think it's important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes," she added.

In an earlier post on Instagram she said she wanted to share the information even though there was a "political risk" in doing so.

When asked if she would run for president in the 2028 elections after being shown polling reflecting her popularity as a potential candidate, Ocasio-Cortez chuckled and tried to sidestep a direct answer.

"I'm focused on winning the mid-terms, I'm running for Congress right now," she said.

But when pushed as to whether she was open to it and whether it was a realistic prospect, she said: "I haven't ruled out the possibility and I'm very humbled to the tremendous amount of support out there."

"We have a responsibility to remain focused on the midterms and not on our individual aspirations or plans," she said.

After she was asked about a possible Senate run against minority leader Chuck Schumer, the US Senate's top Democrat, Ocasio-Cortez replied that "anything was possible".

The midterms are held every two years and fall in the middle of the president's four-year term of office.

They are due to be held in early November. Votes will be cast for all 435 seats in the US House of Representatives, and a third of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for grabs.

News.title: Thai school shooter learnt how to use guns via social media
News.content:
A teenager who opened fire at his home and school in Thailand, killing eight people and himself, had taught himself how to use a gun via social media, police have said.

The boy's consumption of violent social media content, anxiety over his studies and family issues, and conflict with friends might have also fuelled his actions, authorities said.

Senior police official Atthapol Anusit told reporters on Sunday that they have questioned 17 witnesses so far while investigating the 14-year-old's motive.

Thailand's leader has vowed to introduce new gun laws as the country reels from its deadliest shooting in years.

Eight people have died after the shooting in Thailand's Nonthaburi province, which borders Bangkok.

Authorities say the student at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School - a local branch of a prestigious secondary school - had shot dead his grandparents at home using a handgun owned by his grandfather, before heading to school where he opened fire at teachers and students.

When asked by reporters if the act was premeditated, Atthapol said that was "probably" the case.

Evidence that police have gathered include the firearm used by the teen in the shooting, cartridge cases, his mobile phone and a knife found in the bag he had carried to school.

His computer at home indicates that he had accessed violent content on social media, police say.

Forensic officers previously said that the gunshots were "quite accurate", with several hitting "vital spots" on victims' bodies.

Atthapol said on Sunday that the police investigation did not find evidence that the teen had practised shooting or trained at a firearms range.

However, the teen's teacher had previously confiscated a BB gun that he had ordered online and brought to school, Atthapol said.

News.title: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
News.content:
Three artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost Â£150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than Â£85,000.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent Â£50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further Â£35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.

The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.

Banksy, who emerged from Bristol's graffiti scene in the 1990s and became one of the world's most famous street artists, is known for murals and installations that often appear overnight and attract large crowds.

The latest costs relate to a mural depicting a judge in a wig battering a protester with his gavel, which appeared on the Royal Courts of Justice in London on 8 September 2025.

Banksy claimed the image as his own work, by posting it on his website and Instagram account.

News.title: Holiday 'completely overshadowed' by loss of airport luggage
News.content:
Travellers have described struggling to enjoy their holidays, days after hundreds of people flying out of Birmingham Airport were left without their luggage.

While it seems the issues that first emerged on Friday are yet to be remedied completely, the airport said the "vast majority" of baggage was now travelling as planned with passengers, and it was working to reunite others with their luggage.

Louise Fenton said she and her family had had no communication from the airline, holiday company or the airport after their luggage failed to arrive in Gran Canaria on Friday.

She is travelling with three teenagers, and said her daughter, who is autistic, had "struggled enormously" with replacement clothes, and had "barely slept because she is unable to tolerate the alternatives".

"We are staying in a tourist area where the shops are predominantly beach shops, with very limited clothing options, particularly for someone with sensory sensitivities," the mum explained.

"We still have no luggage and, no meaningful information about where it is."

She added the situation had "completely overshadowed" the holiday.

"We have worked hard and saved for this holiday, and we simply don't deserve to have the entire experience taken over by something that isn't our fault."

Speaking to the BBC on Friday and Saturday, travellers variously described the situation as "absolute chaos" and "carnage".

Other flights affected include ones to Turkey, Cyprus, Glasgow and Rome, covering a number of airlines.

News.title: Harry Potter fans force diversion of UK-Ireland power link to avoid 'Dobby's grave'
News.content:
He said a colleague told him the nature of the calls, and that "apparently we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave".

"I said 'Dobby, who's Dobby? I don't know Dobby?'

"I said 'he's a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious what are you talking about?'

"[The colleague] said 'no it's very, very serious'."

Ludlam said he then discussed with planners "exactly how to reroute the cable so we wouldn't go anywhere close to Dobby's grave".

He added: "A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby's happy."

The Bronze Age remains the cable went close to were mentioned in Pembrokeshire council planning documents, external about the power link.

It said archaeological trenches dug near the route of the underground cable "contained the rim of an inverted pottery vessel whose fabric suggests a Bronze Age collared urn circa 1700-1500BC, typically associated with human burial".

The cable diversion is not the first time Dobby's grave has been saved.

In 2022 the National Trust agreed it could remain in place following a consultation, but urged visitors not to leave souvenirs.

Fans were asked not to leave socks on the mock grave, made of pebbles with messages written on them, because the beach was environmentally sensitive.

News.title: Parents fear being left behind in screening for rare condition after Jesy Nelson campaign
News.content:
Parents of children with a rare genetic condition say they fear Wales is being left behind as other parts of the UK introduce routine screening for newborns.

After widespread campaigning, including by former Little Mix star Jesy Nelson, testing for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) will happen in England and be trialled in Scotland but not in Wales.

Warren Davies, whose three-year-old daughter Ophelia-May has SMA type 2, external, said it felt like the Welsh government was "playing God because they have the opportunity to effect change and are choosing not to".

The Welsh government said it had followed UK National Screening Committee (NSC) guidance that had not recommended routine newborn screening for SMA.

Newborn screening for SMA is also not in place in Northern Ireland, external.

News.title: Rare turtle to be sent back home in 5,000-mile 'incredibly emotional' trip
News.content:
It has taken almost two years to plan, including building a special temperature-controlled crate for him, and co-ordinating complex paperwork across two countries.

Rhossi normally lives in the sea, but has to travel out of the water â first by helicopter from Anglesey to London, then by cargo flight to Houston, Texas, USA.

It means the journey needs to be completed as quickly as possible, and staff have to be constantly on hand to make sure he does not dry out or dehydrate.

Davidson said: "We have to make sure that the shell is really well lubricated, so we spread Vaseline all over to stop it drying out and flaking off.

"The same for the skin â it's really delicate â and especially the eyes, which both have to be lubricated before he goes into the crate and again just before takeoff, or he will start to peel like someone getting sunburned.

"But I have had to go to the checkout in a chemist's with about eight tubes of KY Jelly and three tubs of Vaseline and explain what's happening when I get strange looks."

News.title: Kellie Bright to leave EastEnders after 13 years
News.content:
EastEnders star Kellie Bright is to leave the soap after playing one of its key characters, Linda Carter, for 13 years.

She arrived in Albert Square with on-screen husband Mick, portrayed by Danny Dyer, when they became the new owners of the Queen Vic pub.

Carter's matriarch character has been central to major storylines including plots about murder, sexual assault and alcoholism.

Bright said she made the "tough decision" to leave more than a year ago but "happily" agreed to stay on to be part of an "exciting storyline".

The BBC has promised "unmissable drama" before her on-screen exit, which is said to be a "while away" yet.

Executive producer Ben Wadey described the actor as being "the beating heart of EastEnders" and said she had become "a classic EastEnders icon".

Viewers have seen the much-loved character at the heart of many emotional storylines including in 2014 when she was raped by her brother-in-law Dean Wicks.

More than 7 million people watched the episode which prompted dozens of complaints. The sexual assault led to long-running story arc about family conflict and trauma.

News.title: Hot weather reveals hidden history across the South
News.content:
As the south of England continues to enjoy an unusually warm and dry summer, parch marks on lawns across the region have revealed the hidden histories of their location.

Among the sites which have seen the outlines of historic installations exposed by the hot weather are Portchester Castle and Blenheim Palace.

At Blenheim, the footprint of an 18th Century garden - which had once stretched across the width of the entire palace - has revealed itself on a lawn.

Andy Mills, the Unesco World Heritage Site's head gardener, told the BBC it was "absolutely magical" to see the outlines of the historic parterre - 260 years after it was demolished.

Mills explained that the original parterre - which is a French word meaning "on the ground" - had been constructed in 1705, and would have "cost an absolute fortune to install".

"It was a very large extravagant thing to do, but it was a way of showing your wealth and importance and that sort of thing," he said.

News.title: Attempted murder arrest after three hit by car
News.content:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and dangerous driving after three pedestrians were hit by a car following reports of a disturbance.

The incident happened on Stokes Croft in Bristol at about 06:30 BST, according to Avon and Somerset Police.

A spokesperson for the force said one of the pedestrians was taken to hospital, but their injuries were not considered to be life-changing or life-threatening. The two others were not seriously injured.

A man police believe to be the car's driver was treated for facial injuries after his arrest.

Thomas Street, Hepburn Road, Stokes Croft and City Road are all closed while police make enquiries, with more officers than usual in the area as investigations continue.

The Best Off Licence in Stokes Croft was also damaged in the incident.

Bristol Supt Matt Ebbs said: "We would like to assure the public we do not believe there to be any wider threat.

"Anybody with concerns is welcome to speak to officers on the ground, but we would also appeal to anybody with CCTV, dashcam or mobile phone footage which may assist our enquiries to contact us."

Jason Arday has cancelled a series of events promoting his forthcoming memoir after his resignation over a high-profile plagiarism row.

A bookshop event in Edinburgh and a conference speech featuring the former Cambridge University professor have been called off “on the request of the speaker”.

Prof Arday stepped down from his high-profile position on Wednesday after the prestigious institution launched a probe into his "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".

The resignation follows a series of media reports alleging that Prof Arday, who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, plagiarised his PhD thesis, completed at Liverpool John Moores University, and other research.

In his open resignation letter, published on the Good Law Project’s website, Prof Arday said that the "only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away".

"This decision should not be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge,” he said.

“Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me. It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure."

Prof Jason Arday resigned from Cambridge on Wednesday ( PA )

His memoir, Great And Unfortunate Things, is to be published in the UK on August 27.

Further questions were asked in the press about the truth of other claims he made, including saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5 million for charity.

At the start of the week, publishers Simon & Schuster said that Prof Arday’s memoir was to go ahead as planned.

Prof Arday was due to attend Topping and Company Booksellers in Edinburgh on September 18, but the event has now been cancelled.

He was also booked for a “fireside chat” at the Royal Geographical Society.

On their webpage, it says the conversation has been cancelled “on the request of the speaker”.

In a statement released on Friday, Cambridge confirmed: "As has been widely reported, Jason Arday has resigned from his post at the university with immediate effect. Regardless of this, and for clarification, the university will continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday’s appointment and tenure.

“The findings will feed into a review of the process for the appointment of senior academic roles. In addition, and as previously stated, the university’s Research Policy Committee will review the misconduct in research policy."

More than a million people were evacuated in eastern China as Typhoon Dolphin, the most powerful storm to hit the country this year, came ashore over the weekend.

The typhoon crossed the coast near the city of Yuhuan in Zhejiang province at about 5.30pm local time on Sunday with sustained winds near the centre of 150kmph, equivalent to a category one hurricane, before making a second landfall at Wenzhou about an hour later, the National Meteorological Centre said.

Forecasters had issued a red alert, the highest of China’s four typhoon warning levels, but downgraded the system to a tropical storm on Monday morning.

Several areas of central and eastern Zhejiang were forecast to receive between 250mm and 500mm of rain, close to a full year's rainfall in London at the upper end.

Wenzhou, a city of nine million on the Zhejiang coast, moved more than 900,000 residents and opened over 1,000 emergency shelters. The nearby city of Taizhou evacuated some 390,000 people while Fujian province to the south moved 98,900 out of areas judged to be at risk, and Shanghai at least 30,300.

Nearly 1,500 flights were cancelled at Shanghai's two main airports and a further 270 at Hangzhou. Train services in the region were suspended and the port of Yangshan cleared its berths and moved more than 500 smaller vessels into shelter.

open image in gallery People look inside a car pinned by a fallen scaffolding structure after Typhoon Dolphin ( AP )

In Hangzhou, the Zhejiang capital, authorities waived parking charges across public spaces so drivers could move vehicles away from the wind and floodwaters, and closed the docks and sightseeing boats at West Lake, one of China's most visited sites, where trees were braced with props.

Fujian's maritime authorities suspended 55 coastal ferry routes, halted all 115 offshore construction projects, and moved 290 construction vessels to sheltered water.

The heaviest rain was moving north, with torrential downpours forecast through Wednesday across Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, and Shanghai, and as far as Tianjin and Beijing.

The water resources ministry warned that the Qiantang, Yong, Jiao, and Shuiyang rivers could flood badly and that smaller rivers in the worst-hit areas could rise above danger levels. People in parts of Zhejiang under a red warning for mountain torrents were told to follow local evacuation orders.

Chinese officials reported no casualties, though several state media outlets said a nine-year-old boy from Wenling in Zhejiang was missing after being swept into the sea.

Authorities, meanwhile, detained two people for spreading misinformation about the storm, according to state media. A 60-year-old man was accused of using AI to fabricate a video showing someone falling from a building in Shanghai while a 32-year-old was accused of re-editing footage posted by other users in a way officials deemed misleading.

open image in gallery People use umbrellas to shelter from the rain as they walk on the Bund a day after Typhoon Dolphin ( AFP/Getty )

By Monday morning, the storm had already crossed Japan's southern islands, where it injured seven people in Okinawa and cut power to more than 50,000 buildings. Among those hurt was a man aged over 100 who was blown over by a gust and hit his head, according to the prefectural government. It also brought heavy rain to the Philippines and northern Taiwan.

Dolphin’s arrival has pushed up temperatures hundreds of miles to the south. Air sinking on the outer edge of the system left Hong Kong reeling at 36.9C on Sunday, the highest temperature measured at the city observatory's headquarters since records began in 1884, above the previous record of 36.6C set in August 2017 days before Typhoon Hato struck.

A station at Sheung Shui in the north of the territory reached 39.8C and the observatory expected the heat to hold until Tuesday.

Dolphin travelled about 6,000km before reaching China, giving it a lifespan more than three times that of an average typhoon and an unusually large circulation, state broadcaster CCTV said. It hit two weeks after Typhoon Noul killed three people and damaged hundreds of homes in Guangdong in the south.

Scientists say a warming climate is making the most powerful typhoons and the most extreme heat more likely.

Sadie Sink has hinted at what she described as a “clever” plan to introduce X-Men into the Marvel Cinematic Universe, saying that she is being kept “a little bit separate” from the casting process as speculation grows over who will play Cyclops.

The Stranger Things star, 24, made her Marvel debut as Jean Grey in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, featuring alongside Tom Holland as Peter Parker, Zendaya as MJ, Jon Bernthal as the Punisher and Jacob Batalon as Ned Leeds.

Brand New Day, directed by Destin Daniel Cretton, is set four years after Spider-Man: No Way Home and follows Peter Parker as he continues fighting crime after Doctor Strange’s memory spell erases him from the lives of MJ, Ned, and the rest of the world, while his spider powers begin evolving beyond his control and a mysterious new villain emerges.

In a new interview, Sink said she wasn’t completely involved in the casting process as Marvel began folding X-Men into its wider cinematic universe.

“It’s a little bit separate. So I’m finding out through Jake,” she told Vanity Fair, referring to director Jake Schreier.

“There’s also so many online rumours but it’s coming together. I think the timing of it’s so exciting, and the way they planned it out is really clever just with introducing one of the mutants, a very important mutant through Spider-Man. I think a great cast is coming together and I think people are going to be really excited about it when it’s all announced.”

open image in gallery Sadie Sink hints at what she describes as a ’clever’ plan to introduce X-Men into the Marvel Cinematic Universe ( Reuters )

It was reported last week that Heartstopper actor Kit Connor was in the running for the role of Cyclops in the MCU’s first X-Men film. The reboot is in early development, with Jake Schreier attached to direct and casting now under way.

Sink did not confirm if Connor had been cast. “There’s always the rumours, and I just never know what’s official,” she told Vanity Fair.

Reports from last month stated that Ready or Not star Samara Weaving would be taking on the role of the mutant Emma Frost, first played by January Jones in X-Men: First Class in 2011.

The X-Men’s screen rights were originally sold to 20th Century Fox in the late 1990s when Marvel was in financial trouble, leading to Fox’s long-running X-Men franchise beginning with X-Men in 2000.

This changed in March 2019, when Disney completed its acquisition of 21st Century Fox, returning the rights to Marvel Studios and clearing the way for the mutants to be integrated into the MCU.

open image in gallery Kit Connor is reportedly top choice for Cyclops in new 'X-Men' film ( Getty )

The first mutant introduction came in 2022 with a cameo by Patrick Stewart’s Charles Xavier in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, which was followed by a brief appearance from Kelsey Grammer as Beast in The Marvels.

In 2024, Deadpool & Wolverine saw Hugh Jackman return as Wolverine alongside Ryan Reynolds’s Deadpool. Several other X-Men characters – James Marsden as Cyclops, Rebecca Romijn as Mystique, and Alan Cumming as Nightcrawler – are set to reprise their roles in Avengers: Doomsday.

Film critics have been raving about Sink’s performance in Brand New Day. The Independent’s Clarisse Loughrey described her as “excellent” in her four-star review of the film and admitted that she couldn’t say more about her role “without giving the game away”.

Brand New Day is showing in cinemas now.

The biggest stars in European athletics head to Birmingham for the 2026 European Athletics Championships with continental titles and in some cases world records on the line, just a week after the close of the Commonwealth Games.

Coming in a fallow year between World Championships and Olympics the Europeans are the major target for most eligible athletes over the outdoor season and the competition is set to be fierce as ever.

Here are the major athletes and races to watch ahead of the week’s action.

Race of the season: the women’s 800m

The women’s 800m is the headline event, even in a stacked programme. Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson has had a stop-start outdoor season, suffering surprise back-to-back defeats and withdrawing in tears from British national championships earlier this summer after tweaking her hamstring. But she returned to winning ways on home soil at the London Diamond League last month, and starts as one of the favourites in a glittering field.

Switzerland’s Audrey Werro has been the surprise package of the season and is the outright favourite after running the fastest in the world this year, but Femke Broeders-Bol - having converted her brilliance in her normal discipline of 400m hurdles to the 800m - is also a potent force. Birmingham’s Alexander Stadium could yet see one of track and field’s oldest world records fall: the controversial 1:53.28 set by Czechoslovakian athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova in 1983.

Hodgkinson had initially targeted the London Diamond League to attempt to break the record, having smashed the world indoor record in March last year. But it now looks as though Werro, who became the first woman since Kratochvilova to run under 1:54 - twice - in Paris and Stockholm this year, is the best placed to finally topple that mark.

The stage is set for a hugely entertaining race - the only drawback is that newly crowned Commonwealth 800m champion Georgia Hunter Bell is opting not to compete over the distance in Birmingham, focusing on the 1500m instead and avoiding a mouthwatering four-way clash.

open image in gallery Hodgkinson returned to winning ways at the London Diamond League last month ( Getty )

Jakob Ingebrigtsen makes long-awaited return

Norwegian great Jakob Ingebrigsten has not raced at all in 2026 after undergoing surgery on his Achilles tendon in January, with his grand comeback taking place this week as he runs in the 5,000m. The injury also heavily impacted his 2025; he obviously struggled with it at the World Championships in September, when he failed to make it out of the 1,500m heats and finished a distant 10th in the 5,000m.

He is the reigning European champion in both the 5,000m and 1,500m but has opted to focus on the longer distance only as he returns to competition, writing on social media: “Anyone who has watched me race over the years will know that competition is what drives me. I am healthy, training has been going well and after discussing with my team, we reached the conclusion that there is no reason not to race.

“What better way than to return to the European Championships, where I have so many golden memories. I’ll be lining up for the 5000m August 10th.”

Ingebrigtsen has never been defeated at a European Championships, winning both the 1,500m and 5,000m titles at each of the last three editions, going back to when he was just 17 in Berlin in 2018, and made history in Rome two years ago as the first man to win six gold medals.

open image in gallery Jakob Ingebrigtsen will make his comeback in Birmingham ( Getty )

Mondo Duplantis bids to shake off rare defeat

One constant of athletics in recent years has been Mondo Duplantis’ crushing supremacy in the pole vault. But the world record holder suffered a shock defeat - his first in three years - at this summer’s Diamond League event in Stockholm, with Australian Kurtis Marschall beating him on Duplantis’ home soil.

The Swede never really looked himself and failed at 6m and 6.05m, only finishing second as he cleared 5.80m with two-time world bronze medallist Marschall clearing 5.90m.

Duplantis set a new world record of 6.28m at the same arena last year but his aura of invincibility took a huge dent this time around, while he then withdrew from the London Diamond League with a thigh strain, after a long conversation with his father and manager on the sidelines.

With the European Championships looming the decision was made to withdraw as a precaution, but the events of the last few weeks mean that - for once - the men’s pole vault title isn’t sewn up before the athletes even step onto the runway. Duplantis arrives in Birmingham looking to win a fourth successive European title and re-establish his supremacy after that blip, setting up a fascinating battle with the likes of major rival Emmanouil Karalis of Greece.

open image in gallery Duplantis' aura of invincibility was dented by defeat in Stockholm before he pulled out with a minor strain in London ( Reuters )

Brits renew rivalry in stacked 100m

While Hodgkinson and Hunter Bell headline the longer distance races for the home nation, there is a raft of British interest in the sprint events, most notably in a stacked women’s 100m field.

Defending champion Dina Asher-Smith has won six European golds and could become the most successful athlete in the history of the event if she wins one more, doubling up after glory in Rome two years ago. She pulled out of the Commonwealth Games with a focus on defending her title but will face opposition from rival Daryll Neita, who is second behind Asher-Smith in the all-time list of fastest Brits over the distance and is a two-time European individual medallist herself.

World 200m silver medallist Amy Hunt is competing in both events in Birmingham; her slow start may rule her out of contention over the shorter distance but her immense closing speed makes her a major favourite in a fascinating 200m race, where she will also come up against former world champion Asher-Smith. British national champion Success Eduan will also be in action, giving the home crowd in Birmingham multiple athletes to cheer on.

open image in gallery Commonwealth 100m silver medallist Amy Hunt is among several British contenders ( Getty )

Josh Kerr holds off on more records

One major absence from Birmingham is new mile world record holder Josh Kerr. The Scot won the 3,000m world indoor title in March, but his season was entirely built around a tilt at Hicham El Guerrouj’s 27-year-old mile record, which he shattered in stunning fashion at the London Diamond League, running it in 3:42.66.

The 28-year-old is always one to talk a big game and his tilt at the record was rarely out of the spotlight as he shared his training for the catchily named ‘Project 222’ - the number of seconds he would have to run to break it - in the build-up. He wrote “I ran 3.42 at the London Diamond League. July 18th, 2026” in his notebook every day; he would plunge in an ice bath for 222 seconds, living and breathing the project.

His superb form carried him into the Commonwealth Games, another important target for him, especially as they were held on home soil in Glasgow. The mile there was a very different race - he won in 3:54.12 and had time to gee up the crowd as he surged clear down the home straight - but the gold was what he came for.

open image in gallery New mile record holder Josh Kerr will not compete in Birmingham ( PA Wire )

There had been talk that having completed those two goals he would turn his attention to the 1,500m world record, also held by El Guerrouj, of 3:26 flat. But that is unlikely to happen this year, despite his blistering form, and nor is an appearance in Birmingham at all. He told The Guardian: “I will hold the 1500m world record in my career. But I’m not in a rush to do that. I think we are flying a little close to the sun at the moment.” His absence opens the door to compatriot Jake Wightman, who was sixth in the mile in Glasgow.

News.content:

When Kat Frize was diagnosed with ADHD at 37, after facing challenges with exhaustion, relationships, communication and accidental injuries, the diagnosis – and the access to treatment that followed it – felt life-changing. But, still, there are points in her cycle when medication is so ineffective she questions whether she’s taken it at all. “Some months, it can feel like there are a good few days where it’s not kicking in like it usually would,” she says.

Despite women positing to their doctors, friends, and support groups online that their hormones exacerbate their ADHD symptoms and make medication less effective, there’s been little research to explore the connection. But now, in a first-of-its-kind study, academics at Queen Mary University and King’s College London have asked 50 women who take medication for ADHD to track their cycles and the impact that has on their neurodevelopmental condition, as well as their daily lives.

“For me, it’s just another part of being a woman with ADHD that I have to navigate,” says Frize, who has never been to her GP about the issue, due to the lack of support she’s experienced around ADHD from doctors in the past. But when it comes to the long-awaited study, she says: “Knowledge is power and research genuinely helps to make navigating life a lot easier.”

When the diagnostic criteria for ADHD were established around the late Sixties, it was mostly based on external hyperactive symptoms frequently present in boys and men, rather than symptoms more common among girls, who may appear inattentive, or mask and internalise their condition – until events like pregnancy, perimenopause or postmenopause disrupt the facade. “Women with undiagnosed and diagnosed ADHD can be very vulnerable at those times because of the hormone changes,” says consultant psychiatrist Dr Shevonne Matheiken.

open image in gallery The interaction between hormone fluctuation and ADHD is under-researched, but doctors suspect estrogen’s impact on dopamine signalling could be significant ( Getty )

The interaction between hormone fluctuation and ADHD is under-researched, but what doctors know, Matheiken explains, is that dopamine is “one of the significant neurotransmitters in the brain, important for things like attention, motivation and executive functioning”. Female hormones, particularly estrogen, can impact dopamine signalling in the brain. There are also theories that phases in a cycle, when estrogen is low, can impact dopamine, which could, in theory, alter medication impact or intensify symptoms.

Without diagnosis (it’s estimated that 50 to 75 per cent of women with ADHD are undiagnosed), these symptoms can generate self-blame. “Like a lot of women I assumed I just needed to try harder, or be more organised, or better at managing stress, or less emotional,” says Frize. “When you don’t have an explanation, it’s really easy to internalise those struggles and see them as personal failings. When you don't understand why things feel disproportionately difficult, it's easy to conclude that the problem is with you…That’s why research like this is really impactful – it empowers us with evidence to explain why we might be feeling the way we feel.”

Like a lot of women, I assumed I just needed to try harder, or be more organised, or better at managing stress, or less emotional Kat Frize

In 2023, doctors decided to conduct a study after noticing that several women at their clinic in the Netherlands described exacerbation of their ADHD and depressive symptoms or an insufficient effect of their medication in the premenstrual week. They increased nine participants’ dosage during their period and monitored the response and side effects across six to 24 months. All nine women’s ADHD and mood symptoms improved with minimal adverse events. The entire group opted to continue with the elevated premenstrual dose.

“Increased dosage may help combat premenstrual worsening of cognitive and emotional symptoms in women with ADHD, with significant clinical implications,” the researchers concluded. “However, implementation should be individually explored. Further investigation of luteal phase psychostimulant dose adjustment is required for safe, optimal and individualised treatment for women with ADHD.” Years on, progress remains slow.

open image in gallery The number of middle-aged women being prescribed ADHD drugs has soared by 40 per cent over the past year ( Getty )

Matheiken says this snail’s pace is, to put it lightly, “unfortunate”. “I think that’s why it’s really important that, despite the lack of robust research evidence, we need to find a way to be able to listen to women and their lived experience while waiting for research to move in the right direction and research findings to translate to change in clinical practice,” she says.

Frize has never experimented with upping her medication dose, but always ensures she takes her pills as prescribed when she notices the effectiveness drops. “There are other times when I may not take my full dose, for example at the weekend if I’m having a couple of days away or my routine has changed,” she says. “When my meds feel less effective, I would rarely reduce or drop a dose like that.”

I think it’s really important that we listen to women and their lived experience while waiting for research to move in the right direction Dr Shevonne Matheiken, consultant psychiatrist

In the UK, there are waiting lists of up to half a million seeking an ADHD assessment, with patients in Leeds and York told in 2024 to expect a 10-year wait for care, as hospitals across the country stopped accepting referrals. In the absence of access to diagnostic tests and treatment, information is spread anecdotally from person to person – and to the hundreds of thousands (or even millions) online.

One academic study even suggested last year that social media content is “romanticising” ADHD as a “cute” disorder and pathologising “normal everyday experiences” like forgetting house keys or having a messy room as symptoms.

“I’m not keen to totally dismiss social media,” says Matheiken in response to the negative criticism. “It has helped increase awareness and reduce stigma. In any other condition that we treat in psychiatry, we would see those two outcomes as a positive thing, but there seems to be a lot more harsh criticism about social media platforms in terms of misinformation, particularly with seemingly trendy conditions like ADHD.”

open image in gallery Symptoms such as impulsivity could be intensified in certain phases of the menstrual cycle ( Getty/iStock )

When it comes to ADHD and menstruation, there’s a rabbit hole of online content to fall down. “What!” one girl lip-syncs in frustration with her hands clutched to her head in a TikTok video captioned: “POV [point of view] you tried to speak to me, but I’m PMSing, which means my ADHD symptoms are intensified and I’m in a constant state of overstimulation.” One girl replies to the video: “Oh my god, why is it so hard to research the correlation between ADHD and the menstrual/hormone cycle?!” This comment was shared in 2023.

Psychiatrist Sally Cubbin, who worked on the King’s College study, told the BBC she believes that women are more likely to make “dodgy decisions and take risks” like not taking contraception, binge eating or spending money when dopamine decreases during their cycle. Matheiken prefers to refer to this symptom as “impulsivity or worsening executive decision-making” theoretically incurred by estrogen dropping. “I’m not a big fan of words and labels that tend to point fingers at people,” she says. As Frize notes, women with ADHD are, often, already busy blaming themselves for their perceived faults, which can include overwhelm, chronic exhaustion from masking, and emotional dysregulation.

Frize, and women like her, can’t do much to change the physiological impact their hormones have while they wait for ADHD research to translate into treatment. “But I can be mindful of what’s happening to my body and what I’m asking of myself each week,” she says. “I can be kinder to myself if I ever struggle or feel like I could have done better. Accepting the fact that I can’t and won’t be at my best all the time is difficult but important – and it’s something that’s taken me a long time to do.”

News.title: Staying in a traditional hanok revealed a refreshingly slow side to Seoul
News.content:

“Shh!” A tour guide raises her index finger to her lips, signalling for my group and I to keep it down. We are in the Bukchon Hanok Village in central Seoul, next to the famous first palace of the Joseon Dynasty, Gyeongbokgung. Hordes of tourists, charmed by the area’s low-rise, wing-tipped houses and hilly streets are wielding selfie sticks. Many are clad in hanbok (traditional dress) from nearby rental shops.

Wearing the hoop-skirted dresses or flowing wraparound jackets is a popular sightseeing activity, but this isn’t technically a tourist attraction – the neighbourhood is residential; a labyrinth of around 900 tightly-packed hanoks (traditional houses).

My guide was not simply a spoilsport either; the nearly 6.4 million tourists who descend on the area annually has led local authorities to deploy uniformed rangers to manage the overtourism. There are signs imploring people to “talk quietly please”, and curfews too.

The area is just as novel to most locals as it is to visitors. Only around 4,500 hanoks remain in the city, mostly scattered across pockets in the central Jongno-gu area. The majority of the nearly 9.6 million locals reside in high-rise apartment blocks, or apateu, which shot up apace after the 1960s – to the sacrifice of historical and traditional building,; many of which were already destroyed during the Korean War and the Japanese occupation.

Museums like the Namsangol Hanok Village offer the chance to see painstakingly restored single-storey hanoks, made from all natural materials: wood, clay, stone and paper; and laid out as they would have been used during the Joseon Dynasty.

However, there is a way to get a much more intimate glimpse into life in a hanok – by staying in one.

open image in gallery Old meets new: Namsangol Hanok Village and the Seoul Tower in the background ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

ead more: Hot springs, shrines and sake: This diverse part of Japan is perfect for first-time visitors

On my final night in the city I had chosen to book one of the remodelled and restored hanoks located in Anguk near the Palace. Following a stay in a towering hotel with bustling corridors and sweeping views of the skyline, a private hanok offered the chance to sample a slower pace of life in the city.

My taxi driver had dropped me off beside an alley, signalling I’d arrived with a shrug. I couldn’t see another soul in the vicinity. I wandered down an alley, toward the pin drop on my maps app, until I reached an imposing wooden entrance gate, and heaved my 19kg of luggage over the threshold to find two smaller locked doors.

Once I’d successfully discerned which was mine (named “Stay Sunshine”), I tapped in my entry code, and ducked through the gate into a neat Taoist-inspired garden (designed as miniature, idealised versions of nature), before lowering my head again to go through the front door.

I discovered a cavernous, minimalist space. The kitchen-diner was equipped with all the useful items I could – and would never – have thought of. In a basket there was a steamer and indoor shoes. A tea set was waiting on the dining table. The bedroom even had an adjoining walk-in closet.

open image in gallery The miniature garden in a rental hanok in Seoul ( Butler Lee )



My hanok’s layout and style had been specifically designed for 21st-century living, though a few days earlier at the Namsangol Hanok Village, my guide Meggie Yu had explained how the the homes used to look, laid out to reflect Confucian social order, based on gender, age and status (no prizes for guessing whose quarters were largest). In all the kitchens, huge gamasots (cast-iron cooking pots) were the centre-piece.

I was taken by the ornate folding screens hand-painted with vibrant motifs, which would have reflected the occupant's wishes or ideals – mandarin ducks for marital harmony, and mountains for protection, for example.

The homes were positioned according to baesanimsu – a principle to ensure harmony with nature, meaning "mountain in the back, water in the front". And South Korea’s history of ingenuity is demonstrated perfectly in how they were adapted for the seasons, with ondol (underfloor heating) for harsh winters and wooden-floored maru halls for summer cooling.

My home for the night had plenty of mod-cons, from central heating to a Toto heated toilet, and a projector. Though it nodded to the past with a mattress close to the floor (previously a way to maximise that ondol heat), the low front door (to minimise how much cold air could seep in) and a traditional square soaking tub for jok-yok (ritualised baths or foot soaks).

Slowly, the numbers of people living in hanoks is rising. Meggie explained how more locals are now yearning for the way of living they offer versus the prevalent high-rise homes. “Korean people are enthusiastically returning to traditional styles and aesthetics, with an enhanced passion for wellbeing, as well as the younger generation's turn towards ‘slow living’. They are reinventing traditional buildings to suit the modern era.”

As well as the efforts to protect the community and homes of Bukchon, the government has been introducing more measures to help preserve hanoks across the city in recent years. Owners have been eligible for grants and low interest lows to restore them since 2002, and recently, the strict definitions (including the need to abide by baesanimsu) have been loosened in more hanok hotspots to allow more people to carry out renovations, and to build them anew.

open image in gallery The bedroom of Hayley's modernised hanok stay ( Butler Lee )

It’s also common for Seoul residents to take "healing trips" to hanoks in the countryside in order to “relax and enjoy the quiet and clean air”, Meggie explained. I could see why.

After spending my evening in the neon glow of Seongsu – arguably the coolest neighbourhood of the moment, packed with fashion and beauty lovers attending its graphic pop-up shops and arty installations – I returned to my little residence and was struck by how peaceful the nearby streets were, lined with hanok tea houses and cafes.

To wind down, I soaked my feet in the bath, made tea and fired up the projector while cocooned in bed to watch Beef, the Netflix show set between Southern California and Seoul. I fought off sleep as long as I could, in denial that I was leaving the city in the morning.

The hanok was the homiest place I had stayed in the city. I had lapped up the gleaming and edgy sides of Seoul – its spas, shops and late-night scene – but my final night was an opportunity to slow down, feel grounded and peek into its past. The perfect send-off.

Hayley travelled as a guest of Inside Asia



How to do it

Inside Asia can arrange hanok stays as part of a cultural adventure to South Korea.

Stay Sunshine is managed by Butler Lee who have around 50 hanoks in central Seoul.

How to get there

Virgin Atlantic operates direct daily flights from London Heathrow to Incheon International Airport in Seoul, starting at £889 economy. Flight time is around 15 hours.

Russian forces will relinquish control of two strategically vital Mediterranean coastal bases, Syria's foreign ministry says, and they will be transformed into joint training centres under a new bilateral agreement.

The development signals a significant recalibration of Moscow's military footprint in the region.

The Hmeimem air base and the Tartus naval base served as crucial Russian military outposts in the eastern Mediterranean throughout Syria's civil war.

Russia was the primary political and military ally of former president Bashar al-Assad, who was ousted in December 2024 by Isis-affiliated insurgents led by now-leader Ahmad al-Sharaa, known by the nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, and subsequently sought exile in Russia.

Under the terms of the new accord between Damascus and Moscow, Syria will assume control of the Hmeimem base and the commercial berth at Tartus port, integrating them into its civil administration.

The military facilities at both locations will transition into "joint training" centres, according to Syria’s foreign ministry.

The ministry characterised the new arrangements as a “reorganising of the Russian presence” along Syria's coastline. A statement from the ministry underscored the gravity of the shift, declaring: "This move marks the most significant development since negotiations began approximately a year and a half ago, paving the way for a new phase in Syrian-Russian relations."

Moscow is yet to issue an immediate comment on the agreement.

Despite its long-standing support for Mr Assad, Russia did not intervene during the swift insurgency that led to his overthrow, though it did grant asylum to the former Syrian leader and his family.

Following Mr Assad's departure, most Russian troops gradually withdrew from Syria, with the exception of those stationed at these key bases.

Syria's new leadership has sought to maintain robust bilateral ties with Moscow. Mr Sharaa has visited president Vladimir Putin in Moscow twice since assuming power, with the future of the Russian bases reportedly a central topic of discussion.

Concurrently, since Mr Assad's ouster, Syria has moved to strengthen its relationships with the US, Europe, and neighbouring Arab countries. Many of these countries had severed ties with Damascus during Mr Assad's rule. Washington has since lifted the majority of its stringent sanctions on Syria, and French president Emmanuel Macron visited the country in July and announced the appointment of respective ambassadors for the first time in 14 years.

News.title: Arsenal lose second successive pre-season friendly after parading Guimaraes
News.content:
Premier League champions Arsenal continue their preparations for the new season as they take on Borussia Dortmund in the Emirates Cup. Arsenal beat Spanish side Athletic Bilbao 3-0 in the 2025 edition, with goals from Viktor Gyokeres, Bukayo Saka and Kai Havertz sealing victory. These sides met during the 2014/15 Champions League group stages, with both games being won 2-0 by the home side.

Arsenal beat Girona 4-1 just over a week ago but fell to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night. Reflecting on that defeat, Mikel Arteta expressed his frustration at the way his side conceded the goals.

“I am disappointed with the result,” Arteta told Arsenal’s in-house media. “We are here to win football matches. We had some fantastic moments in the first half, the way we played, the way we opened them up. We have to score first, clearly, in the two chances that we had before the score.

“I am very disappointed in the manner that we conceded the first goal, the two giveaways leading to the other two goals. It is true that the finishing quality from them was exceptional, but to win a football match, you have to compete at a different level, especially in those areas of the pitch and that is the learning from today [last Wednesday].”

This is in fact Arsenal’s first game at the Emirates since being crowned Premier League champions, as they sealed the title with a game to spare, with that final match of last season being away at Crystal Palace. After today, Arsenal have two more games, including the Community Shield in a week’s time, before they kick off the defence of their Premier League crown at home against newly-promoted Coventry. The likes of Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Martin Zubimendi are still yet to return after their World Cup exploits.

Dortmund, led by Niko Kovac, finished second in the Bundesliga last season, 16 points off winners Bayern Munich. They have played four pre-season friendlies thus far, winning twice and losing twice. The likes of Karim Adeyemi, Julian Brandt and Niklas Sule have left the club this summer.

Team news to follow shortly.

News.title: Andoni Iraola: Liverpool cannot ‘sustain the level’ I want
News.content:
Liverpool 2 Monaco 3

Andoni Iraola has conceded that Liverpool cannot currently “sustain the level” he expects after his side squandered a two-goal lead for the second match in a row.

In the Spaniard’s first game at Anfield since becoming manager, Monaco fought back to win 3-2 by virtue of Paris Brunner’s late glancing header seven days on from Leeds United’s 4-2 victory in Chicago, emphasising Liverpool’s alarming lack of depth, particularly in defence.

“We played a good first half, especially a good 30 minutes. Right now we probably don’t have much more, in terms of the levels required to play like this. They deserved to turn around the game.

“We won the first two pre-season games, but the last two we cannot sustain the level we want for all of the game. As soon as we made some changes, players start to get tired and we cannot sustain that level. So, we have work to do.”

News.title: Chelsea’s feisty friendly ends in penalty shoot-out confusion
News.content:
Chelsea’s pre-season tour of South East Asia ends today with a match against Johor Darul Ta’zim in Malaysia. The clash comes barely 24 hours after the west Londoners beat AC Milan 3-0 in Jakarta, a much-needed win coming on the back of defeats against Juventus and Tottenham.

A fine volley from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to victory in the Indonesian capital.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head into the break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

Alonso’s side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto.

Just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

Today, the west London side face Malaysian powerhouses Johor at the Sultan Ibrahim Stadium, more on them later, but considering the tight turnaround from yesterday’s match today’s clash will provide a stern test.

“The idea, with the game against Milan and then one in Johor, was to arrive at this weekend with players not being ready for 90 minutes until now,” Alonso explained after the win in Jakarta.

“We wanted to have a logical progression in their loads; so we had our plan and we’ve stuck to that.

“We have another idea [against Johor]; that was decided yesterday [Friday]. The idea is that many young players were coming to have chances to play tomorrow. If not, we’d have been short, as playing two games in two days is quite intense. So we will need them.”

Stay here for all the team news and action with kick-off set for 1pm.

News.title: Israel’s mental health time bomb
News.content:
This month alone, three Israeli soldiers are reported to have died by suicide, two of them young women. It takes to 17 the number who have taken their own lives since the start of the year, a rate higher than at any point in the last 15 years.

The month was made worse by the news last week that the boyfriend of Liron Barda, who was murdered at the Nova music festival during the October 7 massacre, had died beside the grave of his sweetheart.

Bar Asraf, 30, was having trouble coping. He had recently told his mother he was struggling without his girlfriend, reportedly saying, “there’s no one who can replace her, no one to cheer me up”.

These high profile tragedies are but the tip of a mental health crisis that is sweeping Israel, according to data collected by Clalit, the country’s largest health provider.

The study found post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in the general population had increased by 70 per cent in the wake of the October 7 attacks and subsequent conflict.

News.title: I’m a professional cleaner and I swear by this three-ingredient carpet stain remover
News.content:
However effective your vacuum cleaner, there will always be those unfortunate spills and baked-in stains that need closer attention. I run a commercial cleaning business and rely on a homemade paste to remove the most stubborn marks from my carpets (and deploy it after any accidents). It’s inexpensive and you will probably have the ingredients in your cupboards already.

It won’t achieve a deep clean, though. If you’re looking to tackle bigger areas and own – or can hire – a carpet cleaner, I also have some fail-safe advice to ensure a pristine finish.

Spot clean stains with a homemade paste

For small stains, this quick concoction is all you need. Simply mix the following ingredients together slowly until they form a paste:

Half a cup bicarbonate of soda

1 tbsp mild washing up liquid

1-2 tbsp of warm water

Avoid brightly coloured washing up liquids, especially if you have lighter-coloured carpets, as the dye may transfer onto the fibres. Before you start, there’s one step that applies to any carpet cleaning; always test your cleaning solution (homemade or otherwise) on a small, hidden area of flooring to check for colour-fastness and compatibility.

News.title: Wildfire forces thousands to evacuate in Canada
News.content:
A fast-moving wildfire in western Canada forced more than 20,000 people to evacuate on Saturday.

The fire in Bald Range, British Columbia, doubled in size on Friday night as Canadian officials declared a state of emergency.

It spread rapidly to cover about 23,500 acres, prompting evacuation orders across the province, including the districts of Summerland, Peachland and other areas to the west of Okanagan Lake.

David Eby, the British Columbia premier, told a press conference on Saturday that one fire official had compared the blaze to a “bomb going off”.

News.title: Argentina rugby fans display Falklands banner in defeat by South Africa
News.content:
Back-to-back world champions South Africa have travelled to Buenos Aires to take on Argentina. Argentina have beaten South Africa just four times in 40 meetings between the nations, with their last win over the Springboks coming in September 2024 when they won 29-28 in Santiago del Estero.

Argentina’s Nations Championship games on home soil last month did not exactly go to plan. They fell to defeats to Scotland and England, with their only win coming against Wales. The loss to England was a particularly fiery affair, a few days after Argentina beat England in the Fifa World Cup semi-finals. Argentina were denied a late try which could have earned them a draw and led to chaos at the full-time whistle at the end of an ill-tempered match. After today, Argentina have two home games against Australia in a few weeks’ time, which will be their final games before the second half of the Nations Championship takes place in the northern hemisphere in November.

South Africa won all three games in the first half of the inaugural Nations Championship, beating England, Scotland and Wales on home soil. The Springboks have a four-match series coming up against New Zealand over the next couple of months. They have welcomed back a number of key players from injury including captain Siya Kolisi, Lood de Jager, Eben Etzebeth and Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu. Head coach Rassie Erasmus has decided though to rest a number of players and keep them back in South Africa to prepare for the Greatest Rivalry Tour against New Zealand, including Cheslin Kolbe, Damian Willemse and Jesse Kriel.

“We tried to get the balance right between giving some guys who are returning from injury and who have not had too much game time in our last four matches a valuable run against Argentina, while at the same time managing the players who have played a lot of rugby this year,” said Erasmus. “The guys who have recovered from their injuries have been training hard and are ready to go, so it will be great for them to get a tough Test match under the belt before we face New Zealand.

“The Argentineans are very similar to South Africans in many ways. Their passion and patriotism for their country and people, and the way they give everything on the field and keep fighting is a testament to the type of Test match we are expecting this weekend. They have beaten us twice in Argentina before and they delivered brave performances in their Nations Championship matches, and will have a point to prove on Saturday, so we are fully aware of the challenge ahead.

“They have a strong forward pack and dangerous backs, and they will have a very passionate crowd behind them, so we will have to be at our best to win this match. We have had to grind out results against them on several occasions in the past, so it will take a proper 80-minute effort this weekend, and we are looking forward to the challenge.”

Kick-off from Buenos Aires is at 8pm BST.

News.title: Man Utd impress in draw against PSG but injury worries mount
News.content:
Manchester United continue their Sweden sojourn with match against Paris St-Germain in Gothenburg.

Clearly a clash against the back-to-back Champions League winners is a step up from their previous two pre-season friendlies (victories against Rosenborg and Atletico Madrid), but at the same time this is more a chance for players to get miles in the legs and see how new signings and possibly some young guns fit in.

One of those new signings is Youri Tielemans, and the Belgian international is in line to make his debut after his move from Aston Villa. Other team news is that Bruno Fernandes is back and ready to captain the team.

Michael Carrick has also been boosted by the returns of Matheus Cunha, Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui after their post-World Cup breaks.

Cunha, however, will not play a part in today’s match because of a “minor illness” according to the MUTV website. He is expected to link up with the squad in Ireland, where they face Leeds United at Croke Park, after the match.

This will be Man Utd’s first outing since the 2-1 win over Atletico, a performance and result that pleased Carrick.

“I enjoyed it, I thought there was a lot of good in things that we are looking to improve on,” the United manager said. “Building on what we did for the last seven months, I think there is a lot of good signs for us, it’s never going to be the exact stage we want to be at. But I thought there was really a lot of positives to take out of the game, individual, collectively as a team, senior players looking strong and fit, and the younger players doing really well.

“The spirit and the camaraderie is so important for the team, it’s great to see the boys getting on so naturally and enjoying each other’s company. Collectively we looked strong as a team, which is always the most important thing, and individual performances seeing the young players come on to have an impact.”

Kick-off is set for 4pm so stay here for the build up, team news and action.

Sports.title: Today on Sky Sports Racing: Badri chases four-timer at Windsor
Sports.content:
Windsor takes centre stage on Monday with a six-race Flat meeting live on Sky Sports Racing.

7.15 Windsor - Badri seeks four-timer in Sprint Series Final

Badri seeks a four-timer in the feature race at Windsor, the Fitzdares Sprint Series Final Handicap over six furlongs.

This horse has been a credit to connections, winning 15 times in 75 starts with his last three runs resulting in success, all at Pontefract. That has taken him from 89-rated up to 99 which is his best mark since March 2024.

Another Abbot returns to Windsor looking to follow up his course-and-distance success two weeks ago after previously running a creditable race in behind Amazing Journey, who went on to to win the International Handicap on King George Day at Ascot. That form reads very well and he could be hard to beat.

Sudden Flight is a model of consistency, finishing second in his last three starts which included in behind Another Abbot two weeks ago. He does find winning hard to come by, though, having not won since July last year, but is now better off at the weights with William Haggas' charge and looks sure to run his race.

6.15 Windsor - Harry Knows and Keep Kicking On feature

Previous-winners Harry Knows and Keep Kicking On lock horns in the Fitzdares Nursery Handicap.

Harry Knows won in stylish fashion last time out at Windsor and received a three-pound rise for the success which might not be enough to stop him from continuing the winning sequence.

Keep Kicking On also arrives off the back of his first success over this track and trip when hitting the line readily three weeks ago and there could be more to come.

This Moment represents the connections of Bow Echo, dropping into a nursery for the first time and must be respected off 79 given the form of George Boughey and Billy Loughnane this season. He is interesting first time out after a gelding operation too.

5.45 Windsor - Mythological Star bids to defy penalty

Mythological Star headlines in the Find Us At fitzdares.com Apprentice Handicap where he carries a six-pound penalty for his success at Ffos Las.

Gelded before his first run, this half-brother to Astro King made it fourth-time lucky last time out when he won a shade cosily. Narrowly beaten on his penultimate start, that win came as no surprise as he was well supported and justified favouritism in good style for Daniel and Claire Kubler.

Hello Cotai disappointed at Epsom last month but this had followed a win here at Windsor and then a commendable third at Epsom before he finished last of four. He may prove best of the opposition.

Sports.title: Brennan secures FedEx Cup Playoffs spot with Wyndham Championship win
Sports.content:
Michael Brennan secured his place in the FedExCup Playoffs as he won the Wyndham Championship by three strokes from Beau Hossler.

Brennan had a run of five straight birdies between the fourth and eighth holes, and recovered from a bogey on the 11th by picking up further shots on the 13th and 18th holes, saving par on the 17th with an excellent second shot after running into the rough with his tee-shot.

Hossler, who shared the overnight lead with Brennan, had kept himself in touch with a birdie on the third and an eagle at the par-five fifth, but then bogeyed the ninth and 12th holes as Brennan surged forward.

"I did great for nine holes," Brennan said. "I felt really good on the front nine. Just playing my game, I was really staying within myself, hitting good shots.

"Felt like I was really in control. Got a little nervous around 10 and 11. I made a really nice par putt on 12 and that kind of steadied me a little bit going through and I'm just glad to make a few putts coming in.

"It's everything. I mean, I don't want to be done playing golf. I feel like I've played the best golf I have all year the last couple weeks.

"Unfortunately, a couple tough Sundays, but outside of that, I've been playing really solidly. This is my sixth week in a row and so seven's a lot, but I think I'm going to be perfectly happy running on fumes next week."

England's Harry Hall finished with a round of 65 to take a share of fifth place, one shot clear of compatriot Matt Wallace who had a share of seventh after he also closed with a 65.

Sports.title: Rahm reigns again after Niemann wins LIV Golf New York
Sports.content:
Jon Rahm clinched the LIV Golf season points title for a third straight year despite finishing tied for 41st at LIV Golf New York, where Joaquin Niemann claimed a three-shot victory for his ninth win in the last three years.

Rahm shot 76 in the final round, but it was still enough for the two-time major champion to secure the season crown for the third successive year since joining LIV Golf.

"The last two weeks haven't been the best, have they," Rahm said. "I would say proud of earlier in the season.

"To start off as well as I did with a few second places and not getting the win and then going to Hong Kong and getting it done when I needed to, having a lead and then basically losing it and birdieing four in a row in the last few holes was probably the most proud moment.

"It's been great. It's been a great year. Again, a little sour taste in my mouth because of how badly I played this week. But it's been something to be proud of.

"After last year and not getting the win, having possibly a question mark over the season-long race, to win twice and do it effectively and win it again definitely feels good."
