What the Rio Grande do Sul Storms Left Behind

The storms came from what the state Civil Defense calls a ‘linha de instabilidade’. That’s an instability line linked to a cold front.

That’s different from the ‘ciclone bomba’. That storm caused so much fear in past years.

Defesa Civil RS explicitly said the damage was from the front, not from a cyclone system passing offshore.

The numbers tell the story. As of Sunday morning, 2,686 people were displaced.

That means they left home. They may stay with family or friends.

Another broadcast later gave a different figure. It put the total above 2,300 displaced.

Over 100 were in public shelters. The slight difference reflects reporting times.

Winds hit 120 km/h in several places. Reuters and CNN Brasil reported this.

The wind and heavy rain caused damage. Trees and power lines fell.

Streets flooded in dozens of towns.

The hardest-hit municipality was Minas do Leão, with 500 displaced. Novo Hamburgo followed with 480, and Sapiranga with 360.

Montenegro, where the fatal accident happened, reported one person in a public shelter (desabrigado). Other towns like São Leopoldo were also among the most affected, though exact figures weren’t given in the results.

The Recurring Flood Risk – and the Shadow of 2024

Rio Grande do Sul has a long history of extreme weather. But the floods of May 2024 were in a league of their own.

It was an unprecedented disaster. More than 180 people died, according to official figures then.

Hundreds of thousands were displaced. That catastrophe reshaped how residents think about infrastructure.

Investors also changed their views on climate resilience.

The August 2026 storms are not comparable in scale. The total number of people affected this time is in the thousands, not the hundreds of thousands.

The event still highlights a pattern. A cold front pushes through the state.

Low-lying areas near rivers are especially vulnerable. These rivers include the Taquari, Caí, and Sinos.

Check flood-risk maps before buying or renting property. Have an emergency plan ready.

The takeaway is practical for foreign residents and investors. The state has improved its early-warning systems.

Nature remains unpredictable, though. This weekend’s storms remind us of that.

Even a ’smaller’ event can disrupt lives and businesses.

Defesa Civil has not released a full regional breakdown of rivers, rainfall totals, or evacuation counts beyond the numbers above. So we can’t yet map exactly which river basins were most affected.

But the names of the towns hit — Novo Hamburgo, Sapiranga, São Leopoldo. Are familiar from the 2024 floods, which suggests a similar geographic pattern.

What to Do if You’re in the Affected Area

If you’re in Rio Grande do Sul, follow Defesa Civil advice. Stay informed through official channels.

Avoid driving through flooded roads. Be ready to move to higher ground.

This applies if you live near rivers or hillsides. Those areas are prone to landslides.

The state’s warning systems are active. They are issuing alerts as the cold front moves.

For those watching from abroad, patience is key. Cleanup and recovery take time.

Brazil’s federal and state governments have mobilised emergency teams. According to officials, most areas are under control.

Check with local managers or partners about damage. This applies if you own property or investments there.

File insurance claims as soon as possible. Flood policies may have waiting periods or exclusions.

Many learned this lesson in 2024.

RS the storms displaced 2,686 people: Why It Matters to You

Rio Grande do Sul is a key hub in Latin America. It matters for residents and investors alike.

The state has major ports and food processing. It also has strong manufacturing industries.

When storms hit, supply chains feel the impact. Soybean exports can be affected.

Shoe production in the Sinos Valley suffers too. That’s Novo Hamburgo’s specialty.

The deeper lesson is about climate risk. Extreme weather events are becoming more frequent.

This is happening across the region. Whether you’re a retiree in Porto Alegre or a fund manager in São Paulo, understanding these risks is essential.

It matters for decisions about where to live. It also matters for decisions about where to put capital.

This was a tragic weekend. One person died, and dozens of families were displaced.

But compared to 2024, it’s a reminder. Not every storm becomes a catastrophe.

With good preparation, impacts can be managed.

More: Brazil news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people were displaced in the August 2026 RS storms? The state Civil Defense reported 2,686 people displaced (desalojados) across 117 municipalities as of Sunday morning, 9 August 2026. A later update said more than 2,300 had left home and over 100 were in shelters — the difference reflects when the figures were compiled. What was the cause of the damage? Defesa Civil RS attributed the damage to a ’linha de instabilidade’ (instability line) associated with a cold front, not to the ’ciclone bomba’ system that passed offshore. Strong winds, up to 120 km/h at some locations, and heavy rain brought down trees and power lines. How does this compare to the 2024 floods? The 2024 floods were a catastrophic event that killed more than 180 people and displaced hundreds of thousands. This August 2026 event is far smaller in scale — one death, a few thousand displaced — but it highlights the same vulnerability in low-lying areas, especially river valleys. Which municipalities were most affected? Minas do Leão had 500 displaced, Novo Hamburgo 480, Sapiranga 360, and there were reports of heavy impacts in São Leopoldo and Montenegro, where the one death occurred. In Montenegro, one person was in a public shelter.

Sources: Defesa Civil do Rio Grande do Sul; O Tempo; CNN Brasil.

World.title: Costa Rica Targets Luxury Car Tax Evasion After Ferrari Case
World.content:
A Ferrari declared for a fraction of its real value has become the poster case for a customs loophole that Costa Rica’s vehicle importers say is bleeding Costa Rica of millions in tax revenue. The Asociación de Importadores de Vehículos y Maquinaria, (Aivema), is warning that luxury vehicles worth well over one hundred thousand dollars have been declared at Customs for as little as fifteen hundred dollars, and the Ministry of Finance has confirmed similar cases of its own.

Among the examples Hacienda has publicly cited is a Toyota Land Cruiser with a real market value near one hundred forty thousand dollars that was declared at only twenty thousand, a gap that allowed the importer to avoid roughly twenty six million colones in taxes. In a separate case, a Ferrari’s undervaluation created a tax shortfall of more than sixty seven million colones, or roughly one hundred thirty five thousand dollars.

The heart of the problem traces back to a policy shift Hacienda made in 2024. Import taxes on vehicles used to be calculated against a government table of minimum market prices. Under the new system, importers simply self-declare a vehicle’s value, and Customs calculates taxes from that figure. In practice, many importers have been declaring numbers far below what the vehicles are actually worth.

One widely cited case involved a two thousand twenty five BMW X6 M declared at just over seven thousand dollars despite a real Costa Rican market value near one hundred ninety five thousand dollars. The shift has coincided with a sixteen percent drop in tax revenue collected from vehicle imports, and Aivema’s leadership says the government has known about the problem for roughly a year without implementing a fix.

The issue surfaces as part of a much larger fiscal enforcement campaign. Costa Rica recently unveiled a package of twenty four measures aimed at strengthening tax collection and cracking down on evasion and smuggling without creating new taxes. Hacienda Minister Víctor Julio Carvajal has said tax evasion costs the country more than two point six billion colones annually and has described vehicle undervaluation as theft on a large scale.

Three related bills are moving through the legislative pipeline, including one that would let Hacienda set maximum taxable values by decree, one targeting the sale of fraudulent electronic invoices worth an estimated seven hundred billion colones in circulation, and one meant to speed up judicial collection on roughly four hundred billion colones in unresolved tax debt.

The undervaluation problem also intersects with organized crime investigations already underway. Following raids connected to the so called Lusso case, prosecutors seized twenty one luxury vehicles worth a combined two point seven million dollars, including two Ferraris tied to the alleged leader of a criminal network, several of which were found circulating without registration or tax payment.

Separate audits have found undervaluation of import declarations reaching as high as sixty eight percent of a luxury vehicle’s real value, a pattern investigators now treat as a potential red flag for money laundering rather than simple tax avoidance.

Aivema is pushing for Hacienda to restore a verification mechanism for declared vehicle values and has reminded the ministry that it retains the legal authority to audit declarations and collect any unpaid taxes retroactively.

World.title: Three-term Mayor Rigo Vellos defeats Shajarie Rogers in heated PUP convention in Corozal Town
World.content:
Three-term Mayor Rigo Vellos defeats Shajarie Rogers in heated PUP convention in Corozal Town

By Jose Luis Cruz: Three-term Mayor Rigoberto ‘Rigo’ Vellos has emerged victorious in Sunday’s heated PUP convention in Corozal Town. Vellos defeated Shajarie Rogers against all the odds to remain as the PUP’s mayoral candidate for Corozal Town.

At the close of polls today, officials reported that over 3,400 people had casted their votes. Tensions, which were already high prior to today’s convention, rose to more than once as voting progressed and the vote counting began.

Earlier tonight Breaking Belize News reported that unofficially Vellos was victorious and that the Vellos team for councilors were also leading but that the split ballots remained to be counted

According to PUP Chairman Henry Charles Usher Vellos received 1,790 votes to seal the victory.

World.title: BTL – From Beginning to End: Ashcroft Gets The Last Laugh?
World.content:
BTL – From Beginning to End: Ashcroft Gets The Last Laugh?

The views expressed in this article are those of the author and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Adam Flowers: From the very beginning in 1988, when the Esquivel-UDP first opened BTL to public shareholding, perennial Belizean boogeyman Lord Michael Ashcroft slowly sank his fangs into the company; and now nearly 40 years, several administrations, half a billion dollars and countless controversies later including this latest; he is taking one last bite of the BTL pie and having the last laugh.

After tooth and nail, BTL was finally nationalized in 2009; at an enormous gross nationalization-related outlay to Belize of roughly $564 Million. And even that figure does not necessarily represent the complete bill. Once years of accumulated interest, legal and arbitration expenses, tax concessions and other costs arising from the wider BTL saga are considered, contemporary estimates placed the overall cost closer to $700 Million. Opposition parliamentarians were already warning by 2017 that the final figure could approach $700 Million, though no single audited Government accounting has established $700 Million as an exact final nationalization cost. More than half the big B. The cost associated with liberation from Ashcroft’s near-total control of Belize’s telecommunications sector; only now to once again intertwine itself with Ashcroft-linked interests through the Speednet acquisition through 2030 for almost another $100 Million.

And are we surprised that the maturity of the amortization schedule coincides with the year in which the next general election cycle would culminate in 2030, if the current term runs its full course? It is an $80 Million acquisition with total scheduled payments of $91.46 Million, and for the Briceño shareholders, this represents an estimated total $20.59 Million based on amortization and interest terms for their 22.51% stake in Speednet, if the seller notes and interest are allocated proportionately to their shareholding.

Essentially, once principal amortization begins; BTL will need to pay Speednet shareholders about $5.5 Million every 3 months or almost $22 Million a year with a total interest of $11.46 Million. And the success of the deal hinges on many IFs: Like IF Smart is even worth $80 Million; IF Speednet’s annual free cash flow will meet the $22 million amortization requirement; or IF BTL will need to cover any shortfall; and IF BTL’s projections of cost savings and “synergies” will materialize.

Usually, if a deal seems too good to be true, it normally is. Speednet shareholders assert the company is viable for the foreseeable future but have agreed to unexpectedly favorable terms to BTL; to finance the $80 Million at 4.5% interest with the first year as interest only followed by 16 quarterly principal-and-interest amortization payments.

And as BTL completes the merger; certain jobs could become redundant, integration costs will increase; and in a one-company national mobile market regulated by a Public Utilities Commission (PUC) of Government appointees, who can guarantee that consumers will not eventually face higher service costs to meet payment demands?

It could be Lord Ashcroft’s parting gift to BTL for all the memories. BTL was incorporated in 1987 and by 1988, Ashcroft-alliance company Carlisle Holdings had already bought around 9% of shares. By 1992, Carlisle bought another 15% giving a 24% stake and in 1993, the outgoing George Price Administration gave Ashcroft/Carlisle “permitted person” status, effectively allowing Ashcroft to hold more than 25% of the company, despite the 25% cap that otherwise applied to ordinary private shareholders under the company’s original Articles of Association.

When the Manuel Esquivel UDP came to office later in 1993, it refused to honor the exemption and up to 1998, Ashcroft was blocked from exercising his permitted person status even though he continued buying shares, though they could not be registered against the 25% ownership cap. By the time the PUP under Said Musa came back to power, the stage was set. In 2001, Carlisle Holdings bought MCI’s roughly 25% block, bringing its total shareholding to 48.4%. Carlisle then bought about another 3% from other BTL shareholders, bringing its total to roughly 52%. The Musa administration allowed Carlisle to register all its shareholdings giving it majority control of BTL. Government even appointed Ashcroft Chairman of the Board.

The Telecommunications Act of 2002 provided for competition and new licenses and in 2002 Speednet is incorporated. By late 2003, Ashcroft agrees to sell his majority stake in BTL. Enter Jefferey Prosser. In 2004, Government buys Carlisle’s shares for US$57 Million, combines them with other shares and sells roughly 84% of BTL in a transaction worth approximately US$89.7 Million. However, by 2005, Prosser defaults on a US$57 Million payment and GOB takes back control of majority shares.

By the time Government finished disposing those shares, Ashcroft’s companies once again re-emerged as the controlling interest of BTL. By March 2005, SMART goes live. And as history records, in September 2005, Prime Minister Said Musa signs the infamous, secret Accommodation Agreement; guaranteeing BTL a minimum 15% annual rate of return, favorable tax treatment and import-duty concessions, restricted the granting of telecommunications licenses to any new competitors other than SMART and limited government interference. The Agreement did not merely give BTL favorable tax treatment. It also created a mechanism through which shortfalls under the guaranteed 15% rate of return could ultimately be set off against taxes otherwise payable to Government, including business tax, while also providing specific tax exemptions. By 2008, millions of dollars in taxes had already been offset under the arrangements. Years later, Barrow’s own Government placed an extraordinary value on getting rid of the Agreement: in 2016 Barrow put the savings attributable to its elimination at around $202 Million, and later described almost a quarter-billion dollars of the BTL award as being attributable to the Accommodation Agreement itself. Of incredible note, during this period of time, the Leader of the Opposition also acted as attorney for Ashcroft’s ECom in BTL litigation during the months leading to the signing of the Accommodation Agreement.

Between 2006-2007, the assets, rights, obligations and liabilities of Belize Telecommunications Limited were transferred to its successor, Belize Telemedia Limited and then the Dean Barrow administration comes to power in a red wave, owed significantly to public fallout over some of the very BTL deals made by the former PUP administrations. Barrow rejects the Accommodation Agreement and in August 2009 moves to nationalize BTL. But there is an extraordinary footnote to that morning. On August 24, 2009, the very day Barrow took the acquisition legislation to the House, lawyers acting for Telemedia and the Ashcroft interests formally communicated that they would accept Government’s repudiation of the Accommodation Agreement and treat it as terminated — effectively arguing that Government could get rid of the infamous Agreement without taking away the company. Barrow proceeded with the acquisition anyway, maintaining that Belize’s problems with Ashcroft’s control of Telemedia went far beyond the Accommodation Agreement. Government acquired approximately 94% of Telemedia’s shares and related interests. By around this same time, three Ashcroft-linked companies — Heaver Holdings, Callerbar and Riddermark Ventures — held around 77.38% of Speednet.

In 2011, the Court of Appeal strikes down the Government’s takeover of BTL. Within weeks, Barrow’s UDP passed new acquisition legislation and subsequently enshrined Belizean majority ownership and control of BTL in the Eighth Amendment to the Belize Constitution. The next few years are filled with legal battles and arbitration in which firms associated with members of the Barrow family act as counsel for the Government of Belize, with substantial legal fees being paid along the way; but ultimately Belize forked over roughly $564 Million in nationalization-related compensation and settlement payments tied to the Ashcroft alliance.

Now, to rid BTL of the Ashcroft-linked majority ownership in Speednet for good, BTL could pay another near $100 Million if the deal closes on the disclosed terms. It is a feather in the cap of Belize’s pied piper. And shockingly, despite opposition from the unions, civil society and the Chamber of Commerce, the wider public response to the new Speednet acquisition has been remarkably muted. It is as if we are resigned or sensitized to the Ashcroft feeding frenzy. Are we simply too cynical, or disinterested to care? Perhaps the lack of response to this issue is because the current voting generation, were in school during the early 2000s and only vaguely heard of the BTL-saga but never knew the intricacies, or because the upcoming generation have never heard of the boogeyman Lord Michael Ashcroft. But the time to have taken a stand against the Speednet acquisition may already have passed. The BTL board has already voted to proceed, though the PUC review and final transaction documents remain outstanding, and approval seems imminent at this point. If the deal closes on the disclosed terms, this money must be paid by the end of 2030.

But thank the good Lord for the laughs and the memories! But is it he who indeed has the last laugh?

There is, however, another uncomfortable reality that deserves consideration: Belize may simply be too small a market to sustainably support two completely duplicated national telecommunications networks indefinitely. Competition sounds good in theory and has undoubtedly benefited consumers, but if two companies continuously cannibalize an already tiny market until neither generates enough profit to properly invest in infrastructure, the consequences are different when one of those companies is BTL. If SMART crumbles, its private shareholders lose. If BTL crumbles, Government loses, Social Security loses and ultimately the Belizean public loses. From the narrow financial perspective of BTL and the Social Security Board, therefore, acquiring SMART and eliminating duplicated operating costs may actually make business sense. The larger national question is what Belize replaces that competition with. If BTL becomes the single domestic national mobile operator, then Belize must ensure genuine outside competition remains possible — whether through Starlink, other international providers or future entrants — while the PUC must enforce prices, service standards, consumer protections, privacy and open access. The real danger may therefore not be the merger itself, but allowing a Government-controlled monopoly to emerge without strong enough competition and regulatory safeguards around it.

World.title: Police went searching the bushes and found seven little bricks waiting
World.content:
Police went searching the bushes and found seven little bricks waiting

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in Orange Walk have cleared yet another hidden stash spot, this time pulling seven small bricks of suspected crack cocaine from a bushy area along Naranjal Street during a late-night search, with no one around to claim them.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Friday, August 7, 2026, at about 11:00 p.m., members of the Quick Response Team attached to the Orange Walk Police Formation conducted a search of a bushy area on Naranjal Street.

During the search, an officer found a small transparent plastic containing seven small bricks of a buff substance suspected to be crack cocaine.

No one was in the immediate area at the time of the discovery, and the suspected drugs were taken to the Orange Walk Police Station as found property.

At the station, the suspected crack cocaine was weighed on a working digital gram scale, amounting to 4.3 grams. The drugs were placed in a labelled envelope and deposited as found property.

No arrests have been made, and the matter remains under police attention.

World.title: 18 year old bolts from station yard and stays free for six weeks before police find her
World.content:
18 year old bolts from station yard and stays free for six weeks before police find her

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A young woman who bolted from the compound of the Orange Walk Police Station moments after being brought in, outrunning pursuing officers into the night, has been recaptured nearly six weeks later and formally charged with escape from lawful custody.

According to the Belize Police Department, the saga began on Sunday, June 28, 2026, at approximately 11:45 p.m., when officers on mobile patrol along Maskal Street spotted a group of women sitting inside a park on the street. Officers approached and asked each individual for her name, and in doing so, one officer recognized a young woman who was wanted in connection with a cybercrime matter.

She was informed she would be detained and taken to the Orange Walk Police Station pending charges, and was escorted to the police mobile without incident. The compliance lasted exactly as far as the station yard. Upon arrival, she was instructed to exit the mobile, which she did, and while an officer was opening the other door, she ran out of the police station compound toward Democracia Street. Police gave chase, but she made good her escape into the night.

The trail stayed cold through July. Then, on Friday, August 7, 2026, she was detained once more, this time with no door left ajar. At the station she was read and issued her suspect’s rights in custody acknowledgement form, signing voluntarily, and was placed into custody pending charges.

In the early hours of Saturday, August 8, at 5:05 a.m., police obtained a warrant in the first instance and formally arrested and charged Kailyn Jacobs, an 18-year-old unemployed woman of Liberty Avenue, with the crime of escape from lawful custody.

It should also be noted that the cybercrime matter for which she was originally wanted remains exactly that in the report, a matter for which she was sought, with any charge on that front still to be confirmed.

Escape from lawful custody stands as its own offence regardless of the underlying matter, and Saturday’s charge carries its plain arithmetic: the June dash bought six weeks, and its price is now an additional count before the court that the original detention never carried.

World.title: Orange Walk parking lot fight proves saying “excuse me” can apparently get very expensive
World.content:
Orange Walk parking lot fight proves saying “excuse me” can apparently get very expensive

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Friday morning scuffle in an Orange Walk business parking lot has ended with both women involved formally charged with harm, after a confrontation that began with a shove and a request for basic courtesy left each with injuries certified by a doctor.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 23-year-old woman of San Pablo Village reported that on Friday, August 7, 2026, she and her sister were standing in a business parking lot eating meat pies when two women passed by, one of whom she has known for about two years.

According to the report, one of the women pushed herself between the two sisters, prompting the complainant to tell her to say excuse next time. The woman then turned around, came at them, pushed the sister out of the way, grabbed the complainant by her hair, and scratched her below the left eye. The complainant fought back, scratching the woman on both hands and her face. The sister jumped in and tried to separate the two but could not, and the complainant called her father, who brought her to the Orange Walk Police Station. Police brought the other women to the station as well.

At the station, both injured women were issued medico-legal forms, and a doctor certified both of their injuries as harm. Statements were recorded from both, and both were detained pending charges.

On Friday, August 7, police obtained a warrant in the first instance and formally arrested and charged both Angelina Gonzalez, a 23-year-old of San Pablo Village, and Merari Ramirez, a 27-year-old supervisor of Chan Pine Ridge Village, with the crime of harm. Both were cautioned and chose to remain silent, and both were granted bail to appear before the Magistrate Court on Monday, August 10, 2026, at 9:00 a.m.

On Monday morning, both sides of Friday’s parking lot quarrel will stand before the same magistrate, and the shove that started it all will be measured at its full price.

World.title: Boss sent employee on a sales run, but the pickup and cash ended up in Mexico
World.content:
Boss sent employee on a sales run, but the pickup and cash ended up in Mexico

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): An Orange Walk Town company is counting its losses after an employee sent out on a morning sales route failed to return with the company pickup or the cash he had collected, and immigration records confirm the man left Belize and entered Mexico that very day.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 50-year-old supervisor of a company operating in Orange Walk Town reported the matter on Thursday, August 6, 2026.

He told police that on Tuesday, August 4, at 8:00 a.m., an employee reported for duty at the company’s premises and was tasked to conduct sales within Orange Walk Town. The employee took the key and drove away in the company’s grey 2006 Nissan Frontier four-door pickup, valued at $20,000, approximately US$10,000, to commence his sales.

By about 6:30 p.m. that evening, the supervisor was informed by a colleague that the employee had not returned with either the company vehicle or the undisclosed amount of cash he had collected during the day. The supervisor further reported that company vehicles are for business use only, must be returned by 5:00 p.m. unless otherwise authorized, and are not permitted for personal use.

Police recorded a statement and circulated information to all border points, and the response settled the question of the man’s whereabouts: the northern border confirmed that the employee left Belize on August 4 and entered Mexico.

Several business places have been visited as part of the investigation, and a message for the man’s detention has been circulated to all police formations.

The border crossing places the case in increasingly familiar territory, joining a growing file of matters this season in which persons of interest have left the country as investigations opened, a pattern that tests the reach of Belizean officials and their cooperation with neighbouring states.

Anyone with information on the whereabouts of the company vehicle is asked to contact the Orange Walk police.

World.title: The weekend ends as it began: bright and hot
World.content:
The weekend ends as it began: bright and hot

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The weekend finishes the way it started, under sunshine. Mainly fair weather prevails across Belize this Sunday, with the familiar 95-degree inland heat, manageable seas, and one small twist: the northern districts may catch slightly more showers later today.

According to the National Meteorological Service, skies will be sunny with a few cloudy spells today and partly cloudy tonight. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated, with slightly more possible over the northern districts later today, a change of assignment from the south, which has carried the shower duty most of the week.

Temperatures along the coast will reach a high of 89 degrees Fahrenheit (32 Celsius) and a low of 83 (28 Celsius). Inland areas will climb to 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 Celsius) before dropping to 74 (23 Celsius). In the hills, expect a high of 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 Celsius) and a low of 68 (20 Celsius). The Sunday advice holds steady: water close, shade often, especially through the afternoon peak.

At sea, conditions run from a light chop to choppy, with easterly winds of 10 to 15 knots and waves of 2 to 5 feet, workable water for the weekend’s final boat runs with the usual care on smaller craft.

On the tropical front, the calm continues. Tropical cyclone formation is not expected in the region over the next 48 hours.

Looking ahead, Monday stays mainly fair with isolated showers or thunderstorms, before a few showers and thunderstorms may develop along the coast and some southern areas on Monday night, easing the country back into the working week.

Today’s high tides are at 6:11 AM and 8:32 PM, with a low tide at 2:10 PM and another low at 12:43 AM tomorrow. The sun rose at 5:34 AM and will set at 6:21 PM. The forecast was issued by forecaster Crystal Rosalez.

World.title: Two reportedly killed in fatal motorcycle collision on Mahogany Street
World.content:
Two reportedly killed in fatal motorcycle collision on Mahogany Street

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Breaking Belize News has received reports of a serious traffic accident involving motorcycles on Mahogany Street in Belize City during the early hours of Sunday morning.

Preliminary information indicates that the accident occurred at around 2:00 a.m. and involved at least two motorcycles. Images from the scene show multiple persons on the roadway as bystanders and other individuals gathered nearby.

Initial reports indicate that at least one person may have died, while there are also unconfirmed reports suggesting that two persons were killed in the collision.

The identities of those involved and the circumstances leading to the accident have not yet been confirmed.

Breaking Belize News will provide additional information once an official report becomes available.

World.title: Lionel Messi bids farewell to father who guided his glittering career
World.content:
ROSARIO, Argentina (AFP) — Argentina football icon Lionel Messi bid farewell Sunday to his father Jorge, the global star’s emotional anchor and agent since childhood who passed away following a battle with cancer aged 68.

The eight-time Ballon d’Or winner touched down on a private flight from Miami late on Saturday with his wife Antonela Roccuzzo and their children.

A private ceremony with close family and a few Argentina teammates took place at a cemetery in the town of Perez, adjacent to Rosario, later Sunday.

The gates of the town’s El Prado cemetery displayed handwritten messages from fans — “Stay strong, Leo, we love you” and “Stay strong, Messi family” — alongside a large floral wreath.

Messi’s teammates rallied around their captain following the announcement that Jorge Messi had passed away late Friday at a clinic in Rosario.

“It will surely do him good for us to be there,” Boca Juniors midfielder Leandro Paredes told journalists after his team’s match on Saturday.

“I need to speak with a few of my teammates to see if we go now or sometime tomorrow.”

According to media reports midfielder Rodrigo de Paul — a close friend of Messi and his Inter Miami teammate — travelled to Argentina.

After scoring a goal in a 2-1 defeat to Monterrey in Miami on Saturday, De Paul paid tribute by taking off his shirt to reveal Messi’s number 10 jersey.

There was a handful of fans outside the cemetery, including 15-year-old Lucas Blanco, who hung a sign reading “Stay strong, Messi” on the gate.

“He has brought so much joy to this country, now it’s our turn to give a little back and offer him some comfort,” he said.

“We drove 700 kilometres to be here. We wanted to stand by Leo during this time,” said Carlos and Ana, a couple who travelled from Tres Arroyos, a town south of Buenos Aires.

The cause of death was not disclosed, but local media reported that Jorge Messi had been suffering from cancer.

His unusual absence from the World Cup in June had already attracted attention.

Messi’s family asked the media for “humanity” during the tournament amid persistent rumours over Jorge’s health.

After bursting into tears after scoring against Algeria, 39-year-old Messi had admitted to dealing with “a situation outside of sports”.

“I went through a few difficult, complicated days,” he later acknowledged. “But I am grateful to the entire delegation and my teammates, because they stood by me, as always.”

Immediately after the World Cup final defeat against Spain, Messi returned to spend a few days with his family in Rosario.

– Humble beginnings –

A guiding figure throughout his son’s career, Jorge Messi was his first coach who left everything behind to accompany his son to Spain.

A metalworker in Rosario, 340 km north of Buenos Aires, Jorge managed youth teams at the small local club Grandoli.

He was the one who introduced Argentina’s future captain to the game aged four on vacant lots where local kids played.

His life changed course in 2000 when Barcelona invited the young prodigy, then aged 13, to Catalonia to continue treatment for a growth hormone deficiency while playing for the club’s youth teams.

Jorge left behind his job in Argentina, his wife, and his three other children to settle in Spain with Lionel.

“When we arrived in Barcelona, I used to lock myself in my room to cry alone, and my father did the same — either without me seeing him or thinking I didn’t see him. We pretended we were both fine, but we were struggling,” Messi later said.

His father was later the agent who negotiated contracts on his behalf, from Barcelona to Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami.

Messages of sympathy have poured in since Saturday from the football world, including from the clubs Messi played for and the Spanish Football Federation.

The Argentine Football Association (AFA) ordered a minute’s silence before matches and that black armbands be worn at games across all age groups for the week.

World.title: Bravery born of pain
World.content:
HIGGINS...I will do whatever I can to protect the kids of our society

FUELLED by her own childhood experiences with sexual assault and incidents of incest that she’d witnessed, Susan Higgins helped track down Troy Ellis, the man accused of the rape and murder of eight-year-old Talia Thompson in Discovery Bay, St Ann, in 2023.

Just shy of three years later, her actions have earned her national recognition. Higgins is among four Jamaicans slated to receive the Badge of Honour for Gallantry at this year’s national honours and awards ceremony scheduled for October.

Ellis, while receiving treatment at hospital under police guard following Talia’s death in September 2023, reportedly escaped. But Higgins later encountered him on the road and played a key role in getting him back into police custody.

For the 50-year-old, the national recognition is deeply personal.

“I feel happy and blessed to know that I can be a help to the helpless and a voice of the voiceless,” she told the

Jamaica Observer.

“When I opened the paper [last Thursday] and I saw Susan Higgins, mi dear! It was 140 people and fi mi name in there, me seh! No man, me feel good,” she added, erupting in laughter.

Talia was allegedly raped and murdered on September 23, 2023. Ellis, who was reportedly known to the family, was subsequently taken to hospital after allegedly injuring himself.

When Higgins heard that he had escaped from police custody, she said she immediately felt a sense of urgency to do something.

She said she was on her way home and her daughter was with her. When they got to the vicinity of the Firearm Licensing Authority office in Discovery Bay, she noticed a man attempting to conceal his face when the motor vehicle headlights illuminated him.

She said she immediately became suspicious and asked the driver to turn the vehicle around.

When they approached the man, Higgins said she began questioning him about his injury, deliberately remaining calm and acting as though she was simply curious about why he was on the road so late. She recalled Ellis telling her that he had recently been discharged from hospital.

Higgins said she continued to speak with him through the window of the vehicle while it drove slowly beside him, at the same time her daughter was conducting a quick online search. The search, she said, confirmed that the man she was speaking to matched the description of the escapee.

“I told him to pull up his shirt to let me see his wound. I was just playing slick because I wanted to see if he had a gun on him. When I saw that he didn’t have a gun, I asked him where he was going, and he said ‘Portland Road’,” she recalled.

“I said, ‘Do you need a ride?’ And he said, ‘Yes,’ not knowing it was the police me a carry him to. I said, ‘All right, when you reach your destination you tell me.’ During the ride, he was talking so intelligently to me. He didn’t show any sign of [being of] unsound mind, so I talked to him and talked to him until he said, ‘Me a come off here so.’ When he said that, me dumb, deaf, and blind, and stopped talking. I took him straight to Discovery Bay police,” said Higgins.

When they arrived, Higgins said the station’s door was closed, so she instructed her daughter to knock.

A cop came outside and Higgins said the driver immediately announced that they had found the man wanted in connection with Talia’s death. At that point, Higgins said Ellis became aware that he had been identified and attempted to resist.

She said she struggled to restrain him before eventually getting him into the police station, after which his identity was confirmed and he was returned to police custody.

For Higgins, the decision to intervene was not about recognition or praise, it was about doing what she would hope someone else would do if her child was in danger.

“Too many times children are being murdered, raped, left abandoned. As a woman, I didn’t get the love and the care of a parent. I actually grew up in the wild because my parents gave me away to a family, and [a man] attempted to rape me. It made me so aggressive, and I said if anybody ever do this to any pickney, if me catch them, me a go unalive them, but I did my best that night to not do what I wanted to because my little daughter was there and I couldn’t bear to do it,” she told the Sunday Observer.

“So many kids get raped and murdered, and so many of these cases go unanswered. I said, I am going to stand up and be a voice for the voiceless and a help for the helpless,” said Higgins.

“I will do whatever I can to protect the kids of our society,” she said. “I didn’t know the parents or the grandparents of that child, but I feel elated that I can help a mother to get some form of justice,” said Higgins.

“As I go along, I will always try to help somebody. My living will not be in vain,” she declared.

World.title: Running dry
World.content:
Paul Williams rinses a vehicle moments after it exited a drive-through car wash. (Photos: Naphtali Junior)

FACING the annual prospect of cutting staff or paying to truck untreated water just to keep their businesses afloat, car wash operators across Kingston and St Andrew say they are once again bracing for a difficult period as stricter restrictions loom.

Several operators told the Jamaica Observer they fear they may be forced to temporarily shutter their operation or find alternatives to clean vehicles if the drought persists, though many remain hopeful that rainfall will ease the situation before the restrictions intensify.

Last week, Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda warned that full prohibition orders on the use of potable water are possible by August 10, if weather conditions remain unchanged or worsen.

Samuda made the announcement after the Meteorological Service of Jamaica projected prolonged dry conditions stretching into October this year.

Under a prohibition order issued by the National Water Commission (NWC), the use of treated water for non-essential activities is banned during periods of severe drought. Prohibited activities include watering gardens, lawns and farms; refilling tanks, ponds and swimming pools; and washing vehicles with a hose. Breaches may result in a fine or imprisonment for up to 30 days.

Speaking at a Jamaica Observer Press Club earlier this year, Samuda said efforts are under way to strengthen the country’s water infrastructure, so Jamaica can avoid imposing similar restrictions during future dry spells. However, until then, restrictions will be in place.

David Chambers, manager of an auto spa, said he has worked in the industry for 30 years and is no stranger to water restrictions, describing them as one of the inevitable challenges the business faces whenever drought conditions arise.

He said the business typically copes by purchasing untreated water sourced from rivers. While the additional expense of trucking water significantly increases operating costs, Chambers said the auto spa absorbs the cost rather than passing it on to customers, fearing higher prices could drive away business.

“People have to still eat food, and the workmen have their families to feed, so it’s not a situation where we can just shut down the car wash. We have to find ways and means to operate,” he told the Sunday Observer.

He said that if trucked water is no longer available, he may have no choice but to close his business, a decision he would make with a heavy heart because of its impact on his employees. However, he said he is researching alternatives.

Chambers said he discovered waterless car-washing products that could allow the business to continue operating, but the specialised chemicals would have to be imported and come at a high cost, making the option difficult to sustain.

“Right now we are in a situation where we have to just watch and see what is happening more than anything else… We are praying for some rain because with rain we know that the water situation will go away because the [catchment] areas will have water, so that will be good for us,” said Chambers.

The cry for rain is also being made by Paul Williams, team leader at One Wash, a drive-thru car wash in the Corporate Area. Williams said currently, One Wash has three water drums on the premises which cost about $18,000 to refill. That will allow them to wash up to 20 cars.

“It affects us a lot, so we have to just try to wash off the cars fast. Luckily, the machine we use recycles water. We have a drum on the inside where it recycles, but for the machines that we use to rinse off the cars, we use the drum, and that takes water, so we try not to waste it,” said Williams.

“If it gets worse, we have to close until the water situation gets better. I’m not prepared for that. I have to go home and sit down and have no work. I don’t know how I am going to manage. I hope rain falls so we don’t have any more water restrictions because right now, I don’t have any water at my house. I got up this morning, and no water, and it’s going on two months now,” he told the Sunday Observer.

Williams appealed for improvement in Jamaica’s water resilience to ensure that businesses that rely on the supply do not have to close their doors.

“We need to find a fix. It cannot be that every year we have to lose business,” he argued.

Chenell Allison, a supervisor at Ten-O-Let Car and Carpet Care, said the company is often forced to make staff changes.

“We try to cut where we can, so maybe staff that is on weekly we give them fewer days,” Allison explained.

She added the company also has contractual workers who get paid per car, so it is less burdensome when business is slow and restrictions are in place.

Allison noted that the company currently trucks water to fill two tanks to stay afloat, but it cannot afford to do so for an extended period.

“If our budgeted amount for purchasing is exceeding profits, then we have a problem, but we are not there yet. We are used to it. It hasn’t come to that yet, so hopefully we can get some rain before it does and we have to shut down,” said Allison.

Another car wash operator said he does not believe it would be worth continuing the business if the drought worsens. He said he is prepared to conserve, because he has other businesses that are more profitable and do not require water usage.

He, too, called for measures to protect water-reliant businesses during a drought.

Samuda said the Government has several major projects under way aimed at making Jamaica more resilient during periods of drought. Among them is the Rio Cobre Water Treatment Plant, now under construction in Content, St Catherine, which he described as a game-changing investment.

The facility will treat raw water from Rio Cobre and inject 15 million gallons of potable water into the NWC’s distribution network each day, supplying more than 150,000 customers across St Catherine, Kingston and St Andrew. The project remains on track for completion in May 2027.

He said the Rio Cobre development forms part of a broader national strategy to strengthen Jamaica’s water infrastructure rather than relying on emergency measures whenever drought conditions arise. According to Samuda, investments made since 2015 have significantly improved water efficiency in Kingston, St Andrew and Portmore by reducing leakage across the network from 71 per cent to 37 per cent. As a result, the system now loses approximately 12 million fewer gallons of water per day than it did in 2015.

In addition, work is progressing on the Western Water Resilience Programme, while plans are advancing to construct new treatment plants and expand water catchment systems, including the Hermitage Dam.

Expanding water catchment capacity is one solution that motorist Miguel Brown believes could help Jamaica better withstand future droughts. Brown, who regularly uses a car wash to maintain his vehicle, argued that the island has ample underutilised land that could be used to capture and store rainwater for use during dry periods.

“We have a lot of springs, we have a lot of rivers, we just need somewhere for the water to stay so we don’t have the problem every year,” he reasoned.

He noted that he washes his car twice a month but is willing to cut down to once a month to help conserve.

“All of us know that we have to save in a crisis like this; in the dry season, we have to save. Once everybody has the understanding and sees what is happening — the entire Jamaica should see what is happening in the dry times and we must get used to it by now,” said Brown.

Conrad Malcolm washes his car once per week. He said he is prepared to clean his car himself using recycled water from home or seek out car wash operators who have access to untreated water and are prepared for the drought.

He urged greater investment in water storage facilities, given the increase in the number of households.

“We have more households coming up and each household will use more water. We need to invest in more water facilities. There are rivers; we have the sea; we can treat the water. We can do much better to alleviate the problem rather than every year we are at the same place,” he stressed.

World.title: Plie’s AMALGAMATION Gala set for 10th anniversary finale in Jamaica
World.content:
Plie Collective .

Jamaica is set for an electrifying celebration of dance excellence as Plie’s AMALGAMATION Gala returns to the Little Theatre on August 29 and 30.

Marking the 10th anniversary of Plié for The Arts, this milestone edition promises to be its most spectacular staging yet.

Held under the distinguished patronage of Misty Copeland, AMALGAMATION Gala 2026 will close its Caribbean tour in Jamaica after performances in Trinidad and Tobago and Barbados.

This year’s gala will honour Desmond Richardson, the iconic American dancer, choreographer, co-founder and co-artistic director of Complexions Contemporary Ballet.

The full company will headline the programme, bringing the Caribbean première of Dwight Rhoden’s show-stopping Love Rocks, set to music by Lenny Kravitz, along with Rhoden’s other breathtaking works Ave Maria and Mercy.

Audiences will also see New York City Ballet’s Christopher Grant in a duet with the stunning Ashley Green of Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater. The ever-spectacular Caught by Parsons Dance, as well as Suite Etta, a stunning piece performed by Adji Cissoko, recently named associate artistic director, and her electrifying dance partner, Shuaib Elhassan from Alonzo King LINES Ballet.

Adding to the excitement, the Plié Caribbean Collective, now featuring exceptional dancers from across the region, will share the stage with these international stars. The Collective will perform powerful works from its repertoire with the Caribbean première of On the Verge of Ascending, created by Swedish choreographer Jon Ole Olstad and Carmina Burano choreographed by Ilya Jivoy delivering a true fusion of Caribbean talent and global brilliance.

At the heart of AMALGAMATION is a bold vision of bringing the best of the world together with the best of the region.

Beyond the stage, the gala creates opportunities for training and artistic exchange through workshops and masterclasses led by participating global companies. As part of the celebration, Complexions Contemporary Ballet will host free masterclasses, with outstanding participants eligible for immersive scholarship opportunities with the company.

With a different experience offered each night, AMALGAMATION has grown into a regional destination event with global ambition. Founder and Artistic Director Marisa Benain says the gala is built to stand among the world’s best: “The Amalgamation Gala offers audiences a programme and an experience that is hard to match anywhere in the world. We have what it takes to produce a dance gala at an international standard, and our aim is always to make each Amalgamation Gala more spectacular than the last.”

World.title: Jamaica leads Caribbean in Airbnb emergency housing
World.content:
This house in Parottee, St Elizabeth, crumbled during Hurricane Melissa.

MORE than two-thirds of the 1,500 nights of emergency housing provided for families displaced by natural disasters across the Caribbean by Airbnb.org since 2020 have been utilised in Jamaica.

Christoph Gorder, executive director of Airbnb.org — the independent non-profit founded by Airbnb to provide emergency housing in times of crisis — puts the figure at more than 1,000 nights.

“The vast majority of that housing was provided in the wake of Hurricane Melissa, reflecting the scale of the storm’s impact,“ Gorder said in an e-mailed response to the Jamaica Observer.

He said the non-profit is proud of the role its community has played in supporting people in Jamaica during emergencies.

“And as our partnership with the Caribbean Disaster Emergency Management Agency (CDEMA) and other partners like IOM, Church World Services, and All Hands and Hearts demonstrates, we stand ready to help in the future,” Gorder said.

Last month, Airbnb and Airbnb.org signed an agreement with CDEMA to accelerate access to temporary housing for disaster victims across the agency’s 20 Caribbean member countries. The agreement is designed to help mobilise available housing support after a disaster, helping close temporary housing gaps that often emerge in the immediate aftermath of a crisis.

The partnership is anchored by a memorandum of understanding (MOU) that addresses roles, coordination, and activations during the critical early days of a disaster response. CDEMA will help coordinate with local responders to identify people with emergency housing needs, while Airbnb.org will support these efforts by helping provide free, available emergency housing.

Airbnb.org leverages the Airbnb platform to help connect people who need a place to stay with listings on the platform, enabling guests to book homes that meet their needs, including kitchens, laundry rooms, and pet-friendly spaces. All stays are offered at no cost to guests and funded by Airbnb.org.

According to CDEMA’s Executive Director Elizabeth Riley, the partnership represents a valuable addition to the region’s disaster preparedness and response framework.

“As we enter the 2026 hurricane season, the MOU strengthens our ability to support people affected by disasters through innovative solutions and enhanced regional collaboration. By combining CDEMA’s regional coordination capacity with Airbnb.org’s emergency housing support, we are expanding the resources available to communities when they need them most,” Riley said. “It also reflects a shared commitment to ensuring that affected populations can access timely assistance and recover more quickly following disasters.”

Additionally, Airbnb, in collaboration with CDEMA and the Caribbean Tourism Organization (CTO), launched a hurricane safety guide to support communities and educate the public about what to do before, during, and after a hurricane. It also includes emergency contact information for multiple Caribbean islands. Airbnb said it will provide the hurricane safety guide to hosts in the region so they can share with their guests.

“Safety in the Caribbean is a top priority for Airbnb. By collaborating with expert organisations like CDEMA and the CTO, we are ensuring our hosts and guests have access to vital, locally sourced resources to prepare for and navigate hurricane season,” said Carlos Muñoz, Airbnb’s director of public policy for the Caribbean and Central America.

World.title: SALMON FINDS A WAY
World.content:
Jamaica’s Joseph Salmon competes in the men’s discus throw qualification at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon, on Saturday. Salmon qualified for today’s final with a mark of 62.10m. (Photo: Paul A Reid)

OREGON, USA — Inspired by his teammate Michael Andre Edwards’ last-round heroics in the men’s triple jump final on Friday evening, world leader Joseph Salmon pulled off a similar nervy feat on Saturday to qualify for today’s men’s discus throw final on the final day of the World Athletics Under-20 Championships here at Hayward Field.

After two fouls and on the brink of failing to qualify, Salmon threw 62.10m on his final attempt in Group B, qualifying to join Kamari Kennedy who had qualified in the first group with 60.65m. Both surpassed the automatic qualifying mark of 60.50m.

Meanwhile, Jamaica will hope to defend both 4x100m relay titles today after qualifying on Saturday.

All four Jamaican relay teams, including the two 4x400m teams, advanced to their finals.

On Friday, Edwards pulled off a final-round miracle to win the men’s triple jump, and Salmon said although he was not expecting to need all three qualifying attempts, he was inspired by what he saw.

“I am really confident. What Michael did [Friday], he gave me a boost, gave me a boost, man so we’ll see. It’s going to be a show [Sunday],” he said after qualifying.

Salmon fouled his first two attempts, saying his technique was not the best, while his second attempt was ruled a foul for stepping over the board.

“In the third round I got everything together and just sent it out there,” he said, adding that he was not thinking about any particular distance but was simply focused on qualifying. “I am pleased to say I’m not really throwing at my full potential but just to get into the final.”

Kennedy was delighted with his third throw, which was over the qualifying mark.

“I was really happy. I’m glad that I got the qualifying mark and so now I can prepare for the finals,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

Kennedy had failed to advance from the first round of the shot put earlier in the championships but said the discus qualification made up for that disappointment.

Strong legs from lead-off runner Kyle Bodden and anchor Sanjay Seymore helped the Jamaican men’s team win their heat of the 4x100m in 39.51 seconds.

Nyrone Wade, who was part of the team that won in Lima, Peru, two years ago, and Nathaniel Martin were also part of the team that beat Japan, which finished second in 39.65 seconds, and Hong Kong, which set a national Under-20 record of 39.66.

The women’s team of Samoya Brown, Theianna Lee Terrelonge, Natrece East and Renecia Edwards finished second in their heat in 43.61 seconds, behind Australia which ran a national Under-20 record 43.44. Nigeria was third in 43.65.

East told the Sunday Observer that the team was happy to advance to the final.

“I think we performed well. I mean, it’s the first three that advance to the finals so we did enough to make it to the finals. And, I feel like when we run in the finals we can do better,” she said.

East said they were going after medals and, while admitting the baton exchanges were good, hoped they could be better today.

“Yeah, I feel like they were good. I mean, there’s always room for improvement so in the final we have to make even better changes and we will be good.”

Earlier, the team of Daniellia Dixon, Kristen Herbert, Davine Dickenson and Shanika Lindsay finished third in the women’s 4x400m, qualifying in 3:35.93 behind Germany, which won in 3:34.35, and Slovenia, which ran a national Under-20 record 3:35.60.

The men’s team of Nishawn Walker, Jordan Rehedul, Jaeden Campbell and Jabulani McLeod also placed third in their semi-final heat in 3:06.44. The USA led with a World Under-20-leading 3:04.55 while South Africa was second in 3:05.08, with both teams being gold-medal prospects.

World.title: COCKTAILS With…
World.content:
(Photo: Marz Jackson)

ANNALISA “@annaixe” GUTHRIE

Designer | Creative Practitioner

We’re stirring things up.

The Style Observer serves up Cocktails With with a twist.

For Independence 64, designer Annalisa Guthrie is toasting the icons, influences, and cultural greats who helped shape Jamaica — and, in turn, shaped the woman she is today.

Known for her knack of transforming the most unexpected materials into high-fashion statements, Guthrie is turning heritage into a silhouette, history into a statement, and Jamaican pride into something wearable.

Style Observer: What was the inspiration behind the new looks?

Annalisa Guthrie: “Our greatness today is a result of who we have been and who we continue to be. Here’s my way of celebrating the greats who helped shape the culture; the same culture that has made me who I am and what I’ll always be proud to be — Jamaican,” she shared.

SO shares the three-piece collection.

Asymmetrical Mesh Merino Dress

A staple in Jamaican fashion is the mesh marino, most commonly worn in the context of streetwear, and which has been styled in many ways, especially by male reggae artistes. I thought it would be interesting to make something of a gown out of different cut-up pieces of several merinos, but in a very raw and rugged way to keep in line with the tradition of “tun yuh hand and mek fashion”. I didn’t want this piece to feel as refined, but I still wanted it to feel flattering and unique and fashionable for the female form while still being raw.

Dancehall Queen 2.0

Nineties dancehall fashion has always been the blueprint for so many internationally, and I thought it was very important to pay tribute to not only original Dancehall Queen Carlene and some of her iconic golden looks, but also to pay homage to Spice, the queen of dancehall. The bejewelled bra has diamond shapes that meet the eye immediately, but If you look closely at the end of the chains you can see symbols (clubs, hearts and spades) to represent the symbols in a card pack — a nuanced way to honour Spice as “queen inna di deck”.

Bandana

For far too long I’ve heard criticism about the Bandana being outdated or not seen as beautiful, despite it being our national dress. I think it is our responsibility as artists to create and help others view things through a different lens. I made this video originally for the purpose of reimagining the Bandana print in a way that felt reverent, but modern. It was meant to be the main attraction. Jamaican folklorist Louise Bennett-Coverley championed for our cultural pride in a way that inspired me deeply and she wore the bandana proudly. I wanted to honour her by carrying the torch and using my creativity to represent her national pride in present day. I hope people are able to feel her spirit and reignite their own love for this little island when seeing this piece take form.

World.title: Jamaica’s Edwards snatches triple jump gold at World U20 Champs
World.content:
In this March 2026 file photo, Jamaica College star Michael-Andre Edwards displays his gold medal after winning the Class 1 Boys’ triple jump final, with a leap of 16.25m., to close out his Champs career. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

OREGON, USA – Michael Andre Edwards thought he would be able to jump “about 16.80m” but surprised himself with a dramatic final round 17.08m (1.1m/s) leap to snatch the gold medal at the World Athletics Under- 20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon.

Edwards, who started slowly, trailed his good friend American Miles Nesmith going into the final round, when he produced the jump of his life on the biggest stage.

After his dramatic win, he said he never expected he would be jumping this far this soon but never thought 17.00m was out of his reach.

He twice bettered his previous personal best of 16.30m set in July, with 16.71m in the fifth round and then his big jump a round later. He joins national under-20 record holder Jaydon Hibbert,17.87m, and James Beckford, 17.29m, as the only Jamaican juniors to jump over 17.00m in the triple jump.

Edwards is also the second Jamaican man to win the triple jump after Hibbert won it in 2022.

This was Jamaica’s first gold of the champions and third medal after Gary Card and Shanoya Douglas won silver medals in their respective 100m finals on Thursday.

Nesmith, who was second to Edwards at the Penn Relays in April, took the silver medal with a personal best 16.79m (1.0m/s) and China’s Zhuoyue Wang was third with 16.36m (0.9m/s).

Edwards, who needed just one jump, 16.00m, to qualify from the prelims, started slowly with a 13.76m (1.4m/s) but qualified for the final with a 16.23m (-0.3m/s) in the third round before he got into second place with 16.71 (0.5m/s) in the fifth round.

-Paul A Reid
