World.title: Why Poland’s right-wing split may not save Tusk
World.content:
However, the departure of former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki from PiS complicates the balance of balance of power on the right.

PiS, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, formally ruptured last month, when Morawiecki stormed out, taking 40 MPs with him to form the new Development Plus party, leaving PiS with 147 deputies.

The split between him and party founder and leader Jarosław Kaczyński quickly became acrimonious.

Morawiecki criticized his own government’s decisions on Covid-19 restrictions and its push to tighten Poland’s abortion law, which outraged many women and saw PiS take a long-term hit in public support.

“Although I oppose abortion, I believed the change would lead to catastrophe — a polling collapse. Unfortunately, I was right,” Morawiecki said on the popular YouTube show Rymanowski Live this week.

He is now trying to set up a more moderate center-right party focused on economic growth which is less partisan than PiS. “Today, Poland does not need to get bogged down in ideological disputes,” he said in Monday’s interview. However, he has ruled out ever working with Tusk in the future.

World.title: A new rival is forcing Italy’s Meloni back to her far-right roots
World.content:
While France and other countries tightened border checks, Italy went further and announced it had suspended the EU’s free-movement Schengen agreement with Madrid. Now, in Italian airports, passengers from Spain are asked to join a different line.

Meloni’s office has made clear it has no intention of lifting the controls until at least Aug. 15, escalating the clash with Spain, which retaliated by imposing checks on travelers from Italy.

“We will not back down one millimeter on illegal immigration,” Meloni posted on X while her allies attacked the socialist Spanish government, accusing it of failing to manage migration flows. “Defending our borders, stopping human traffickers, and ensuring effective repatriation will continue to be this government’s policy,” she added.

The clash with Spain is just the latest sign that the Italian leader is doing all she can to secure her core, hard-right electorate in the face of a challenge from the right by Roberto Vannacci, a former general and member of the European Parliament.

With an election expected as early as next spring, Vannacci’s far-right National Future party has been advancing in the polls, overtaking one of Meloni’s coalition partners, the far-right League party, and gaining on another, Forza Italia, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.

For Meloni, who began her political career in the youth wing of Italy’s post-fascist movement, the challenge strikes particularly close to home.

World.title: Israel rejects Trump’s peace plan for Gaza
World.content:
Hamas has said that it would begin disarming, but in recent days an Israeli official said the country still had “serious security concerns.”

The rejection is a blow to peace negotiations the Trump administratoin has been brokering since September. The U.S. president had described the plan, now rejected by Israel, as a “critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government” and giving Israel “the security it deserves.”

Israel appears unlikely to pull back significant forces or make other concessions ahead of legislative elections scheduled for October. Netanyahu faces a tough reelection battle, with his far-right coalition partners urging him to keep up the pressure on Hamas and leave forces in Gaza. Opponents also accuse him of failing to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack when Hamas-led militants attacked Israeli communities, killing about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and taking 251 others hostage. Israel responded with a punishing military offensive that has killed more than 73,000 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.

Netanyahu said on Sunday that he is now in discussions with U.S. officials about how to move forward. “They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us, and we know how to stand up to these things,” he said.

World.title: Russia and Ukraine exchange overnight strikes, WHO confirms warehouse destroyed
World.content:
Another overnight strike on the Zhytomyr region injured three people, Ukrainian emergency services said.

Meanwhile, five people died in a Ukrainian overnight drone attack on the Russian city of Belgorod, the regional crisis centre said on Sunday. Acting governor Alexander Shuvayev said earlier on Sunday that three people were killed and 25 others injured in the “massive terrorist drone attack” by Kyiv. The death toll later rose to five.

Zelenskyy condemned what he described as “ballistic terror” attacks on Odesa, Kharkiv, Pavlohrad, and other regions. “Every such attack on human life serves as a constant reminder – we need more pressure, more sanctions against Russia, and more air defense for Ukraine,” he said.

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director-general of the World Health Organization, said on Sunday that a WHO warehouse in Dnipro in Ukraine was destroyed by a strike on Friday.

The warehouse held humanitarian supplies for frontline health facilities. No casualties were reported, as a WHO staff member and drivers managed to evacuate 130 of approximately 300 pallets and left the area before the attack.

“I cannot say loudly enough: attacks on health care MUST STOP. Otherwise, people are deprived of lifesaving healthcare,” Tedros said.

World.title: Germany battling ‘daily’ hybrid warfare attacks, minister warns
World.content:
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt speaks to the media during a news conference at Leipzig airport on Aug. 5, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images

Last week’s drone incident in Lepizig just the latest example.

Germany is being hit by hybrid warfare attacks from foreign powers on a “daily” basis, the country’s interior minister has warned, after a drone packed with explosives was found at Leipzig Airport earlier this week.

Espionage, sabotage, cyber attacks and covert actions “with the aim of destabilizing Germany or directly harming it” are a “constant reality,” German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told BILD in an interview on Sunday.

Dobrindt suggested on Thursday that a drone incident at Leipzig Airport may have been an attack by a state actor. The minister has stopped short of specifying which foreign powers are behind the hybrid attacks.

World.title: Magyar’s party backs former supreme court head for Hungarian president
World.content:
The Hungarian Parliament is set to vote on András Baka's candidacy next Tuesday. | Tibor Illyes/EPA

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s ruling Tisza party said on Saturday that it had nominated former Supreme Court President András Baka to become the country’s next president.

Baka, who worked as a judge on the European Court of Human Rights before being elected to head the Supreme Court, was removed from his post by the Fidesz government in 2011 — a move the ECHR ruled was unlawful.

“Throughout his career, Dr. András Baka has considered the principle of the separation of powers to be of paramount importance and has consistently stood up for the rule of law and judicial independence,” Tisza said in a Facebook post.

World.title: Sánchez-Meloni clash brings back borders — and headaches for tourists
World.content:
Madrid has pushed back forcefully against that narrative, and noted that the migrants could not leave the North African territory because they lack valid IDs required to travel on ferries to mainland Europe.

Spanish authorities and the European Commission this week confirmed that none of the 72,000 people who surged into Ceuta have crossed the Strait of Gibraltar. During a meeting of EU interior ministers on Tuesday, Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi publicly praised Spain for its handling of the situation and expressed Rome’s “sincere solidarity” with Madrid.

Yet despite requests from Madrid, the Italian government has declined to end border checks even after it became clear that there was no risk of the Ceuta crisis spilling into the rest of Europe. Rome’s inaction prompted Spain to issue a statement on Friday threatening to adopt “proportional measures” if Rome did not change course by Aug. 9.

After Meloni’s office responded by declaring “Italy does not accept ultimatums or demands from abroad regarding national security and border control,” Madrid moved to reintroduce its own controls.

Magnus Brunner, the European commissioner for internal affairs and migration, sought to mediate in the dispute.

“I was in contact with both the Spanish and Italian Interior Ministers today. Both confirmed that the internal border controls are temporary,” Brunner said in a post on X. “I stressed the progress we’ve made on tackling illegal migration and that trust between Member States is our most valuable currency.”

World.title: Human hair used as protective barrier in oceans
World.content:
As the Portuguese saying goes: "At first it feels strange, then it gets under your skin." The same happens when you first hear about a project that turns human hair into a barrier to filter oil and plastics from the ocean.

 

The technology, already used in other countries such as Chile and the United States of America, inspired Mariana Robrahn, founder of the non-governmental organisation (NGO) Fiotrar, to create and develop this project in Brazil.

The tests were carried out for the first time in Enseada de Bom Jesus, on the shores of Guanabara Bay in the state of Rio de Janeiro, where a rubbish containment barrier was already in place.

"These filters are fixed to the orange floating barrier that retains rubbish, and we use it as a support for Fiotrar's barrier," explains environmental engineer Ana Beatriz Gonçalves, who is responsible for the weekly maintenance of the new barriers.

So, in Guanabara Bay, instead of small boats with crews casting nets to catch fish, it is now common to see a kind of cylinder packed with hair, also known as a "blanket", being thrown into the water to form a barrier that traps oil, biodiesel and other polluting substances.

The barriers can remain in the sea for up to four months, capturing pollution "from vessels, illegal discharges and other sources of contamination", explains chemist Caroline Carvalho.

The project was born in a country with a high number of hair salons, which gives it major potential, as its main raw material is almost inexhaustible.

Around a dozen hair salons donate the cut hair that will not be used to make wigs, for the production of these "eco blankets".

Animal fur can also be used to filter and absorb oil.

Mariana Robrahn, the NGO's founder, is no stranger to using hair for good causes: in 2013, she launched the solidarity project "Cabelegria", aimed at making wigs from donated hair for cancer patients.

Oil spills harm fishing activity

Because of heavy maritime traffic, with ships constantly coming and going, Guanabara Bay has been suffering from various types of pollution for decades and was therefore chosen as one of the sites to test the project.

In an interview with AP, local fisherman Sérgio Carvalho described the serious pollution problem affecting the area.

"When we go out to fish with nets, we come across many oil spills that harm our work. The oil stays on the surface but affects everything down to about a metre and a half in depth. The fish disappear," he says.

The hope of the fishing community, as well as of all the environmental groups involved in the project, is that these hair barriers will help restore ecosystems and contribute to reducing pollution in the bay.

World.title: Three midlife health factors could delay dementia by 13 years, study finds
World.content:
Having normal blood pressure, no diabetes, and not smoking from age 48 to 68 are associated with nearly 13 additional years, on average, of dementia-free life, according to a new study.

 

Dementia is one of the fastest-growing health burdens worldwide. Every year, 10 million new cases are diagnosed globally, according to the World Health Organization, and that number is projected to surpass 150 million by 2050.

The rising toll has prompted researchers to focus on prevention and the modifiable lifestyle factors people can adopt in midlife for healthier ageing.

The findings, published in the journal Neurology Open Access, showed that maintaining good vascular health — defined by the absence of diabetes, hypertension, and smoking — during middle age directly influences the number of years a person can expect to live without developing dementia.

“Our findings argue that people need to actively avert these factors in midlife as a strategy for preserving brain health for more than a decade,” said study senior investigator Josef Coresh.

By analyzing data from over 12,000 participants, researchers found that individuals with diabetes, hypertension, or smoking habits experienced significantly shorter dementia-free life.

Participants with three midlife risk factors faced nearly three times higher hazard of developing dementia, compared to those with no risk factors.

Individuals with zero vascular risk factors at age 55 could expect to live an average of 30 years without dementia.

Those with one risk factor could expect 26 years without dementia, those with two had 21 years, and those with three had just over 17 years — meaning people with no risk factors lived roughly 13 years longer without cognitive impairment than those with all three conditions.

Sex differences also emerged. Women generally lived more years dementia-free than men; among those with three risk factors, for instance, women averaged 18 years compared to 16 years for men.

“Hopefully, these results will encourage people to stop smoking and watch their vascular health closely from age 48 on,” Coresh said.

World.title: Most of the Maldives may be unliveable in 50 years – but these kayaking islanders aren't giving up
World.content:
A group of young people in the Maldives recently paddled kayaks to protest land reclamation work that was cutting through protected mangrove wetlands in a UNESCO biosphere reserve, even spray-painting “ECOCIDE" on a reclaimed patch.

 

The nonprofit Project ThimaaVeshi, which means “self and surroundings”, is part of a new generation of activists in the Indian Ocean island nation tackling issues that are part of their daily lives: coastal erosion, plastic pollution and development-damaged ecosystems.

In Addu City in the south, the activists have focused on overdevelopment, documenting the impact on wetlands and reefs. In the capital, Male, others are tackling the plastic waste suffocating streets, hangout spots and swimming areas.

As they team up with surfers and others for cleanups, picking fishing lines out of coral reefs and piling up discarded water bottles, the groups educate youth on their right to a clean and healthy environment.

They are united in knowing that, unlike with previous generations, climate change and environmental damage are no longer a distant threat.

The Maldives has championed itself as a country fighting its vulnerability to climate change and sea level rise, but the government has said sacrifices must be made at times in favour of development, and the activists say protective measures are not happening fast enough.

Experts have said the country south of India and Sri Lanka is expected to be around 80 per cent uninhabitable within the next 50 years due to rising sea levels.

Buildings stand on Male, the capital city of the Maldives, June 19, 2026. AP Photo/Sophia Nasif

Youth push back against a sense of helplessness

“It was just us and a bunch of hopes and dreams,” says 21-year-old co-founder of Project ThimaaVeshi, Yameen Maumoon.

Maumoon along with Mishal Mushahid started their activism as student leaders working with the Addu City council. What started as a group of friends became a movement and a registered nonprofit after they graduated from high school.

In Male and neighbouring Hulhumale, another youth group seeking formal registration, Ripple, started when friends noticed the trash building up in areas where they hung out.

“One day when we were playing Minecraft, we were joking around, saying we should start making TikToks and we should start cleaning up," says co-founder, Mariyam Maasha Waheed. What began as an informal cleanup grew after their TikTok videos gained traction.

Members of Project ThimaaVeshi, team up with Veshi Saafu, a group of older women, to demonstrate against reclamation projects in Addu City, Maldives, June 5, 2026. AP Photo/Sophia Nasif

The group now organises weekly cleanups and campaigns against plastic pollution, collaborating with others to recycle the plastic they collect.

Founders say they want environmental action to feel less intimidating and more communal.

A co-founder of the newest group seeking registration, Barnacles, Yania Hussain Ishan, became interested in environmental issues while preparing a presentation for school on protecting nature. The group focuses on climate education and youth leadership.

The constant talk on social media and elsewhere about a climate emergency has led to their generation's feeling of a lack of agency over it, Ishan says.

A hawksbill turtle swims at Addu Nature Park, a protected UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, off the coast of Addu City, Maldives, Feb. 23, 2026. AP Photo/Sophia Nasif

The groups have faced criticism over their youth

The age of the activists has drawn comments, even from government officials, that youth equates to naivety and ignorance. All three groups have been told their work is pointless, and that something as simple as a beach cleanup will not fix the overall challenges.

Young people have too many emotions and can’t be trusted with decision-making, the country's minister of climate change, Ali Shareef, last year told a public forum.

The activists say they know they cannot solve Maldives's problems alone. But they believe waiting for the bigger problems to be solved isn’t an option. They want to shape a generation who understand their rights and pass the responsibility to future ones.

“We are deciding what kind of ancestors we will be," Ishan says. “We are defending our home, our heritage and the right of every Maldivian child yet to be born to stand on these shores, look out at the sea and feel the same wonder and security that defines who we are.”

World.title: From Scotland to Austria: Europe's best destinations for a 'stillcation'
World.content:
In a world that rarely slows down, perhaps the greatest holiday luxury isn’t doing more, but instead opting to be "still"?

 

For many travellers, the idea of truly switching off and simply existing is more daunting than boarding a flight. And that’s where the idea of a “stillcation” comes in.

Rather than packing getaways with itineraries of activities, a stillcation prioritises slowing down and being more present.

According to tour operator Inghams Walking, the best destinations for this type of intentional travel are the ones where the environment helps the brain truly unwind.

Inghams analysed nearly 100 European destinations, ranking them by six factors, including the number of walking trails per square kilometre, air quality, birdsong richness, stargazing quality, human density per square kilometre, and total forest cover.

These features help the brain activate the “default mode network”, a resting state which, despite its name, involves the brain consolidating memories, processing emotions, problem solving and developing greater self awareness.

Eloise Skinner, a UK-based psychotherapist, said this has a positive impact “helping us move into a state of 'rest and digest' rather than 'fight or flight', and reducing our stress response and cognitive fatigue”.

She added: “Being surrounded by natural landscapes removes many obstacles and distractions, allowing us to turn our attention inward and feel a sense of greater connection and calm.”

Keen to plan a stillcation? Here are the destinations in Europe that scored highest for helping travellers truly just “be”.

Europe’s top 15 ‘stillest’ destinations

1. Wester Ross, Scotland: 44.74 / 100

2. French Pyrenees, France: 41.20 / 100

3. Abisko, Sweden: 40.86 / 100

4. Engadin Valley, Switzerland: 39.44 / 100

5. The Dolomites, Italy: 39.20 / 100

6. Picos de Europa, Spain: 39.05 / 100

7. Outer Hebrides, Scotland: 38.96 / 100

8. Corsica, France: 38.18 / 100

9. Gotland, Sweden: 37.95 / 100

10. Kitzbuhel, Austria: 36.86 / 100

11. Kranjska Gora, Slovenia: 36.38 / 100

12. St Anton, Austria: 36.32 / 100

13. Skane, Sweden: 35.05 / 100

14. Bled, Slovenia: 33.80 / 100

15. Neustift im Stubaital, Austria: 33.65 / 100

Wester Ross, Scotland

Crowned as the “stillest” destination in Inghams’ survey, this remote region in the northwest highlands of Scotland boasts dramatic mountain peaks, deep sea lochs, and pristine coastline.

The region is so remote that Inghams found just 1.6 inhabitants per square kilometre and also found it to have very low light pollution on the Bortle Scale. It is the perfect dwelling for a diverse range of local flora, fauna and wildlife, including otters and black-throated loon birds that can be seen in the waters of Loch Maree.

Its vast area of high-quality natural landscapes and biodiversity is paired with cultural heritage, where visitors can enjoy Gaelic music and observe traditional activities kept alive today, including Scottish “crofting”.

French Pyrenees, France

The vast Pyrenees mountain range stretches more than 430 kilometres between France and Spain. Inghams highlighting that the varied terrain offers something for every type of stillcation traveller to enjoy.

Travellers can hike across an array of trails, including the Andreyt ridges from the Col d’Aubisque, a 8.7 kilometre path of sweeping views over green hills.

Although second overall in the survey, the French Pyrenees is home to more than 319 bird species and ranks one of the highest in Ingham’s survey as a natural soundscape destination. The tour operators pointed to research that suggests the sounds of nature help people feel stillness and more relaxed, lowering heart rate.

Abisko, Sweden

This small village in Sweden is north of the Arctic Circle and famed as one of the best places in the world to see the shimmering Northern Lights from September to April.

Abisko also ranked highest in Ingham’s survey as a walking trail destination, thanks to its abundant paths and network of mapped routes – making it easy for travellers to explore without extensive planning.

World.title: Western Europe sets new temperature record as heat waves continue to pummel region
World.content:
The European Climate Office Copernicus reports that the average temperature record for the June–July period set in 2022 was overturned by the heatwaves plaguing Western Europe this summer.

 

Since it started in May, the intense heat has caused many wildfires, a protracted drought, new national temperature records throughout the region, and thousands of anticipated heat-related deaths.

Globally, so far this is the third-hottest year, behind 2024 and 2025, climate statistics show. But 2026 still has time to catch up.

There is a growing possibility that by year's end, 2026 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record, or at least come close, due to the combined effects of accelerated human-caused global warming and a supersized El Niño, a periodic warming of parts of the Pacific that causes temperature variations worldwide, according to scientists.

Last month saw the highest average sea surface temperature ever recorded for July across the extra-polar oceans, or the oceans free of seasonal sea ice, Copernicus said.

That was partially fueled by developing El Niño conditions in the equatorial Pacific, the service said. The new average record for July is 20.96 degrees Celsius, which beats the 2023 record of 20.89°C.

However, according to Copernicus, this month's average worldwide surface air temperature was 16.90°C, making it merely the second-warmest July on record and tied with July 2024.

The average temperature record for the June–July period in Western Europe was 21.62°C.

“Persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over western Europe; the extreme temperatures also amplified widespread drought. As soils dry out, they lose their ability to provide natural cooling, allowing heat to build more readily,” said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

“This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another.”

Wildfire burning near Tirana under control

Firefighters, helicopters, and the military worked through Sunday to contain a large wildfire burning on Mount Kruje as authorities evacuated residents from several villages and arrested a man suspected of accidentally sparking the blaze.

Three military helicopters have been assisting ground crews in efforts to bring the blaze under control, with firefighting operations continuing both on the ground and from the air as steep terrain has made access difficult.

Residents from the Barabit-Lluban area in the municipality of Kruje were evacuated overnight after the fire spread toward populated areas.

Police said they arrested a man suspected of causing the wildfire after allegedly setting fire to dry grass near his home on Saturday.

According to police, the flames spread out of control because of strong winds and reached Mount Kruje, threatening nearby communities.

The wildfire, about 38 kilometers north of the capital, Tirana, had been burning since Saturday afternoon.

Fire in Andalusian province continues to spread

Authorities in the southern Andalusian province of Huelva, halfway between Seville and the Portuguese border, on Sunday prompted the evacuation of some 470 locals over a fire that broke out and continues to spread, reaching nearly 4,000 hectares with shifting winds.

"The fire remains complex. We still have work to do and a tough day ahead, involving a great deal of intervention, but today we are somewhat more optimistic," said the Andalucia region's minister for emergencies, Antonio Sanz.

More than 500 firefighters, including 60 members of the Military Emergency Unit, aided by around 20 waterbombing planes, are battling the flames against volatile winds.

Spain is enduring a tough summer for wildfires, with various blazes having forced the evacuation of thousands of people, especially in the centre of the country.

World.title: Holiday affordability in Europe: Where can people afford a break?
World.content:
Summer is holiday season across Europe, yet millions of people still cannot afford to take a week away from home. However, the share of Europeans unable to afford a holiday has fallen significantly.

 

In 2025, 27.5% of the EU's population aged 16 or older were unable to afford one week of annual holiday away from home. This was 35.2% in 2015, representing a decline of 7.7 percentage points and a significant improvement in holiday affordability.

In five countries, the share of people unable to afford a holiday increased over the past decade, although the rise was marginal in some cases. These were Norway, Sweden, Finland, Germany and Austria. The three Nordic countries saw the largest increases, but their rates remained among the lowest in Europe.

Germany and Austria also bucked the broader trend, with around one in five people unable to afford a week-long holiday in 2025. The share increased by 1.2 percentage points in Germany and 0.3 points in Austria over the decade.

Holiday economics

So, which European countries have the highest share of people unable to afford one week of annual holiday away from home? Which countries saw the biggest improvements in holiday affordability over the last ten years? What factors affect holiday affordability?

As of 2025, the share of people who are unable to afford one week's holiday varies widely across Europe. It ranges from 9% in Switzerland and Norway to 61% in Romania.

More than half the population was also unable to afford a holiday in Montenegro (58%), Albania (53%) and Turkey (51%). North Macedonia (48%) and Greece (47%) were also close to that level.

It is also above one in three in Bulgaria (39%), Hungary (39%), Serbia (36%) and Italy (36%).

The share unable to afford a holiday was below the EU average in Portugal (33%), Croatia (33%), Spain (32%), Lithuania (31%), Slovakia (29%), Latvia (29%), Cyprus (28%) and Malta (28%).

At the other end of the scale, the share was 15% or below in Luxembourg, Sweden, the Netherlands, Denmark, Finland and Slovenia, in addition to Switzerland and Norway, where it was 9%.

This share was 21% in Germany and 23% in France.

Southern and Southeastern Europe have the highest levels of holiday deprivation. This includes EU candidate countries. Northern Europe, in particular the Nordic countries, and Western Europe record the lowest levels. Central and Eastern Europe generally fall between these two regions, but with considerable variation between countries.

Role of GDP and economic disparities

Explaining the 2023 figures, experts emphasised the role of income levels.

Professor C. Michael Hall from Canterbury University pointed out that the level of disposable income is clearly important, as this allows people to spend money on holidays. "Disparities with holiday taking and expenditure reflect some of the broader economic disparities within the EU," he said.

Professor Lynn Minnaert from Metropolitan State University of Denver stated that the differences between nations are typically related to the strength of a country's economy. She noted that countries at the higher end of holiday deprivation have lower GDPs than those at the lower end.

The chart above shows this trend, presenting the share of people who are unable to afford a holiday alongside annual net earnings for a single person without children earning the average wage.

Fifteen years ago, almost 2 in 5 people (38.8%) in the EU were unable to afford a week-long holiday. This gradually declined after peaking in 2012 at 40.5%, reaching 28% in 2019. Since then, it has remained relatively stable at around 27-28%.

Comparing 2015 and 2025 figures, 25 of the 30 countries recorded a decline in the share of people unable to afford a holiday, while five recorded an increase. Three Nordic countries showed the highest increases in percentage-point terms, with Norway up 3.8 points, Sweden up 3.2 and Finland up 1.5.

However, these countries started from relatively low levels in 2015. For example, the share unable to afford a holiday was just 5.3% in Norway and 9.2% in Sweden. These increased to 9.1% and 12.4% respectively in 2025.

In Germany and Austria, where around one in five people are unable to afford a holiday, this rate rose by 1.2 points and 0.3 points respectively.

On the other hand, the share of people who are unable to afford one week's holiday away from home fell by 33 and 32 points in Croatia and Serbia.

The decline was 26 points in Cyprus, 22 in Ireland, and 21 points in Bulgaria and Turkey. Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Malta and Hungary also recorded significant declines, of more than 15 points.

World.title: A unique ninety seconds in the 21st century: Spain prepares for historic eclipse trio
World.content:
On 15 April 1912, just two days after the sinking of the Titanic in North Atlantic waters, Spain experienced its last total solar eclipse for just a few seconds, classified as hybrid because of the unusually narrow width of its path of totality. Issue 33 of the magazine of SAE, the Spanish Astronomical Society, recorded the event with testimonies from several Galicians who witnessed this fleeting phenomenon.

 

"The landscape looked sad and wan, and the cold was quite intense. The hens were looking for their roost and one that I saw, which had her chicks, sheltered them beneath her wings," recounted Tomás Martínez, a teacher from O Barco de Valdeorras, about the event he witnessed at 11:49 from his latitude in Ourense.

For the first time since then, the country is preparing to host this phenomenon in two consecutive years (on both 12 August 2026 and 2 August 2027), plus a third annular solar eclipse on 26 January 2028, which together will form a unique trio of eclipses in 21st-century Europe.

The next solar episode will only be seen in totality from northern Siberia, the east coast of Greenland and western Iceland before crossing Spain through up to 12 autonomous communities in a band 293 kilometres wide. A real astronomical lottery, yes, though also an economic one because of the geographical circumstances.From Canada, the north-east coast of the United States and north-west Africa it will also be visible, but only partially.

The darkest band marks the path of totality, where the Sun will be completely obscured. The contours within that band indicate how long totality lasts Observatorio Astronómico Nacional / eclipses.ign.es

The term eclipse comes from the Greek 'ekleipsis', meaning disappearance, and has several forms. Solar eclipses occur only at new moon, when the disc of our satellite exceptionally manages to cover the Sun completely. This produces a sudden spell of darkness for a few moments while a black sphere can be seen. If the Moon's orbit were not tilted, this phenomenon would occur twice a month in specific areas of the Earth, both at new and full moon.

_"_As soon as the Moon completely covers the Sun, the brightness decreases. We can start to pick out the brightest stars and planets in the sky. If we are in the countryside, we will hear the birds singing. And just as totality begins, the birds stop singing because they think night is falling," explains César González, an astronomy populariser at the Madrid Planetarium, putting into professional words the testimony that teacher Martínez gave 114 years ago to the SAE.

"The temperature drops. It can fall by as much as five degrees, and a slight breeze always starts to blow," adds this scientist. It is in that brief moment that lucky observers can remove their special, fully approved glasses (this can be checked by the ISO 12312-2:2015 certification on one of the arms), since during the partial phases the risks to eyesight are high.

Without the glasses, ultraviolet radiation will damage the eye's photoreceptors (cones and rods), while infrared energy will produce a direct thermal effect on the retina, causing solar retinopathy. The symptoms of this condition, which will take time to appear, can include blurred vision, spots or scotomas at the point of greatest visual acuity, metamorphopsia (a distorted perception of shapes) and a reduced tolerance to light, or photophobia, which can cause headaches.

The total phase will not exceed 1 minute and 48 seconds - the closer you are to the line of totality, the more seconds you will be able to enjoy the phenomenon - anywhere along its path over Spain, so it is important to time it and to bear in mind that, depending on where it is observed, the event will start and end at different times.

The trajectory of the eclipse enters Spain through north-west Galicia at around 19:27 and will end in the Balearic Islands at around 20:35. Cities just outside the band, such as Madrid or Salamanca, will see a deep partial eclipse (at least 92% dimming across the whole Peninsula) but not totality. So how do scientists calculate all this?

"We know the laws that govern the movement of planets and satellites and, in inverted commas, it is not too difficult to work out when they are going to happen, even in the distant future (...) By using computer tools to find out about eclipses in the past and comparing them with historical events, it is possible to link phenomena together," explains César González.

Long before modern calculations, scientists already knew that eclipses follow certain patterns. González points out that the Sumerians, around 5,000 years ago, may already have identified them. The best-known cycle is the Saros, of approximately 18 years, 11 days and 8 hours, because after that period the geometry between the Sun, the Earth and the Moon becomes very similar again, but there is also the exeligmos, which is equivalent to three Saros cycles and makes it possible to calculate more precisely from the place where it is observed.

Hotel bookings fully taken in Spain's emptied-out interior

The eclipse passes directly over provinces such as Soria, Guadalajara and Teruel - the area known as Spain's Siberia because of its low population density - as well as the four Galician provinces, all of Castile and León except Salamanca, the Principality of Asturias, Cantabria, the Basque Country, Navarre, Aragon, Castile-La Mancha (in Guadalajara and Cuenca), the south-west of Catalonia, the Valencia region (Castellón and Valencia) and all of the Balearic Islands.

The Spanish Rural Development Network estimates that the trio of eclipses could generate an economic impact of close to 1.4 billion euros, which, with the exception of the coastal provinces, will be spread across areas generally far removed from the interests of the bulk of foreign tourists. The second solar eclipse, in 2027, will last longer (up to five minutes) but over a smaller geographical area (Cádiz, Málaga, Granada, Almería, Ceuta and Melilla), and will also be competing with other Maghreb countries.

In April, the Presidency Councillor of Castile and León put the estimated number of visitors to the region attracted by this first eclipse at two million. And the tourism portal of the Generalitat Valenciana forecast an 80% surge in bookings in inland Castellón, in a region where tourism is concentrated on the Valencian and Alicante coasts.

For those visitors who cannot come to Spain to enjoy the total eclipse, ESA will broadcast the phenomenon live from the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory in Teruel, as well as organising a free public observation programme in the city of León in collaboration with the university and the city council.

World.title: Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy
World.content:
The launch of the Yeni Party in Turkey promises to energise the country's struggling opposition. But while some polls show it leading, it remains vulnerable – already beset by arrests it says are "politically motivated".

Advertising

In a glitzy video, set to pumping music and shared widely across social media, Ozgur Ozel launched the Yeni Party – "New Party" – vowing to usher in a new era in Turkish politics and end President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s long rule.

Ozel founded the New Party after a court removed him from leading the main opposition party, the Republican People’s Party (CHP).

His rival, former party leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu, 77, who lost every election during his decade in charge of the CHP, replaced him.

Many in the country believe Erdogan played a role in the removal of Ozel, as his popularity grew thanks to tireless campaigning.

Riding the wave

The New Party is settings its sights beyond the CHP’s usual supporters.

"It covers the whole political spectrum in Turkish political life," explains Ozel's advisor Ilham Uzel.

"There are critical elements like democratisation, rule of law, secularism and a pro-Western approach, so we maintain these main pillars. But it is not confined to social democracy; we reach out to every section of Turkish society, including Islamists and conservatives, nationalists and liberals. We have Kurdish supporters."

The New Party is riding a wave of excitement. Ninety-one out of 135 CHP parliamentary deputies have defected to its ranks, joined by dozens of mayors and it is swiftly becoming the main opposition in parliament.

Turkey opposition worries that Europe is sacrificing democracy for security

Some polls show the party soaring above 30 percent, leaving Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party behind, while the CHP’s support has collapsed.

The New Party’s broad approach is finding fertile ground. "Even those who still support the governing coalition, the AK Party and MHP, are unhappy with how things are or how politics is practised, especially regarding economic issues. So there is a push towards change," says political commentator Sezin Oney.

"There is a yearning to change things at the grassroots, and the New Party may be the only party that can represent a new way of doing politics. But they have to live up to it, of course."

Corruption charges

Erdogan has remained in power for more than 20 years partly by exploiting divisions within the opposition, which is made up of conservatives, hardline secularists, and both Kurdish and Turkish nationalists.

The New Party has a key advantage over the strongly secular CHP, whose history is linked to past policies targeting Turkey’s large Kurdish minority and religious conservatives.

"CHP is identified with many bad experiences that the Kurds and conservative people had in past decades," said Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

"If you look at what Ozgur Ozel says during his speeches, you may clearly see the Yeni Party doesn’t have the baggage of CHP."

Erdogan has also often exploited the CHP’s history, painting it as anti-religious and hostile to Kurdish minority rights. The New Party faces the tricky task of keeping CHP loyalists on board while reaching new supporters.

But for now, simply staying out of jail may be the most pressing concern for its representatives.

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Several mayors who joined the New Party have been arrested on corruption charges, widely seen as politically motivated. In the past two years, 26 opposition mayors and hundreds of officials have been imprisoned on corruption allegations, compared to two mayors from Erdogan’s AK Party.

"They are cracking down on our party – every other day, mayors are arrested," says Uzgel. "They filed another charge against our leader. Nobody is safe in this authoritarian regime. So Mr Ozel is on the spot, definitely."

Ozel is protected by parliamentary immunity, but Oney warns he may be running out of time.

"Ozgur Ozel might be imprisoned himself once his immunity is removed by a parliamentary vote, that's a possibility. The only immunity he can have is the immunity bestowed upon him by the people. So only public opinion is protecting him. How much can it protect him? We'll see."

With parliament about to break for summer until October, Ozel has a brief window to strengthen his party and rally public support.

World.title: Iran War:  Is Iran’s middle class being pushed into poverty?
World.content:
The war has intensified Iran’s economic crisis, squeezing household budgets, hurting businesses and raising fears that millions of middle-income families are slipping closer to poverty.

For Mina, a housewife in Iran, the war is no longer measured by air strikes or military statements. It is measured by what has disappeared from her family's dinner table.

"Since the war started last year, we have become poorer every day,” she told DW. "I honestly can't remember the last time I bought red meat. We replaced it with chicken, but even chicken has become a luxury. We no longer think about saving money. We only think about paying the rent and buying food.”

The International Monetary Fund forecasts Iran's economy will contract by 5.4% this year, while inflation is expected to approach 69%. The World Bank has also warned that conflict, weaker trade and prolonged uncertainty are weighing heavily on the country's economy.

For economist Ahmad Alavi, a Sweden-based researcher, the war did not create Iran's economic crisis, but sharply intensified it.

"Iran entered the conflict with inflation already above 40%, a weakening currency, chronic budget deficits and years of sanctions,” he told DW.

"The war acted as an external shock. Damage to infrastructure, disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz, internet shutdowns and rising inflation expectations accelerated the collapse in purchasing power,” he said.

Alavi points to official figures showing annual inflation reaching 66% and year-over-year inflation nearing 88%. Food prices have risen even faster. Bread and cereals have increased by around 140%, meat and poultry by 135%, dairy products by more than 116%, and edible oils by over 200%.

For many families, those figures have meant buying less meat, postponing medical treatment and abandoning plans to save money.

Inflation in Iran is expected to reach nearly 70% in 2026 Image: Fatemeh Bahrami/AA/picture alliance

The war has pushed some 4 million Iranians into poverty

Economists say households often cut spending on travel and clothing first. As inflation persists, however, the cuts extend to food, healthcare and education, placing growing pressure on middle-income families that once considered themselves financially secure.

Alavi says lower-income households have suffered the most but argues that the middle class is increasingly facing the same pressures.

"Many salaried workers and pensioners have fallen below the poverty line for the first time because incomes have failed to keep pace with inflation.”

He estimates that between 3.5 and 4.5 million more Iranians have fallen into poverty since the conflict intensified, bringing the total number of people living below the poverty line to more than 40 million.

To adapt to the tighter cost of living, many households have started cutting meat from their diet Image: Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Businesses squeezed by uncertainty

The pressure is also being felt by Iran's private sector.

Mortaza, an Iranian trader, says regional trade routes changed rapidly after shipping through the Strait of Hormuz became more difficult.

"China moved quickly to fill part of the gap left by suppliers in Dubai,” he told DW. "Unlike Gulf countries, China can also ship goods through rail links across Central Asia, avoiding many of the risks and delays associated with maritime transport.”

He believes the growing importance of these overland routes was one of the reasons the U.S. targeted a railway line near Iran's border with Turkmenistan, although that assessment could not be independently verified.

Even so, Mortaza says the shift has brought little benefit to Iranian traders.

"The collapse of the rial and soaring inflation have prevented the market from growing,” he says. "Merchants are living with constant uncertainty because exchange rates change almost every day. Goods that we bought and sold at lower prices now have to be replaced at much higher costs, and that's only if customers still have enough purchasing power to buy them.”

For Mortaza, uncertainty has become the biggest obstacle.

"With tensions continuing, I honestly don't see a clear future for doing business in Iran.”

What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can the government soften the blow?

Despite higher global oil prices, Alavi says Iran is unlikely to benefit significantly because sanctions, export restrictions and higher transport costs continue to limit its oil revenues.

He argues that government measures, including subsidies, price controls and intervention in the foreign exchange market may ease some immediate pressure, but are unlikely to address the underlying problems.

"Without restoring confidence, reducing sanctions and addressing structural problems, these policies remain short-term responses rather than lasting solutions.”

Economist Dr. Ahmad Alavi says rebuilding confidence in the economy is likely to take much longer than repairing physical damage caused by the war Image: Privat

The cost of uncertainty

Alavi says uncertainty itself has become one of the biggest barriers to economic recovery.

According to him, many businesses are delaying investment because they have little confidence in future economic conditions. At the same time, households are becoming increasingly cautious about spending as they expect prices to keep rising and the value of their incomes to fall further.

He says rebuilding confidence among investors, businesses and consumers is likely to take much longer than repairing physical damage caused by the war.

Unless inflation eases, the exchange rate stabilizes and trade conditions improve, Alavi believes many households will remain under financial pressure, even if military tensions subside.

Looking ahead, he expects living standards to deteriorate further if current trends continue.

He says more families are likely to cut spending on protein, healthcare and education, while business closures and unemployment may continue to rise.

"We don't talk about the future anymore,” Mina says. "We only hope we can afford next month's rent.”

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

World.title: Western Europe records hottest June and July on record
World.content:
Drought is gripping large parts of Europe, with soils unusually dry and major rivers running low. A strengthening El Nino could push global temperatures even higher later this year.

Western Europe experienced its hottest June and July on record, according to data released Monday by the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service.

The average temperature across the region for the two-month period reached 21.62 degrees Celsius (70.92 Fahrenheit), breaking the previous record set in 2022.

Copernicus said the figure reflected the "exceptional persistence of heat" in western Europe, where four heatwaveshave occurred since May.

The extreme temperatures have contributed to prolonged drought, major wildfires and new national temperature records across the region, as well as thousands of projected heat-related deaths.

Firefighters battle a wildfire in southwestern France amid hot and dry conditions across the region [FILE: July 28, 2026] Image: Emma Da Silva/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Europe is the fastest-warming continent in the world, though temperatures varied considerably, with eastern Europe and Scandinavia experiencing much cooler conditions. For Europe as a whole, July was only the 11th warmest on record, with an average temperature of 20.49 degrees Celsius (68.88 Fahrenheit).

How are heat and drought affecting Western Europe?

Conditions were drier than average across large parts of Europe in July, including Spain and other areas of the Iberian Peninsula, France, Germany, Austria, Hungary and the United Kingdom.

Ireland and parts of Iceland also experienced unusually dry conditions. Soil moisture in western Europe was significantly lower than in July 2022, when the region last experienced a severe drought.

Hungary's third-largest lake is running dry To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over western Europe, the extreme temperatures also amplified widespread drought," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which operates Copernicus.

"As soils dry out, they lose their ability to provide natural cooling, allowing heat to build more readily," she added.

"This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another."

River flows were also unusually low, with the Seine, Rhine and Danube among the hardest-hit waterways. Low water levels have disrupted transport, irrigation and energy production in several European countries.

The dried-up Danube riverbed in front of the Paks nuclear power plant in southern Hungary [FILE: July 31, 2026] Image: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

The hot and dry conditions have also increased the risk of wildfires. France and Spain have battled particularly severe fires this summer, while serious blazes have also hit other parts of Europe, the northwestern United States and Canada.

Why are global ocean temperatures at record highs?

Copernicus also reported a record for global sea surface temperatures in July.

The average temperature across oceans outside the polar regions reached 20.96 degrees Celsius (69.73 Fahrenheit), surpassing the previous July record of 20.89 degrees (69.60 Fahrenheit) set in 2023.

Record temperatures were measured along parts of the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, accompanied by intense marine heatwaves.

A developing El Niño in the equatorial Pacific also contributed to the record. Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo described the emerging El Niño as "very large" and potentially unprecedented in its strength.

El Nino is the warm phase of a natural climate cycle in the Pacific Ocean that can temporarily raise global temperatures and alter weather patterns around the world.

Could 2026 become the hottest year on record?

Globally, July was the joint second-warmest on record, tied with July 2024.

The average global surface air temperature was 16.90 degrees Celsius (62.42 Fahrenheit), around 1.47 degrees (2.65 Fahrenheit) above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average for July. July 2023 remains the hottest on record, with an average temperature of 16.95 degrees (62.51 Fahrenheit).

So far, 2026 is the third-hottest year recorded globally, behind 2024 and 2025. Scientists say the strengthening El Niño could push temperatures higher later this year.

Buontempo said scientists expect a new global average temperature record to be set either later this year or in early 2027.

The past 11 years have been the hottest on record. "We have not seen a climate that warm during our lifetime, and very possibly our civilisation," Buontempo said.

"And the main driver for this warming — as we know — are the greenhouse gases," he added.

Oceans absorb most of the excess heat caused by human greenhouse gas emissions. Higher ocean temperatures can contribute to heavier rainfall and stronger storms and damage marine ecosystems, including coral reefs.

Copernicus bases its climate analyses on billions of measurements from satellites, ships, aircraft and weather stations around the world.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

World.title: Netanyahu rejects Trump-backed Gaza peace plan
World.content:
The Israeli prime minister says his country will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas fully disarms, putting him at odds with a US-backed roadmap endorsed by the group.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday rejected US President Donald Trump's plan for Gaza, saying Israeli troops would not withdraw from the territory until Hamas was fully disarmed.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu told a Cabinet meeting, referring to the US-backed roadmap agreed to by Hamas in late July.

The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed," Netanyahu said, adding that this included "heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry."

Israel rejects US-led Gaza peace plan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Netanyahu said Israel remained in talks with Washington despite its objections. He described Trump as "our greatest friend in the White House," but added: "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters."

The White House did not immediately comment.

What does Trump's Gaza plan say about Hamas disarmament?

Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough on a 15-point roadmap aimed at ending the war in the Gaza Strip.

The plan drawn up by his Board of Peace calls for Israeli troops to withdraw as Hamas gives up its weapons. An International Stabilization Force would then work alongside a new Palestinian police force to secure Gaza.

Trump hails 'complete disarmament' of Hamas To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hamas is designated as a terrorist organization by Israel, the United States, the European Union and several other countries.

The group has avoided using the term "disarmament." It says it agreed to hand over its weapons for storage under a US-backed Palestinian technocratic administration that would govern Gaza under the supervision of the Board of Peace.

Hamas has said implementation also depends on Israel meeting its obligations, including withdrawing troops and halting attacks.

"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap, and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim said.

Hamas said Sunday it remained committed to the roadmap.

Gaza plan rejected by Netanyahu 'only way forward':

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza, said Israel would face no obligations until Hamas had surrendered all its weapons, including assault rifles.

However, Mladenov told Israel's Channel 12 that Israeli troops would eventually have to withdraw "sector by sector" once Hamas' weapons had been collected and rendered unusable.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative for Gaza, has defended the US-backed roadmap and said talks with Israel are continuing [FILE: May 13, 2019] Image: Mustafa Hassona/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

"The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again," he said, referring to the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, which triggered the war against Hamas in the Gaza Strip.

Mladenov said discussions with Israel were continuing and that he hoped for a "positive outcome."

How are Israel's elections affecting Netanyahu's Gaza policy?

The disagreement comes at a politically sensitive moment for Netanyahu ahead of elections scheduled for October 27, Israel's first national vote since the Hamas led attacks that sparked an ongoing Israeli military campaign in Gaza.

The prime minister is running level with or behind rivals in some polls and faces pressure from far-right members of his government who oppose concessions to Hamas.

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich welcomed Netanyahu's position.

"We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas," he said. "The [military] cannot withdraw even a millimetre from the Gaza Strip."

US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have long presented themselves as close allies, but have recently differed over the way forward in Gaza [FILE: July 28, 2026] Image: dpa

The dispute is the latest sign of differences between Netanyahu and Trump. The two leaders are considered as close allies, but have recently disagreed over how to deal with the conflicts in Iran, Lebanon and Gaza.

The Gaza roadmap builds on a US-mediated ceasefire reached in October 2025.

Gaza health officials say more than 1,250 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since then. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed during the same period.

Despite the ongoing negotiations over the roadmap, Israeli forces continue to control large parts of Gaza, while most of the enclave's more than 2 million residents have been displaced and are living in a much smaller coastal area, many in tents or damaged buildings.

World.title: Alleged Irish crime boss Kinahan charged with directing criminal organisation
World.content:
Daniel Kinahan is accused of leading the Kinahan organised crime group, an international network linked to drug trafficking and money laundering operations,

Suspected international crime boss Daniel Kinahan landed in Ireland on Sunday after being extradited from the United Arab Emirates.

Following his arrival in Ireland, prosecutors charged Kinahan with directing a criminal organization during a special court sitting.

Kinahan, 49, was arrested in April in Dubai after Ireland issued a warrant for "alleged serious organized crime offenses."

He is accused of being the leader of a cartel linked to drug smuggling and money laundering.

Irish authorities deployed an enhanced security convoy to escort the supsected crime ringleader to court Image: Brian Lawless/PA Images/picture alliance

What do we know about the allegations against Kinahan?

The group is thought to be the most powerful criminal organization in Ireland, with Irish police estimating its wealth at more than €1 billion ($1.15 billion).

The alleged crime boss had lived openly in the UAE for about a decade before his arrest. He moved there from Spain around 2016 after the murder of one of his associates and an attempt on his life.

In 2022, the United States imposed sanctions on Kinahan after linking his organization to some of the world's most notorious crime networks and offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest.

The group is linked to a brutal feud with a smaller Irish syndicate that has resulted in 18 murders.

“Since February 2016, the (Kinahan Organized Crime Group) has been involved in a gang war with another group in Ireland and Spain, resulting in numerous murders, including of two innocent bystanders,” the US Treasury Department said.

Kinahan is the second alleged senior member of the cartel to be extradited to Ireland from Dubai. Sean McGovern was extradited in 2024 and was ultimately sentenced to 24 years in prison after pleading guilty to directing organized crime and attempted murder.

Irish media reported that a special security convoy would be deployed to escort Kinahan to the Special Criminal Court, which handles offenses related to terrorism and organized crime.

UAE, Ireland hail judicial cooperation in Kinahan extradition

In a joint statement, the justice minister of the UAE and Ireland called Kinahan "one of the most high-profile individuals sought for prosecution in connection with transnational organized crime."

Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan called the extradition a "landmark of judicial cooperation with Dubai," adding that it "sends a clear message that suspected perpetrators of serious and organized crime will find no safe haven from justice."

Meanwhile, Foreign Minister Helen McEntee hailed the outcome as "the culmination of years of determined work" by Irish authorities under various governments.

World.title: Syria says deal agreed with Russia on future of military bases
World.content:
Under the agreement, Syria will take over management of two Russian bases that were used to support ousted leader Bashar Assad during the Syrian civil war.

Syria and Russia have agreed on the future management of Russian bases on the country's Mediterranean coast.

Russia used the bases to provide military support to former Syrian leader Bashar Assad during Syria's 13-year civil war that ended in 2024.

The Syrian Foreign Ministry announced Sunday that the two nations had signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) after 18 months of negotiations.

The deal effectively means Russia will no longer have military outposts in the Arab country.

Syria says the strategic Mediterranean bases will become joint training centers [FILE: December 2024] Image: Adrien Vautier/Le Pictorium/IMAGO

What will happen to Russia's military bases in Syria?

Syria will take over management of the Hmeimim airport and the commercial berth at Tartus port, Syria's Foreign Ministry said.

State media cited the ministry as saying that the bases would be converted into "joint training and capacity-building centres, within new arrangements that preserve mutual interests."

The facilities will be gradually integrated into the country's civilian administration. The transition is expected to be completed within three months, the ministry said.

Russia has yet to comment on the agreement.

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani visited Tartus port on Sunday Image: SANA/AFP

Russia trying to build relations with post-Assad Syria

During the civil war in Syria between 2011 and 2024, while Assad was president, Russia was Syria's main ally and military backer.

Assad was overthrown in December 2024, and now lives in exile in Moscow. Current Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa led an alliance of Islamist rebel groups that fought against government forces during the war.

Assad's ouster in 2024 dealt a major blow to Moscow's influence in the region.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has been trying to build ties with Syria's new leadership to protect the future of the only two official Russian military bases located outside the former Soviet Union.

Al-Sharaa has met with Putin in Moscow twice since coming to power in January 2025.

During his last trip, Putin said, "much has been accomplished in terms of restoring our interstate relations."

The Syrian government has been demanding that Moscow extradite Assad.

World.title: Denmark: Several wounded in suspected gang shooting
World.content:
Police said they believed that the incident was linked to a "settling of scores" within criminal networks.

Three people were wounded on Sunday in a shooting in Denmark.

They do not face life-threatening injuries, the police said.

Police said in a statement they believed that the incident was linked to a "settling of scores" within criminal networks.

"At this time, we cannot provide further information about their condition. The police presumption is that this is a settling of scores within the criminal milieu," the statement read.

Officers had been called to multiple locations in Holbaek, some 70 kilometers (45 miles) west of the capital, Copenhagen.

The incident was reported to police around 3:45 p.m. local time (1345 UTC).

Before the shots were fired, a fight broke out within a larger group in a residential estate, police said

Police said that the perpetrators were seen leaving the scene in a white car, according to preliminary information.

World.content:
Skip next section The Left could work with CDU to keep far-right AFD out of power

08/09/2026 August 9, 2026 The Left could work with CDU to keep far-right AFD out of power

The co-leader of Die Linke ("The Left") on Sunday said the socialist party would do anything in its power to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) out of office.

Luigi Pantisano's remarks on public broadcaster ZDF come with less than a month to go before elections in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD is polling at over 40% and is poised to win an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.

Were the AfD to win in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, it would mark Germany's first far-right state government since World War II.

To prevent that scenario, Pantisano said he would consider supporting the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, despite Pantisano recently accusing the CDU of implementing "fascist politics."

"We, The Left, have shown in recent years that we take responsibility for this country," Pantisano told ZDF.

If the AfD falls short of an absolute majority, the CDU's incumbent state Premier Sven Schulze would likely have to form a coalition government with The Left.

The AfD has never been in government at either state or federal level, as all other established parties refuse to work with it, under a policy known as the "firewall."

World.title: German kidnapped in Niger released — Algeria
World.content:
Algeria says a German citizen has been released after a "criminal armed group" kidnapped him in Niger two weeks ago.

Algeria said on Saturday that a German citizen kidnapped by an armed criminal group some two weeks ago in neighboring Niger was safe and in the hands of the Algerian military.

The German national was taken in charge by the Algerian army's security services on Friday, according to a statement from the Defense Ministry shared on the official Algerian news agency.

He has now been taken on a special flight from Guezzam in the far south to the Boufarik military base near the capital Algiers, it said, adding that he was in "good health" and would be handed to German authorities "at a later date."

No details were provided on how the German national was freed.

A spokesperson for the German Foreign Ministry told DW it was aware of the case, but added that the government "does not comment on cases involving the abduction of German citizens abroad."

Niger, which has been under military rule since a July 2023 coup, has in the past few years been wracked by violence from jihadis linked to the al-Qaeda or the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist groups.
