World.title: Major Croatian Projects Involve New Bridge, New Tunnel & Railway
World.content:
August the 10th, 2026 – Several major Croatian projects involving a new bridge on Krk, a 14 kilometre tunnel and a railway line to host high speed trains are underway.

By the end of 2029, the reconstruction of the 44-kilometre railway line from Karlovac to Zagreb should be completed. Snjezana Bicak/Poslovni reports that if you want to go from Rijeka to Istria, you will come across a major construction site; there are more and more excavators and tall cranes as you approach the Učka tunnel or exit it, all so that already next year we will have a full-profile motorway and a more comfortable and pleasant drive to the peninsula and along the entire Istrian Y.

You will also encounter works if you travel through Slavonia, especially around Požega. If you fly with Croatia Airlines, its pilots will bring you to your destination in new aircraft. And if you travel by train from Karlovac to Zagreb, for the next four years you will also watch the works from the train, given that, finally, four years after the first tender was announced, construction of the second track on the Hrvatski Leskovac – Karlovac line has begun these days. Thanks to this, passengers from, for example, Karlovac to Zagreb should reach their destination by train in about 20 minutes.

karlovac is going up in the world…

Karlovac Mayor Damir Mandić has said several times so far that this is a big thing for the development of Karlovac, given that a large number of Karlovac residents work in Zagreb, children go to the metropolis to study, and a number of business activities are linked to Zagreb, writes Večernji list.

Karlovac thereby becomes an even more desirable place to live – outside the hustle and bustle of the big city, yet only about 20 minutes away by train, and the same after the construction of the third lane of the motorway connecting the two cities, which is also planned.

Karlovac will truly become a suburb of Zagreb with an excellent transport connection to it, but also to the rest of Croatia, especially towards the Adriatic, which makes it even more attractive for business investments that lead to the opening of new jobs, and then also for living and the arrival of new families.

The start of construction of the lowland railway, at least on this part of the corridor, delights everyone it concerns. This is no small investment; the contractor, the Spanish company Comsa S.A., which signed a contract with HŽ Infrastructure in July for the execution of the project, will reconstruct the existing track, build the second track, carry out the electrification of 44 kilometres of railway, build new bridges, viaducts and power facilities, arrange stations and stops, and construct five facilities for the needs of HŽ Infrastructure in Karlovac. After the works are completed, train speeds of up to 160 km/h are planned. The value is not negligible either: it amounts to 348.5 million euros including VAT, and the deadline for completion of the works is 36 months, i.e. by the end of 2029.

The Hrvatski Leskovac – Karlovac section is only part of the entire lowland railway project that will connect Zagreb and Rijeka on a section 56 kilometres shorter than the current railway connecting the two cities, and the procedures for contracting works on certain sections are underway. The project is complex; the new double-track and fully electrified railway is designed for speeds of up to 160 km/h for passenger trains and 120 km/h for freight trains.

With a total length of about 175 kilometres – 56 kilometres shorter than the existing line – this will drastically reduce travel time. The biggest challenge on the section after Karlovac is overcoming the demanding mountainous terrain, which is why the construction of more than 30 viaducts and tunnels is planned.

a brand new tunnel through velika kapela

The star of the project is the future tunnel through the Velika Kapela massif, 14 kilometres long, which will become the longest in Croatia. For comparison, the Sveti Rok and Mala Kapela tunnels together are a little less than 12 kilometres long. The route also provides for the construction of five new stations and one stop. All of this should be completed by 2036. From just these few points it’s very clear that Croatia is in a major infrastructure boom that has been going on for some time and will last at least another ten years, which is the period planned for the construction of the entire lowland railway corridor that will connect the largest port of Rijeka with the Hungarian border.

“Croatia is currently implementing one of the largest investment cycles in its existence in transport infrastructure, which covers all types of transport, as well as the development of public urban transport and new forms of mobility. Through European sources of financing within the financial periods 2014–2020 and 2021–2027, projects with a total value of around 5.57 billion euros have been contracted and are being implemented in transport infrastructure, of which around 3.45 billion euros relates to non-refundable EU funds.

The stated amount refers exclusively to projects implemented with the support of European funds and financing instruments, through the Operational Programme Competitiveness and Cohesion, the Competitiveness and Cohesion Programme 2021–2027, the National Recovery and Resilience Plan and the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF). The largest part of these investments is directed towards the modernisation of railway infrastructure, followed by the road sector, maritime transport and public urban transport,” the Ministry of the Sea, Transport and Infrastructure told us.

They add that, in parallel with the already contracted projects financed with the support of European funds, the Government is implementing a broader investment cycle of modernisation of the transport system that includes EU funds, the state budget, loans and other sources of financing.

more railway and train projects are in the works

The railway sector stands out in particular, where investments in railway infrastructure worth more than 1.7 billion euros are underway, while an investment cycle worth around 6 billion euros is planned over the decade to come.

This is the total value of planned investments in the modernisation and renewal of the railway network, which will be financed by a combination of different sources, including EU funds. The goal of the investments is to increase the safety, capacity and quality of railway transport and to strengthen Croatia’s connectivity with European transport corridors, the competent ministry adds.

Minister Oleg Butković said that never before has so much been invested in local and regional railways as now, thanks to part of the loan from the European Investment Bank that the Croatian Government secured. He emphasises that Croatian Motorways invest around 50 million euros annually in investment maintenance of motorways, along with investments in the development and modernisation of the motorway network and the introduction of a new electronic toll collection system.

Croatian Roads, for example, have invested around 1.6 billion euros over the past ten years in the construction of new and the reconstruction of existing state roads, while a series of projects with a total value of more than 1.2 billion euros is currently in preparation and implementation.

port infrastructure investments

“We also have a major investment cycle in port infrastructure worth more than 500 million euros, the largest part of which is financed with EU funds. From the Ministry’s budget alone last year, 14.7 million euros was allocated for port infrastructure and the rehabilitation of maritime domain in general use, and a total of more than 118.4 million euros during the terms of this Government. Investments in inland navigation are aimed at increasing navigation safety, improving the navigability of rivers and developing port and berth infrastructure. In the period 2014–2027, more than 200 million euros was invested in inland waterway projects through European funds and other sources of financing, with the largest part of the investments relating to the development of infrastructure on the Danube River and in the Port of Osijek,” the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure adds.

roads and expressways

When it comes to investments in road transport, among the most important projects currently underway is certainly the completion of the construction of the Istrian Y in full profile, including the section from the Učka tunnel to Matulji, with a total value of around 200 million euros.

A network of expressways is also being built across Croatia, among which the most important is the Podravina Y (from Vrbovec – Bjelovar – Virovitica – the border with Hungary), then the Varaždin – Krapina expressway, the Požega expressway with an exit to the A3 motorway, the Solin – Stobreč – Dugi Rat – Omiš expressway, the Nuštar – Vukovar expressway, the Okučani – Stara Gradiška expressway, and the Zlatar Bistrica – Marija Bistrica expressway as part of the Zagreb Ring.

New bypasses are also being built across Croatia: Fužine, Nedelišće, Pušćine, Orebić, Drniš, Zaprešić, Čakovec and other towns, and reconstructions of state roads are underway: the new entrance to Split, the Sisak junction – Sisak, Donja Zdenčina – the bridge on the Kupa, Veli Vrh – Pula, the narrower city ring of Karlovac, the Širina intersection. The introduction of a new toll collection system is underway, and the Križišće – Selce section on the A7 motorway is being built, while the procedure for signing a contract with the consortium of bidders is underway for the Jadranovo – Selce subsection.

A contract has been signed with the contractor for the Križišće – Jadranovo subsection, the first phase of the Selce – Novi Vinodolski section is being built, and project documentation is being prepared for the Novi Vinodolski – Senj and Senj – Žuta Lokva sections. The Rudine – Osojnik section on the A1 motorway is being built, and additional lanes are being added on the Zagreb – Karlovac section of the A1 motorway and the Zagreb West – Lučko section of the A3 motorway. These last two projects in particular will significantly contribute to reducing congestion, especially in the summer months.

For decades, for example, investment in connecting Požega to the A3 motorway was awaited. Požega-Slavonia County Prefect Antonija Jozić said at the signing of the contract with the contractors that the construction of the expressway and the Požega junction will be of decisive importance for the transport accessibility and economic development of Požega-Slavonia County.

“For many years there was talk of a project that is now being realised. Our county will no longer be the appendix of Croatia; we are becoming more accessible by transport, and what we are most looking forward to is that these projects will be a strong driver of the economy,” Jozić said.

Brod-Posavina County Prefect Danijel Marušić emphasised that this project is proof of cooperation and common interests of neighbouring counties. “In my municipality, along this road, economic zones are already slowly being prepared; of course there will be greater circulation of both people and goods, and it is truly a completely different perspective,” Marušić said.

modernisation of the railway system

In addition to roads, the Croatian Government is also investing in the modernisation of the railway system through the renewal of infrastructure and rolling stock.

“In the recent period, the procurement of new trains for HŽ Passenger Transport has been realised, and 70 new low-floor trains are in operation: 55 electric multiple units, 13 diesel multiple units, and one electro-battery and one battery train each. The total value of the procurement amounts to 363.4 million euros,” the Ministry adds.

And they are not stopping there, because a new procurement has already been contracted. Specifically, 6 electro-diesel trains for the Zagreb – Split route, worth 57.3 million euros, which will be put into service this year; then 5 electro-diesel, 4 electro-battery and 4 battery trains with two charging stations, worth €117.9 million, with delivery during 2027 and 2028. There are also 6 electro-battery trains and a hybrid charging station in Kotoriba, worth 53.6 million euros, with delivery during 2028 and 2029. Additionally, by the first quarter of 2029, 228.8 million euros will be invested in the procurement of an additional 25 trains, the competent authorities note.

Preparation is also underway for potential financing of the procurement of an additional 30 new trains from the Social Climate Fund. The new trains will run on more modern tracks, given that major investments in railway infrastructure are also underway.

Specifically, the reconstruction and construction of the second track on the Dugo Selo – Novska line is underway, a project worth around 900 million euros; the modernisation of the Dugo Selo – Križevci and Križevci – Koprivnica – state border with Hungary sections is being completed; and, as mentioned, the modernisation of the Hrvatski Leskovac – Karlovac section worth 280 million euros has begun.

Numerous projects for the renewal of local, regional and international lines are also underway, including the Pitomača – Kloštar, Generalski Stol – Oštarije, Ogulin – Moravice, Karlovac – Ozalj, Knin – Zadar, Osijek – Koška and other sections.

that isn’t all…

“When it comes to investment in port infrastructure, in the previous period 25 projects were contracted through which 14 ports were built or reconstructed, including the ports of Tkon, Crikvenica, Cres, Unije, Sućuraj, Korčula, Baška, Žigljen, Zadar, Split, Stinica, Vela Luka and others. In the new financial period, investment in port infrastructure continues through projects with a total value of 267.64 million euros. These include projects for the reconstruction and expansion of the ports of Novi Vinodolski, Rovinj, Murter, Krk, Rab, Prvić Šepurine, Perna, Prigradica, Split, Kaštela, Vrsi, Ika and others,” the Ministry of Maritime Affairs revealed.

Among the more important projects related to inland navigation, the completion and development of the bulk cargo terminal in the Port of Osijek, the arrangement and improvement of the waterway of the Danube River, and the construction and development of port infrastructure for inland freight transport stand out. The leaders of Slavonian cities and counties are particularly looking forward to these projects, given that they will contribute to the development of economic activities across Slavonia.

Minister Oleg Butković also said that the goal of these significant investments is to increase the share of river transport in total freight traffic, connect Croatian ports with European transport corridors and further relieve road traffic.

World.title: Will New Toll Collection System Reduce Croatian Traffic Jams?
World.content:
August the 9th, 2026 – Will the new toll collection system set to come into force next year actually manage to reduce the infamous Croatian traffic jams on the motorways?

As Poslovni reports, the much anticipated installation of more than 220 portals on motorways across Croatia is currently underway. Appearing on HTV’s programme Studio 4, the director of the Traffic Sector at HAC (Croatian Motorways), Hrvoje Ordulj, touched on the new toll collection system, which is expected to become operational during 2027.

More than 220 portals are currently being installed on motorways throughout Croatia, and a large part of the infrastructure has already been put in place, reports HRT. “We expect all the portals to be installed by October, and the system could go live during next year,” he said. However, he did warn that not even the new system will be able to completely eliminate the country’s well known summer congestion. “Regardless of barriers or the new toll collection system, traffic will stand still if the load is too high,” Ordulj stated.

Major projects: Učka, Novi Vinodolski and Matulji

Speaking about future projects, Ordulj announced the continuation of construction of the Novi Vinodolski bypass, the completion of the Matulji junction, and the connection of Istria and Kvarner with a full-profile motorway.

“We expect that in the first quarter of next year Istria and Kvarner will be connected by a full-profile motorway,” Ordulj said. He added that works on the sections between Križišće, Jadranovo and Selce will intensify after the end of the summer tourist season.

World.title: Croatia Could Face Natural Gas Problems in Autumn
World.content:
August the 9th, 2026 – Croatia could end up facing natural gas problems this autumn, with underground natural gas storage facilities being filled poorly.

As for natural gas prices, Grozdanić says that prices in the European Union have risen to a little over 60 eurps per megawatt-hour (MWh). Poslovni reports that towards the end of summer, concerns about the supply and prices of energy sources in the colder part of the year always begin. This year they have been spurred by the conflict in the Middle East that shows no sign of ending, as well as by the extreme drought that has left river levels at record lows, affecting the operation of hydropower plants and the Krško Nuclear Power Plant.

Midweek, the Krško NPP, the electricity production of which covers 16 percent of domestic market needs, temporarily and preventively reduced the reactor’s output by 20 percent due to the risk of overheating of the water in the Sava River, writes Miroslav Filipović for N1.

“This isn’t a limitation for technological reasons, but for environmental reasons, i.e. for the protection of the bio-environment and the temperature of the Sava River,” energy expert Ivica Jakić explained this move by the Krško NPP to our portal.

the situation with electricity

Neither Jakić nor energy expert Igor Grozdanić expect that, despite all the difficulties, the electricity supply will be endangered this autumn.

“There will be enough electricity on the market thanks to the nuclear power plants over in France, and let’s not forget that the Czech Republic and Slovakia together have eight nuclear reactors which, like the Krško NPP, are cooled by air coolers and are not dependent on the amount of cooling water from rivers or lakes,” Jakić said.

“If nothing extraordinary or catastrophic happens, I don’t expect shortages or problems in the electricity supply. And if prices rise, they will not rise too much,” Grozdanić said. Croatia imports a significant share of its electricity from Bosnia and Herzegovina, where it is produced in thermal power plants that operate without difficulties. In addition, Jakić notes that electricity is purchased under contracts, so-called futures, at a pre-agreed price, whereby the supplier is obliged to deliver it at a fixed price and within a fixed delivery period.

petrol and petroleum products

After four consecutive price reductions, the first summer price increase of petroleum products followed in mid-July — only diesel fuel, and not a large one. But two weeks ago all fuels rose significantly: LPG by five cents per litre, eurosuper 95 by eight cents, and eurodiesel by as much as 16 cents per litre.

Next Tuesday a new price increase is expected, but only for diesel fuel. According to RTL’s unofficial information, a litre of eurosuper 95 should be two cents cheaper, while eurodiesel and blue diesel should rise by three cents per litre. The exact amount will be known on Monday when the Government decides on a possible intervention in prices. Grozdanić doesn’t really expect major shocks regarding fuel prices this autumn.

“As for fuels, the situation is more stable than on the markets of other energy sources in our country. Regardless of the situation in the Middle East, prices are always higher in summer because of the tourist season,” he says.

natural gas is where the problems could arise

However, there could be problems with natural gas, Grozdanić notes.

“The fact is that underground natural gas storage facilities are being filled poorly. But that is expected because prices are very high for this time of year. The American-Iranian war has reduced the gas supply and everyone is waiting to see how the situation in the Middle East develops. The situation is interesting because European natural gas stocks have fallen to their lowest level since 2011. Under current market conditions it does not pay anyone to fill the storage facilities. Gas storage facilities need to be filled before winter, but people are still waiting,” he says. Gas stocks across EU storage facilities are currently a little below 58 percent, Grozdanić emphasises, and the fill level of the Okoli Underground Gas Storage is roughly the same.

On Friday, PSP Okoli was at 57 percent fill. The Croatian Government decided at the end of July that by 1 October the fill level of the Okoli storage must be at least 85 percent, with an allowed deviation of up to five percent.

As for natural gas prices, Grozdanić says that prices in the European Union have risen to a little over €60 per megawatt-hour (MWh). “This autumn the gas price could be in the range of 55 to 75 euros per MWh,” Grozdanić concluded.

World.title: Meet Krapje – The Wooden Croatian Village Hidden Within a Nature Park
World.content:
August the 9th, 2026 – Beautiful, secluded Krapje is often called the wooden Croatian village, and it is hidden deep within a beautiful nature park, far from the coast.

Despite being relatively unheard of abroad, Krapje is actually one of the best-preserved traditional villages most people will ever see. It holds the status of a cultural heritage monument of the Republic of Croatia and is considered one of the pearls of the gorgeous Lonjsko Polje Nature Park.

Posavina is one of the rare parts of Croatia where traditional wooden villages can still be seen today, the kind that were once a common sight along the course of the Sava. Putni kofer writes that charming oak houses, wide courtyards, farm buildings and a way of life adapted to the river have shaped this region for centuries, and one of the places that has preserved this valuable heritage almost in its original form is Krapje. Located in the municipality of Jasenovac, on the left bank of the Sava in Sisak-Moslavina County, this picturesque village is today counted among the finest examples of traditional architecture in Croatia.

most of the houses in the croatian wooden village are over 100 – and still standing despite their construction style…

Nikola Cutuk/PIXSELL

Only about a hundred people actually live in Krapje, and because of its exceptionally well-preserved architecture it was declared a village of architectural heritage in 1995. It is first mentioned in written sources as early as the 14th century and got its name from the fish krap (carp). But Krapje’s greatest hallmark is the traditional Posavina architecture. The village has more than 80 wooden houses typical of central Posavina, holds the status of a Category A cultural heritage monument and is considered one of the pearls of Lonjsko Polje Nature Park.

Most of the houses are more than a hundred years old. They were built from oak planks joined with wooden pegs and are recognisable by their covered external staircases, porches, protective canopies and richly decorated railings and columns. Their facades all face the street, while farm buildings, stables, haylofts and storerooms, are located at the rear.

a true haven for all kinds of birds

Even the method of construction was no accident. Because the Sava frequently flooded the surrounding area, durable oak wood that could withstand water was used for the houses, while living quarters were placed on higher floors. Besides its architectural heritage, this part of Posavina is also known for its unspoiled nature.

Between Krapje and nearby Drenov Bok lies Krapje Đol, a special ornithological reserve spanning an impressive 25 hectares. It has been protected since 1963 and includes an old branch of the Sava and a valuable wetland habitat overgrown with lush vegetation. Thanks to this environment, more than 500 pairs of birds nest there, among which spoonbills stand out in particular.

One of the must-see places in the village is the Krapje Visitor Centre, located in a complex of restored wooden Posavina houses. It houses a multimedia hall, a gallery and a souvenir shop, and you can also rent a bicycle or canoe and set off on the Border Guards’ Trail that begins in the centre’s courtyard.

At house number 48 you can view the ethnographic collection of the Palaić family with more than 170 items that show the everyday life of the former border guards and the traditional crafts characteristic of Posavina. Every year the European Heritage Days in Krapje are also held in the village, dedicated to the preservation of its rich architectural and cultural heritage.

a rich natural world awaits visitors

While you’re there, be sure to try the biggest local speciality, carp on a spit (šaran na rašljama). Finally, a stay in Krapje can easily be combined with exploring Lonjsko Polje Nature Park, one of the largest and best-preserved floodplain areas in Europe. The park is known for its rich plant and animal life, especially storks. It also includes the famous village of Čigoč, which was declared the first European Stork Village back in 1994.

World.title: What are The Main Issues With Summer Traffic Jams in Croatia?
World.content:
August the 9th, 2026 – There are an array of very particular issues causing the infamous summer traffic jams up and down Croatia, with queues stretching for kilometres on the motorways.

The awful queues at Lučko, stoppages near Sveti Rok and kilometre-long traffic jams towards the coast have not spared Croatian motorways this year. Nor have they ever so far. Poslovni reports that Hrvoje Ordulj, Director of the Traffic Sector at HAC (Croatian Motorways), spoke as a guest on HRT’s programme Studio 4 about summer delays being practically unavoidable, but that drivers often make the situation worse by disregarding traffic rules.

“These long queues will remain unavoidable for some time yet. We all want to get to the coast and we all want to return from the sea at the same time,” Ordulj stated, before pointing out that the problems aren’t only at the toll booths themselves, but are a result of the very configuration of the roads and the large number of vehicles that pour southwards through Croatia at the peak of the summer season.

Why do traffic jams form at Lučko and Sveti Rok?

Ordulj explained that at Lučko as many as seven or eight traffic lanes merge and then narrow down to only two. “You can’t reduce traffic from seven lanes to two and expect everything to function normally. A particular problem lies with the Sveti Rok tunnel, where traffic sometimes has to be temporarily stopped for safety reasons. Traffic in the tunnel mustn’t come to a total stop. If an accident or breakdown occurs, the entrance to the tunnel is automatically closed,” Ordulj explained.

He added that HAC operators continuously monitor the situation on the motorways and, when they assess that traffic density is too high, temporarily close the entrance to the tunnel in order to prevent dangerous situations.

“Foreigners respect the limits, croatian drivers much less”

One of the topics of the conversation was also drivers’ traffic culture. Ordulj openly admitted that Croatian drivers often ignore speed limits, especially in roadworks zones. “As a rule, you’ll notice that drivers with foreign registration plates respect the speed limits, unlike a lot of Croatian drivers who overtake until the last moment and cut in front of other vehicles,” he said.

He particularly appealed to drivers to respect dynamic signalling and the rules on forming an emergency corridor. “When traffic stops, the driver can’t possibly know whether it is an accident or just another ordinary jam. That’s why the emergency corridor should be formed immediately,” he concluded.

World.title: Meet the Croatian Dead Sea On a Dalmatian Island Paradise
World.content:
August the 8th, 2026 – There’s a so-called Croatian dead sea, tucked away on a southern Dalmatian island paradise, just a stone’s throw away from the hustle and bustle of Dubrovnik.

Hidden away on an island in the very far south of Croatia lies an unusual lake that shares its name with the saltiest sea in the world. In summer it is a popular swimming spot. Just a few hundred metres from the famous Dubrovnik lies the island of Lokrum. Putni kofer writes that this beautiful little island of small size and great diversity is a must-visit destination for a trip from the Mediterranean pearl and offers peace and beauty that can rarely be experienced elsewhere. But did you know that Lokrum also hides the Croatian Dead Sea? That is exactly what an unusual lake is called that has become one of its most popular swimming spots in the summer months.

The Croatian Dead Sea – 30 metres wide and 10 metres deep

The island of Lokrum itself is believed to have got its name from the abundance of sour wild orange trees that once grew on it, derived from the Latin word for sour fruit, acrumen. Its highest peak, Glavica, is 96 metres high, and on the southern part of the island there is also a small lake. That is precisely the Croatian Dead Sea!

It is 30 metres wide and, at its deepest point, ten metres deep. Its southwestern shore is not kind to visitors, but the northeastern one is. That is why the Croatian Dead Sea has become one of the favourite swimming spots on the island, especially for families with small children.

This natural wonder is actually a saltwater lake connected to the Adriatic Sea by a narrow channel. The enclosed natural cove is ideal for swimming because there are never any waves in it, and the water is shallow and warmer than that on the open sea. In summer the lake on the island of Lokrum is full of bathers and tourists, so it is best to visit it out of season or in the early morning hours. Nearby there is also a natural stone arch that locals call “Buža”, a favourite backdrop for photographs among tourists. The Croatian Dead Sea was of interest to numerous researchers and travel writers who, as early as the 19th century, analysed and described the chemical composition of its seawater. Today this lake is part of the Natura 2000 ecological network, and its condition is regularly monitored.

the island of plants…

Over many millions of years, the rocks have been extremely tectonically disturbed, as evidenced by the systems of cracks and faults that are gradually widened by karstification and the erosive action of the sea. Thus a former erosional depression in the relief, today known as the Lokrum swimming area, was filled with the sea in the youngest geological period, the Quaternary. You can very easily reach the island by regular boat lines from Dubrovnik. This pearl of the southern Adriatic was first protected as early as 1963, and since 1976 it has had the status of a special forest vegetation reserve. Hundreds of plant species grow on it, including 70 species of eucalyptus.

Besides the botanical garden and the beaches, the biggest attractions are also the abandoned Benedictine monastery and the castle on the southern part of the island. You can simply walk across Lokrum, but if you really want to enjoy it and explore it in more detail, we definitely recommend setting aside a whole day.

World.title: Tartu Old Town bar owners concerned about nearby residential development
World.content:
Several bars in Tartu's Old Town are concerned about apartments due to be completed in the heart of the city in a few years and potential conflicts with the new residents who will move into them.

The building on the corner of Gildi and Rüütli streets in Tartu's Old Town, built in 1838, has served as a broadcloth factory, a girls' school and a polyclinic. Now, after standing empty for several years, the building is being converted into office space and 53 apartments, mostly one- and two-room units. Nearby bars are concerned about their potential new neighbors, fearing noise complaints and conflicts similar to those surrounding Genialistide Klubi, which Tartu has been trying to resolve for the past year and a half.

"Rüütli tänav is Tartu's main downtown street. This is where the nightlife is most concentrated. We already have noise problems, which have been discussed extensively in Tartu, so how do you resolve a situation where short-term rental apartments are allowed on the main downtown street, which is the center of nightlife? Why are short-term rental apartments allowed on this street? It's clear from the outset that there are going to be problems here and experience so far has shown that I have to resolve all these problems out of my own pocket, with my own money, nerves and everything else," Kivi bar owner Karin Kiplok said.

Jaan Tover, who owns several bars near the new apartments, said they are also concerned because the city is not taking steps to prevent problems related to nightlife. When problems arise, businesses on Rüütli tänav are left to resolve them themselves. The developer said its plans have taken the location into account.

"These are mostly smaller homes that will probably attract younger people without children who may be less bothered by the associated disturbance. The other thing is that, from a construction standpoint, we have to take great care to make sure the windows are very well insulated. Also, there won't be any ventilation openings in the wall," said Kaarel Kiidron, managing partner at developer Livida.

Although prospective apartment buyers are informed about the bustle on Rüütli tänav, some residents who expected noise and people on the street have encountered issues they did not anticipate.

"The vibration that comes through the window on weekends is actually pretty bad, and it's specifically from the music. I knew there would be noise, but I didn't expect the vibration to come through the walls of the building. It's coming through from the building next door. I knew there would be a lot of people here, and people don't bother me, but there could be less music here," said Triin Varul, a Rüütli tänav resident.

Tartu's Rüütli tänav. Source: Airika Harrik/ERR

Tartu Deputy Mayor Kertu Vuks said the city's vision is for the Old Town to accommodate both housing and bars and cafes. If new Old Town residents encounter problems with noise, the city will address them on a case-by-case basis. At the same time, the city would like bars outside the Old Town to be viable as well.

"The city's hope and vision is also for other locations — not just Rüütli tänav — and neighborhood bars to be viable," Vuks said. She added that, ultimately, bars will not have to leave Rüütli tänav and businesses are free to choose the locations that suit them best.

World.title: Estonia's ruling coalition on thin ice after Eesti 200 member quits party
World.content:
Kalev Stoicescu's decision to quit Eesti 200 means that the Reform-E200 coalition now has only a razor-thin 51-seat majority in the 101-member parliament.

Member of Eesti 200 and Chair of the Riigikogu National Defense Committee Kalev Stoicescu took to social media on Sunday to announce his decision to quit the coalition party. "Done," Stoicescu wrote on social media.

According to Stoicescu, the decision had been a long time coming and he had considered whether he wanted to remain in politics at all.

"I stepped down from the party's board back in February 2024. I did not run in the local elections in October 2025. I thought for a long time about whether to continue in politics at all. People close to me and voters have unanimously encouraged me to continue and run in the next Riigikogu elections. I trust myself and the people close to me," the politician said.

Stoicescu also said he has already received offers to join other parties but has not yet made a decision.

"I want to continue contributing to Estonia's future, particularly in the areas of defense, security and foreign policy," Stoicescu said.

Coalition left with a razon-thin margin in the Riigikogu

The Reform Party parliamentary group has 37 MPs. Since the last Riigikogu elections, Alar Laneman, formerly of EKRE, and Maria Jufereva-Skuratovski, formerly of the Center Party, have joined the Reform Party. This means the Reform Party can count on 39 MPs.

Eesti 200 won 14 seats in the last Riigikogu elections. Züleyxa Izmailova previously left the party and is now a member of the Social Democratic Party. Following Stoicescu's departure, Eesti 200 therefore currently has 12 votes.

Overall, this means that the governing coalition's majority in the 101-seat Riigikogu has shrunk to the narrowest possible margin, with the two parties now holding 51 seats between them. Such a slim majority makes passing legislation difficult and requires strict discipline. It also means the coalition will have to seek support from unaffiliated MPs in important votes.

At the same time, several opposition politicians have said that more MPs are likely to leave the governing parties, whose ratings have fallen, before the next elections. Estonia could therefore see a minority government before the elections, as none of the opposition parties is eager to enter government. Those seen as potential defectors are primarily MPs who want to remain in politics but whose current governing parties' levels of support do not guarantee them a seat in the next Riigikogu.

Prime Minister and Reform Party Chair Kristen Michal and Eesti 200 leader Kristina Kallas had firmly rejected these claims before Stoicescu announced his departure.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) and Eesti 200 head Kristina Kallas. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

After Stoicescu left the party on Sunday, Kallas told the media that the decision had come as a surprise to her.

ERR has been told that Stoicescu is most likely to join the nonparliamentary Parempoolsed (Right-wingers) ahead of the Riigikogu elections. Polling firms Emor, Norstat and Turu-uuringud currently put the party's support at 6–7 percent. Parempoolsed have struggled with a lack of well-known figures and Stoicescu joining would certainly help them.

The next Riigikogu elections will take place March 7, 2027, seven months from now.

It will also be interesting to see how Stoicescu's departure from Eesti 200 affects the dynamics of the Riigikogu's committees, particularly the National Defense Committee, which Stoicescu currently chairs. The National Defense Committee has 11 members, and before Stoicescu left Eesti 200, the governing coalition held a narrow six-member majority.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal indicated to Postimees that Stoicescu could remain chair of the National Defense Committee and vote with the coalition on important issues. However, if Stoicescu does indeed join Parempoolsed or one of the opposition parties currently represented in the Riigikogu, their sharp criticism of the governing parties means the coalition cannot be certain that he would, for example, vote with it on the state budget.

Stoicescu, whose full legal name is Grigore-Kalev Stoicescu, joined Eesti 200 on September 30, 2022. He ran on Eesti 200's ticket in the 2019 Riigikogu elections and received 395 votes. He also ran for the Riigikogu in the 2023 elections, receiving 3,663 votes in electoral district No. 5 (Hiiu, Lääne and Saare counties) and winning a seat. In the 2024 European Parliament elections, he received 1,678 votes but was not elected.

Kristina Kallas and Kalev Stoicescu. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

World.title: Estonia axes unemployment benefit for young people finishing conscription
World.content:
New eligibility requirements mean that young graduates cannot receive unemployment benefits after finishing school or completing military service, unless they have previously worked for at least eight months.

A young person who goes straight from school into compulsory military service may be surprised to discover that, when looking for work after completing their service, they will have to rely on someone else for financial support because the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund will not pay them benefits. The exception is if they managed to work enough while still in school.

Previously, both school graduates and young people completing military service were eligible for unemployment allowance, but that form of support ceased to exist at the beginning of this year. Unemployment insurance benefits are now available, with eligibility depending on a person's previous participation in the labor market, said Kirsti Melesk, head of the employment department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications.

"As with any other type of insurance, the system works so that a person becomes entitled to benefits if they have contributed to the insurance system and the insured event then occurs. In the case of unemployment insurance, that means becoming unemployed. The same principle can be compared with home or auto insurance: If a person has never paid insurance premiums, they cannot claim an insurance payout when an insured event occurs. The purpose of unemployment insurance benefits is to partially replace income previously earned from employment during the period when a person is looking for work, rather than directly guaranteeing an income to everyone who is out of work, including those who did not previously have such an income," Melesk said.

She said conscripts are in the same position as school graduates who also have no previous work experience when they begin looking for work after graduation and have to manage without financial support from the state. Young people can nevertheless register as unemployed and make use of services designed to help them find work.

"We currently have no plans to create any kind of exemption for conscripts. Instead, we consider it important to support young people in their job searches, helping them gain their first work experience and get a foot in the door of the labor market. Since the beginning of this year, for example, the Unemployment Insurance Fund has also had youth counselors who specialize specifically in supporting young people's job searches and providing them with counseling," Melesk said.

In certain cases, however, young school graduates may still be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits if they managed to work while attending school. To qualify, they must have worked during at least eight months over the preceding three years, for at least one day in each of those months.

"A person must have accumulated at least eight months of unemployment insurance coverage. This can be accrued, for example, through employment under an employment contract, and if a person has worked under an employment contract for eight months, the requirement has already been met," said Vadim Djomin, head of unemployment insurance benefits at the Unemployment Insurance Fund. There are, however, exceptions.

"If a person works under a contract governed by the law of obligations, there must be eight payments from which unemployment insurance premiums have been withheld. In the case of employment contracts, a person must have worked for eight months and those months do not have to be consecutive. They can be under different contracts and in different months, but there must be at least eight months in total," Djomin said.

According to Djomin, a young person could accumulate the required eight months by working over three summers and would then be eligible for benefits from the Unemployment Insurance Fund after graduating.

Viru Infantry Battalian conscripts' passout, June 10. Source: mil.ee

The Estonian Defense Resources Agency has not discussed providing conscripts with financial support while they look for work after completing their service. If such support were introduced, it would have to come from the defense budget at the expense of specific military capabilities, the agency's director general, Anu Rannaveski, said.

"What is military service if not another form of training? Just as people study different fields at university, military service itself is training in national defense. Of course, as a society, we want to make it as easy as possible for young people to enter the labor market. I think military service itself already gives a young person a very strong competitive advantage. The studies we have conducted also show that, in the future, young people who have completed military service earn more than those who have not," Rannaveski said.

She said the trend in recent years also shows that a significant number of young people remain in the Estonian Defense Forces as active-duty personnel after completing their military service. They account for around 7.5 percent of conscripts.

World.title: Natalie Mets: Youth unemployment will not fix itself
World.content:
Vocational education must be a deliberate and valued choice for young people in Estonia, rather than a fallback option for those who did not get into university, writes Natalie Mets.

Estonia's youth unemployment rate is at its highest level in recent years, at 18.2 percent. But we should also be increasingly concerned about young people who are not in education, employment or training (the so-called NEET group). In Estonia, approximately one in 10 young people aged 15–26 falls into the NEET category.

Estonia's problems are often blamed on our small population. Yet youth unemployment is also rising in much larger countries. The root of the problem, therefore, is not that there are too few Estonians. The labor market has changed rapidly and getting that first opportunity is becoming increasingly difficult for young people. It is no longer only those who do not want to work who are unemployed — increasingly, even young people who are actively looking for work cannot find a job.

But what lies behind these figures? A young person who is neither studying nor working unfortunately ends up on the margins of society. Inactivity can quickly turn into loneliness and isolation. Days are spent in front of a computer screen and — as anyone who has spent a long time unsuccessfully looking for work probably knows — confidence in oneself and in the idea that there is a place for them in the labor market quickly disappears. The longer a young person remains without work or study, the harder it becomes to enter the labor market later.

Against this backdrop, it was particularly dismaying to hear Tallinn Deputy Mayor for Education Andrei Kante's (Center Party — ed.) explanation for Tallinn Technology College's lack of popularity among girls. In his view, the problem is that the college does not offer enough programs that interest girls. Fortunately, representatives of the college immediately rejected this view, saying that such thinking is outdated and harmful to society.

When a politician in power essentially says that technology-related fields are not meant for girls and that more suitable programs should be created for them, he is reinforcing precisely the stereotypes that Estonia should have left behind long ago. Through the deputy mayor's words, Tallinn is sending the message that higher-paying occupations with better career prospects — engineer, mechanic or IT specialist — are for boys, while girls should choose service, care work or other traditionally lower-paid fields that are supposedly more likely to "interest" them.

This kind of thinking is just as harmful to boys as it is to girls. If a boy wants to study to become, for example, an early childhood teacher, occupational therapist, speech therapist or nurse, prejudice and misplaced embarrassment may prevent him from making that final decision. There is extensive research on this and the OECD has reached the same conclusion: perceptions of which occupations are "women's work" or "men's work" directly influence young people's choices of fields of study.

Yet the fields mentioned above are precisely the ones that need more men. Children benefit when both male and female teachers work in kindergartens and schools. Every field stands to benefit from greater diversity.

There are occupations in which biological differences may, on average, give one sex an advantage, such as strength-based activities at the absolute elite level or the most physically demanding tasks. Most modern occupations, however, require knowledge, teamwork, creativity and dedication, not lifting rocks.

At a time when artificial intelligence will inevitably change the nature of work and affect almost every occupation, politicians should be sending a very different message. Instead of crudely dividing occupations into "women's" and "men's" work, we must do everything possible to ensure that every young person acquires the skills needed to adapt in a rapidly changing world.

Those who know how to use technology, acquire new skills, combine different fields and think critically will succeed. We cannot afford to leave some young people with the impression, while they are still in school, that certain opportunities simply are not for them.

Only systemic change can address the current situation. Vocational education must become a deliberate and valued choice for young people in Estonia, rather than a fallback option for those who did not get into university. That requires closer cooperation with employers, more internship opportunities and greater societal respect for skilled trades.

At the same time, hiring young people must be made more attractive to employers. One option worth considering would be reducing employers' tax burden on young workers, making it less risky for businesses to offer someone their first job.

The Riigikogu's decision to allow 16-year-olds to serve alcohol was also a step in the right direction, but that alone is not enough to improve young people's prospects in the labor market. A broader package of measures is needed to support young people's education and their transition into employment.

Higher education, for example, could be made more flexible so that parents can study part time free of charge and having a child does not mean interrupting their education or facing a financial penalty. The public sector, one of Estonia's largest employers, could also launch a pilot program to create more first-job opportunities specifically for young people.

Youth unemployment will not decline on its own. It requires political decisions that expand young people's opportunities, whether in education or in getting their first job, and that help break down outdated notions about which choices are "right" for them.

World.title: EKRE head: Ülle Madise's election in the Riigikogu could be contested in court
World.content:
Martin Helme said his party would not support Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise as a potential candidate in the presidential election and that the chancellor's conflict of roles in the election could lead to the result being challenged in court.

"Ülle Madise has now essentially declared herself a presidential candidate because she is bargaining with the Riigikogu to secure cross-party support. She does not have that support, because at the very least our party does not support her election," Helme wrote on social media.

"At the same time, she has a very serious conflict of interest by indicating that she wants the support of all parties while serving as chancellor of justice, who oversees the work of parliament," he said, adding that such a conflict of roles could result in the election result being challenged in court if Madise is elected.

The EKRE chair said Madise's potential candidacy creates a bad impression.

"The chancellor of justice is playing a game in which she acts as though she is not a candidate, thereby avoiding the debate and heightened media and public scrutiny that should be a matter of course for someone seeking high office. At the same time, she is consistently signaling that she is interested in the office, provided the votes for her are already secured," Helme said.

He said Madise has systematically passed up opportunities to say that she will not run and is not interested in doing so. "Today (Saturday — ed.), she once again confirmed that she is interested in the presidency, except that she wants to see sufficient support first."

"This kind of game allows her to pop up as a candidate at the last minute and, assuming the votes are indeed secured, walk straight in through the back door of Kadriorg. As I said, all of this is very poor form and flagrantly at odds with the basic principles of democracy," the EKRE chair added.

Helme said EKRE is the only party to have approached the presidential election seriously and professionally, while also treating voters with respect. He emphasized that the party nominated Mart Helme as its candidate in the spring.

"I continue to urge people to support Estonia's only official presidential candidate, Mart Helme," he concluded.

Eesti 200 Chair Kristina Kallas said Thursday that Madise currently has the support of 67 members of the Riigikogu and that Züleyxa Izmailova, who left Eesti 200 and joined the Social Democrats, does not support Madise. Izmailova, however, told ERR that the vote is secret and that she would not stand in the way of electing a president.

The Riigikogu's Council of Elders will discuss the presidential election Tuesday.

At least 21 members of the Riigikogu are required to nominate a presidential candidate. A candidate would need at least 68 votes to be elected president by the Riigikogu.

Key dates:

• Aug. 21-24: Candidate nominations

• Sept. 2: First round of voting in the Riigikogu

• Sept. 3: Second and third rounds of voting in the Riigikogu, if necessary

World.title: Estonia's warming bodies of water catering to fish parasites
World.content:
Although many parasites have always coexisted with fish in Estonia, encounters with heat-loving parasites in particular can pose a serious threat to populations of cold-water salmonids.

An expedition by Estonian University of Life Sciences researchers to Greenland and the Faroe Islands found that the parasite that causes a dangerous and currently incurable kidney disease in salmonids has spread much farther north than previously known. However, Anti Vasemägi, professor of fish genetics and genomics at the Estonian University of Life Sciences, said it is not known when the parasite, Tetracapsuloides bryosalmonae, reached the area. The parasite was first detected in Estonia nearly 30 years ago.

"But we still don't know, for example, when it reached Estonia. In Iceland, meanwhile, the parasite has spread rapidly over the past couple of decades, and this has also been linked to rising water temperatures," Vasemägi said.

Vasemägi noted that in Estonia, both warm-water fish and heat-loving parasites are currently thriving.

"When a cold-water fish encounters a parasite that prefers warmer water, it can end badly for the fish. In Estonia, this parasite causes the greatest mortality among juvenile trout, specifically in rivers where water temperatures have been altered by human activity. As we know, people have built many dams on rivers, straightened large sections of rivers and even cut down trees along riverbanks. All of this warms the water and raises its temperature," Vasemägi said.

According to Vasemägi, recent studies indicate that many parasites found farther south are reaching Estonia via migratory birds.

"For example, our new project funded by the Estonian Research Council will examine the spread of parasites associated with cormorants and a possible increase in their abundance in coastal waters."

The Estonian Federation of Fishing Clubs said there is nothing particularly unusual happening in Estonia. Vasemägi also noted that parasites are found in all fish species in Estonia and that fish generally cope well with them.

"It can be said that an extremely small proportion of our fish parasites can be dangerous to humans, and only if the fish has not been properly prepared. The rule of thumb is that people should avoid eating raw fish and fish roe, but fish that has been sufficiently heated or salted poses no danger to humans. So if fish is properly baked, boiled, salted or dried, there is no danger," Vasemägi said.

Vasemägi added that if anglers notice anything unusual about a fish, they can always send a photo to researchers at the Estonian University of Life Sciences and ask for advice.
