World.title: ‘Unacceptable’ Sydney airport reliability expected for weeks at least
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesAviation ‘Unacceptable’ Sydney airport reliability expected for weeks at least Chris Zappone and Matt O'Sullivan Updated August 10, 2026 — 3:27pm ,first published August 10, 2026 — 9:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two airport workers have been stood down and the chief of Australia’s air traffic control agency has been warned that delays at Sydney Airport have become “unacceptable” as investigators probe the second near-collision between planes on the tarmac in the past two weeks. But passengers, who have had to deal with the delays caused by a shortage of air traffic controllers, will have to wait weeks before a new roster comes into effect in September that Airservices Australia hopes will improve reliability. A Jetstar plane and a Qatar Airways plane on the runway at Sydney Airport on Sunday morning. Nine News An air traffic controller and a ground worker involved in an incident on Sunday have been stood down under their employers’ policies while authorities determine how a Jetstar plane got within metres of striking a Qatar jet. The stand downs, which are common after an incident, come as Transport Minister Catherine King criticised the delays and disruptions after meeting with Airservices Australia CEO Rob Sharp.



“The delays and disruptions we have seen at Sydney Airport over the last three days have been unacceptable and have caused significant disruption to passengers, staff and airlines,” King said. Related Article Aviation Dozens of flights out of Sydney delayed up to 80 minutes Airservices committed to implementing “improved rostering practices” for Sydney’s air traffic controllers that will be in place from early September, King said. “I have made my expectations clear that Airservices must carefully manage the situation at Sydney for the rest of August,” she said. Airservices’ Sharp apologised for the impact “on flight delays” and the impact it has on people’s travel plans.



“I want to assure the public that safety is not compromised when issues with staffing levels occur,” he said, who noted the safety measures can lead to flight delays. The Sunday near miss came just weeks after a similar incident in which planes had been given contradictory instructions by controllers at Sydney Airport. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau is now investigating. Its chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said the incident occurred at low speed but still had the potential to be “very significant”. “Those two aircraft should not have come as close as they did,” he said on Seven’s Sunrise. He would not prejudge his organisation’s investigation, but flagged that the traffic control system had been under significant stress. Airservices has repeatedly reduced flight frequencies at Sydney Airport over the past week due to shortages of air-traffic controllers, leading to major delays. Adding to the difficulty, it can take about 18 months to train a new controller to manage a specific piece of airspace or part of the airport. Airservices has been dogged by capacity since a mass retirement of controllers in 2021 as COVID shut down the aviation sector. Additionally, questions have lingered about the work culture.



Aviation safety specialist Geoff Dell said a shortage of air-traffic controllers risked reducing “redundancy” in the system to deal with incidents. Loading “The reality is that if they are short people, it puts stress on the service, and it puts stress on the individuals,” said Dell, a former airport operations safety manager for Qantas. “If you have a lot of aircraft on the ground because of delays, it becomes a chessboard trying to shuffle them around so you don’t have them conflicting where one aircraft is closer than it should be.” Sydney Airport has about 70 aircraft coming and going every hour during morning and evening peak periods, putting it near the cap of 80 an hour. A further five movements are permitted to help the airport recover from cascading delays caused by bad weather or other disruptions.



NSW Premier Chris Minns expressed concern that the major disruptions at the airport could potentially affect Sydney’s reputation as a global city. Related Article Exclusive

Aviation VietJet to offer international flights from Western Sydney “The onus is on everybody associated with the airport to get it done [to resolve the situation] ASAP,” he said. The airlines’ peak body said it had repeatedly raised the performance issues with Airservices. “Airservices Australia management needs to provide greater transparency about the causes of these ongoing disruptions and, importantly, set out a credible plan to immediately resolve them,” Airlines for Australia and New Zealand CEO Stephen Beckett.



“These operational disruptions are now occurring multiple times a week.” Australian Travel Industry Association chief executive Dean Long said the number of delays caused by Airservices had jumped compared with before the COVID pandemic. Long said that the rest of the travel sector had restored performance since the pandemic but “Airservices, for whatever reason, does seem to be really struggling to get their performance where it needs to be”. World.title: Dalaroo set for first drilling of three key Côte d’Ivoire gold targets
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Dalaroo set for first drilling of three key Côte d’Ivoire gold targets Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright August 10, 2026 — 3:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dalaroo Metals has cleared the final hurdles in its preparation to kick-start a major maiden drilling campaign at its Bondoukou Gold Ridge project in Côte d’Ivoire, with all drill pads and access routes now complete. Following a recent 2.5 million capital raise, the company has expanded the planned reverse circulation, or “RC”, drilling program to 12,000 metres from 10,000m, allowing for a more systematic test of three priority gold targets dubbed Mag, Wilfred and Ali. The three targets are evenly arrayed along a more than 5.25 kilometre stretch of a 7km-long northwest-southeast anomalous gold trend. Dalaroo Metals has completed initial drill pads and access routes ahead of its first drilling campaign at the Bondoukou Gold Ridge project in Côte d’Ivoire. The move comes as the West African nation continues to attract exploration capital, with investors favouring the region’s near-surface, structural gold systems in underexplored belts. Côte d’Ivoire has cemented its reputation as one of Africa’s most active gold jurisdictions, with a pipeline of discoveries ensuring new drill programs remain on the market’s radar. The numbers are hard to ignore. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence’s World Exploration Trends’ 2026 report, Côte d’Ivoire attracted $186 million in mineral exploration investment in 2025, the single largest increase anywhere on the African continent. That figure is up from $102 million in 2024, an 82 per cent hike in a single year.



‘The success of our recent capital raising has allowed us to expand Phase 1 from 10,000 metres to 12,000 metres.’ Dalaroo Metals chief executive officer John Morgan Dalaroo’s campaign is designed as a phased, geology-led strategy to unlock the potential of the Bondoukou project in the demonstrably prospective Birimian Greenstone Belt which extends across five West African nations. The company’s exploration work to date has included soil sampling which uncovered a compelling result of 23.26 grams per tonne (g/t) gold along the 7-kilometre-long gold corridor. The 12,000m Phase 1 program, poised to swing into action within a week, will be the opening stage of a more extensive 20,000m drilling strategy, with initial work to consist of 24 orientation holes for 4200m, averaging 175m deep. The company will use a “scissor-drilling” approach which uses opposing angles to cross-examine the target zone from two directions. This strategy mitigates the risk of drilling parallel to the geology, which can distort results. By cutting across the structure from both sides, Dalaroo can more accurately determine the true width, orientation, and continuity of the mineralisation, delivering a markedly more reliable geological model. Dalaroo Metals chief executive officer John Morgan said: “Completion of the initial drill pads and access routes is a significant milestone for Dalaroo, positioning the Company to commence its maiden drilling campaign at Gold Ridge. This will be the first time the extensive surface gold anomalies at Mag, Wilfred and Ali are directly tested at depth, representing an important step in determining the discovery potential of the broader Gold Ridge corridor.”



Based on geological observations from the initial holes, Dalaroo plans to launch into a 78-hole follow-up fence drilling program for a further 7800m. In total, the phase one campaign is expected to comprise 102 holes across eleven drill fences. The program is designed to be flexible, allowing holes to be relocated, extended or reoriented as the geological picture becomes clearer. Drilling is slated to begin no later than August 15, with initial assay results expected roughly four to six weeks after the first samples are delivered to the Intertek laboratory. The company plans to deliver samples progressively, on a weekly basis, to ensure a consistent flow of results. The campaign will be the first time the extensive surface gold anomalies at the company’s Mag, Wilfred and Ali targets are tested at depth. Dalaroo is aiming to establish the orientation and geometry of the mineralisation before designing subsequent phases of drilling. The program will integrate data from previous soil and auger geochemistry, geological mapping, magnetic interpretation and the distribution of artisanal workings. Geological logging, structural observations and assay results from the RC drilling will be fed into an evolving 3D geological model to guide future work. With the program fully funded and the drill rigs about to mobilise, Dalaroo appears to be on the cusp of a defining period of exploration. As the rods start to turn in one of West Africa’s premier gold belts, all eyes will be on the assay results to see if the high-grade surface anomalies translate into a significant discovery at depth. World.title: ‘Difficult to reconcile’: The Australian council moving to ban data centres
World.content:
NationalWAData centres ‘Difficult to reconcile’: The Australian council moving to ban data centres Indigo Lemay-Conway August 10, 2026 — 2:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Perth’s biggest metropolitan council could soon be among the first in the nation to ban data centres in a bid to preserve its residential amenity. The City of Stirling – Perth’s most populous local government area – will consider a notice of motion from councillor Suzanne Migdale on Tuesday night, urging the council to look into amending a local planning policy and reclassify data centres as being “a prohibited use”. The City of Stirling could be the first local council in Australia to ban data centres. iStock It could make Stirling the first local government in the country to take a hard stance against the data centre boom. Migdale said the motion would benefit both the community and environment.



“The council should consider data centres as an ‘X’ use under LPS4 because they can create impacts that are difficult to reconcile with residential amenity, local environmental management, and sustainable planning outcomes,” she said in the report to council. “Data centres are widely identified as energy-intensive facilities with significant environmental footprints, including large electricity demand, water use, and backup generator emissions.” Stirling councillor’s reasons why data centres should not be allowed in the city Data centres require substantial electricity, and their power demand can increase indirect greenhouse gas emissions where the grid is fossil-fuel dependent.

Many data centres use large volumes of water for cooling, which can place pressure on local water supplies.

Cooling systems, fans, and backup diesel generators can create continuous or intermittent noise that affects nearby residents and businesses.

Back-up generators and associated energy production can contribute to air pollutant emissions, including particulates and other combustion by-products.

Security lighting and 24/7 operational requirements can add to light spill and reduce local amenity.

Data centres can generate substantial waste heat and create an industrial character that is often incompatible with surrounding uses.

Large facilities may increase demands on local roads, utilities, and power infrastructure, with costs and disruptions potentially falling on the community.

Research has linked large data centres to community concerns around air quality, noise, water stress, and broader public health impacts. If approved, Tuesday’s notice of motion would see the council request its chief executive to prepare a report for council’s consideration before an official vote would be made. Stirling is a sprawling local government area that is largely residential, however it does include the industrial and business precinct of Osborne Park, which is home to the headquarters of WA iron ore miner Mineral Resources.



Data centres have been a contentious issue across WA this year. Related Article AI Mike Cannon-Brookes’ fortune jumps $2.6 billion in just hours In May, residents in the neighbouring City of Swan claimed victory after plans for a controversial data centre neighbouring the Helena River were withdrawn following significant community pushback. Sydney-based data company GreenSquareDC applied to build the $600 million, three-storey facility next to the Helena River Waldorf School, on two Aboriginal heritage sites and approximately 40 metres from the Helena River channel. Public outcry against the proposal planned for lots 14 and 15 on Stirling Crescent was aired at several Swan council meetings, with concerns around environmental impacts, noise pollution and cultural insensitivity.



The city received a total of 1890 submissions regarding the proposal, with 1829 opposing the project. In the end the company formally withdrew its application. Related Article AI Rogue AI fakes identities, switches languages to trick humans There are currently 15 data centres across WA, 13 of which are in the Perth metropolitan area. In July, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed plans for legislation around the expectations for large AI data centres, which would be introduced to parliament early next year. “Our Australian standards will also set clear rules for large data centres: where they are built – and the power and water they use,” he said during a speech at the University of Sydney.



“We have a continent to ourselves, one of our big advantages. We have more than enough room for new data centres, without them competing with new housing. And we will work with every level of government to see common sense prevail.” Albanese said the government would also create a legal obligation for the next generation of large-scale data centres to underwrite new power supply. “To pay their full share of grid connection, so no costs are passed on to homes or businesses. And to put at least as much energy into our grid as they take out of it,” he said. Other councils across the country have also faced issues with new data centre builds. In NSW, councils including Penrith in Sydney’s west and Ryde – where the Macquarie Park cluster of data centres live – called on the government to hit pause on approvals of new data centres as part of a parliamentary inquiry into the impact they have on communities.



The councils requested the government freeze approvals until it sets rules to guarantee their power and water usage will have no effect on local communities. Related Article Data centres ‘Significant win’: Helena Valley residents cheer power-down of $600m data centre plans Meanwhile, Melbourne’s current data centre power draw could double if plans for a $1.1 billion campus on the former Ford car factory site get the state government’s go-ahead. The Campbellfield proposal by developer Zerra DC has raised concerns with the community about noise, pollution and fuel storage. Plans submitted directly to Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny under special state planning provisions for big projects would mean that residents wouldn’t be eligible to oppose the development at a state administrative tribunal.



The “Project Dune” proposal would consume 336 megawatts of power once fully operational across six stages, matching the cumulative energy of the 55 data centres currently operating in Melbourne. City of Stirling councillors will vote on the notice of motion at the ordinary council meeting on Tuesday night.

World.title: Kaiser digs deep at historic Victorian Maldon goldfield in Victoria
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Kaiser digs deep at historic Victorian Maldon goldfield in Victoria Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 10, 2026 — 2:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Profitable gold producer Kaiser Reef has fired up the underground developmentat its historic Maldon gold project in Victoria, taking the first cut of a new drill drive in what marks the first development on-site in nearly eight years. The work at the project’s Union Hill gold mine will establish a new underground platform to allow for drill testing of several highly prospective, underexplored reef systems. The company says it has already been stripping some narrow sections at the top of the decline with a view to future ore haulage. Kaiser Reef’s jumbo drill rig breaking new ground at the Union Hill gold mine within the Maldon gold project in Victoria. The new Northern drill drive is designed to give Kaiser its first proper look at the territory north of Maldon’s existing workings. The company is aiming its drill rigs at the interpreted extensions of the Eaglehawk and Linscott’s Reefs, in addition to the parallel Ladies and Sailor’s Reefs. Kaiser Reef is already sitting on a 187,000-ounce gold resource at its Union Hill deposit within the project and operates its own 200,000 tonne per annum processing facility at the Porcupine Flat plant nearby. This latest underground development at Maldon represents a significant milestone for the company as it looks to breathe new life into one of the Victorian Golden Triangle’s richest historical goldfields, which churned out 1.75 million ounces of gold at an outstanding average grade of 28 grams per tonne.



‘It’s a milestone for both the Maldon gold project and Kaiser to have jumbo development underway beneath Union Hill.’ Kaiser Reef managing director Brad Valiukas Kaiser Reef managing director Brad Valiukas said: “Maldon represents a district-scale gold opportunity for Kaiser, with numerous historical mines and lines of working that remain substantially underexplored, despite having produced an enviable 1.75Moz at 28g/t. Crucially, Maldon offers more than just historical pedigree and exploration upside. It is supported by a fully permitted and operating processing plant, a fully permitted mining lease and an existing decline that will allow both access for exploration and potential future production.” While the company has been active with a surface drilling campaign that began in June, with 4350 metres to test its Quill target, and refurbishment works to prepare for underground activities, this latest move marks the first time new ground has been broken in the Maldon underground in the better part of a decade. Kaiser is a multi-asset producer, also operating its flagship Henty gold mine in Tasmania. During the recent June quarter, Henty produced 5563 ounces of gold, while Maldon contributed a more modest 437 ounces. The company has reaffirmed its production guidance of a total of 32,000 ounces across both operations for the 2027 financial year. Featuring a healthy cash balance of $37.2 million at the end of the quarter, Kaiser Reef looks to be well-funded to pursue its growth ambitions at both operations. The move to aggressively explore Maldon follows a change in leadership late last year, with former Northern Star Resources operational boss Brad Valiukas taking the helm as managing director.Valiukas topped up his holding in the company with on-market purchases of shares just last month.



Maldon sits within the central Victorian goldfields, a region that hosts world-class deposits such as Agnico Eagle’s legendary 4.6-million-ounce Fosterville gold mine and has seen a resurgence of exploration interest from players including Southern Cross Gold and Catalyst Metals. With a fully permitted 200,000-tonne-per-annum processing facility and established underground access already in place, any exploration success at Maldon could potentially be fast-tracked into production. The old-timers pulled an incredible amount of high-grade gold from Maldon using little more than picks, shovels and sheer grit. Now with a healthy war chest, modern exploration smarts and the drill rods about to spin, Kaiser Reef is getting ready to find out just how much they may have left behind. World.title: Teens ‘armed themselves’ before attending party where 21yo died, police say
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandCrime Teens ‘armed themselves’ before attending party where 21yo died, police say William Davis and Cloe Read Updated August 10, 2026 — 2:18pm ,first published August 10, 2026 — 7:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Four teenagers charged over the bashing murder of a 21-year-old man were part of a group who went to an Airbnb house party armed with weapons and a plan to harm people, police allege. Detectives from Queensland’s Organised Crime Gangs Group are now part of the investigation into the death of Jongkuch Achiew, who was found lying severely injured in a suburban street by police after they were called to the out-of-control house party. Achiew died at Princess Alexandra Hospital after succumbing to head injuries he suffered at the gathering at Bahrs Scrub, a suburb in Logan south of Brisbane, in the early hours of Sunday, July 26. Loading Four male teenagers, aged 18 and 19 years old, were arrested and charged on August 6 following investigations by homicide detectives.



On Sunday evening, four more teenagers aged 17 and 18 were arrested and charged with murder. A video game was playing on the TV and gaming controllers lay on the floor, as the teenagers were arrested at a Morayfield house about 5pm. The teenagers reside in Acacia Ridge, Sunnybank, Inala and Doolandella. Speaking on Monday morning, Detective Inspector Ian Galpin said police would allege the group had a plan to harm people and armed themselves with various weapons, before attending the party. “What the police will allege is that this group attended this location with a common purpose of causing harm to people at that address,” he said.



He would not elaborate on the types of weapons allegedly carried by the group. When asked whether the alleged murder was gang-related, Galpin confirmed the Organised Crime Gangs Group had joined the police investigation. However, he said police liaison officers had been working closely with community leaders to address any concerns. Jongkuch Achiew, 21, died in hospital less than a week after he was found with significant head injuries on a suburban Logan street. Nine “Together they have done an amazing job at addressing any suggestion or tension within the community,” Galpin said.



“I can tell you that everyone that we have spoken to, they want nothing but peace within their community and that’s why I’m confident there won’t be any further retaliation.” Three 18-year-old men charged on Sunday – Morad George, Jason Marik, and Benito Bikanye – had their charges briefly mentioned in Brisbane Magistrates Court on Monday. Their cases were adjourned to August 24. The case of the 17-year-old boy, who cannot be named under Queensland law, was heard in the Childrens Court. Police were called to reports of an out-of-control party at an Airbnb property in Bahrs Scrub, Logan, just after 2am on July 26. Nine News Police have carried out 14 search warrants across Logan, South Brisbane, and Ipswich as part of the murder investigation. Galpin said it was possible more charges could be laid.



When asked about Achiew’s family, Galpin said it had been a very emotional and difficult time for them. A message attributed to Achiew’s family, and posted to a social media group representing members of the Biong community from South Sudan, thanked police and other first responders for their efforts. “This is a life cut far too short, and a loss felt profoundly by all who knew and loved him,” it said. Loading Police were called to the house party on Discovery Boulevard just after 2am following reports of a large disturbance.



They found significant damage at a house and vehicles along the street. People allegedly fled the scene as soon as officers arrived, and Achiew was found with significant head injuries on a nearby street. He was rushed to Princess Alexandra Hospital in a critical condition but died after his life support was switched off six days later. A 22-year-old Heathwood man has also been charged with one count of contravening an order about information necessary to access information stored electronically. World.title: Penrith can still win the title without Yeo. Could your team survive loss of its best player?
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion Penrith can still win the title without Yeo. Could your team survive loss of its best player? Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist August 10, 2026 — 3:30pm

August 10, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The chance of Isaah Yeo’s pectoral injury ending his season has raised the question of whether Penrith can win the NRL premiership without him. Yeo is line-ball with Nathan Cleary as the Panthers’ indispensable player. What single player’s absence would cancel out the other contenders’ title hopes? Cronulla have won games without Nicho Hynes or Braydon Trindall, but I doubt they could reach the grand final without Blayke Brailey, their quicksilver version of Harry Grant. Newcastle can survive without Dylan Brown but not, obviously, without Kalyn Ponga. The destructive new star Francis Manuleleua is also critical to the Knights’ chances. Loading The Dolphins slumped while Isaiya Katoa was injured and are now roaring back with their recovered playmaker. The Warriors and Roosters, the most likely grand finalists if Penrith miss out, are the least reliant on one player. Still, I can’t see the Roosters winning if they lost Naufahu Whyte. (See how Sam Walker or James Tedesco perform without Whyte’s go-forward.) Victor Radley, who straightens their attack at first receiver, is probably their other indispensable player.



The Wahs have no single linchpin. James Fisher-Harris is still the best prop in the game, but they have such a good pack they could make up for his absence. Maybe Wayde Egan, whose vision at dummy-half sets up those dominant forwards, is indispensable. While the semi-finalists have an even spread of talent, a few of the sides who will be in Bali in September belong to the one-man team league. Related Article NRL 2026 Yeo shock: Panthers hope skipper can return for premiership tilt Bronze medal or fool’s gold? In case you missed it, three weeks ago, England and France were dragged out of their post-semi-final misery to go through the motions of a “bronze medal playoff” in the FIFA World Cup. The Guardian’s Jonathan Liew, calling it “the match nobody wants to play”, was voicing the thoughts of several billion fans. Reflecting the emptiness of the fixture, the coaches put out second-string teams, each making seven changes. France, playing like they didn’t care, let in four goals in the first half. England, playing like they didn’t care, scored six by full-time. Ten goals were scored, and by the end even fewer people cared than at the beginning.



Clearly someone at the NRL did miss it, because they have floated the idea. Imagine the anticipation: two teams of reserve-graders competing for nothing, not even a NSW Cup. Approximately 20 tries scored if they can hang onto the ball, which they won’t. All in the name of “content” but making no-one content, or even half-content. Today’s NRL is good at throwing meaningless chum in the water to stir up news. Let’s just hope this is another example. In the history of dumb ideas, this one gets a bronze medal. Scott stance beggars belief Over in the AFL, there was an extraordinary press conference on Saturday when Geelong coach Chris Scott was asked about the club’s unlawful secret contract with player Jake Kolodjashnij waiving any future claim for the effects of head injuries. It’s about as lawful and ethical as an actor signing on for a snuff movie. Geelong did it in secret, and are now being rightly condemned. Cats coach Chris Scott says he had no involvement or knowledge of the waiver the club signed with Jake Kolodjashnij. Getty Images If that was reprehensible, the reaction of Scott, a two-time premiership coach, was bizarre. Not only did he say he hadn’t known about the contract, but he didn’t want to know, and held this up as a model of governance.



“It’s not 1980. The coach doesn’t run everything these days,” Scott said. “This is deliberate that I’m kept at arm’s length from these things … I don’t want to know too much ... I’m one of the least-informed people … It’s not part of my remit ... I could demand that I be involved in it, but I don’t want to be. It’s not the way our football club or any good football club operates.” Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘It’s not 1980 – the coach doesn’t run everything these days’: Scott speaks on concussion scandal Eh? Was this Sergeant “I Know Nothing! No-thing!!” Schultz? The head coach thinks it’s modern governance for him to not know about unlawful agreements between his players and the club. Even if you believe Scott, it is exactly the type of willed ignorance that has characterised drug scandals in football. These are the same coaches who are always telling us that they care for their players not just as footballers but as human beings. It beggars belief. Over to you, rugby league. Has any club signed a contract with a player who waives future claims for brain injuries? Are head coaches kept in the dark so they can maintain plausible deniability? It is critical for the NRL to clarify this. I trust it has begun its investigation.



Cowboys-Titans shirt show Indigenous Round brings many good feelings (notably how far the NRL has outpaced the AFL in Indigenous inclusion). A highlight was the smoking ceremony before the Dragons-Sharks match; what were those Dragons inhaling? But the lowlight was the jerseys in the Cowboys-Titans game on Thursday. Nothing against the jerseys themselves, but why were the Titans in Cowboys dark-blue and the Cowboys in Titans teal? The panel designs were quite similar, so the only way to tell them apart was the colours – which were the wrong way around. Both teams play in next week’s second part of the Indigenous Round, so they could have worn the jerseys then. Jason Taumalolo celebrates a try against the Titans. Getty Images The head-scratcher is that there had to be a meeting, somewhere, before Thursday’s game, in which someone decided that yes, it was OK to have each team play in the other’s colours. In the end, the only memorable thing about the game was 80 minutes of total bewilderment; the Titans appeared to win 30-8 and the Cowboys to suffer a second straight heavy defeat; but that was just an optical illusion. World.title: Why Australia’s megaproject boom may deepen the housing crisis
World.content:
NationalPlanning Opinion Why Australia’s megaproject boom may deepen the housing crisis Ehsan Noroozinejad Senior researcher August 10, 2026 — 3:30pm

August 10, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia has a building plan for almost everything. We need 1.2 million new homes, new electricity transmission lines, rail and road upgrades, hospitals, schools, and the venues and transport needed for the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Each ambition can be defended. Together, however, they expose a basic problem: Australia keeps announcing projects as if everyone will have their own private supply of engineers, tradies, contractors, machinery and materials. They won’t. The five-year pipeline of major public projects in Australia has reached a record $242 billion. Infrastructure Australia says the five-year pipeline of major public projects has reached a record $242 billion. It estimates the infrastructure workforce is already short about 141,000 people and that the gap could exceed 300,000 by mid-2027. If the federal government decides to cut the immigration program, as is mooted, that figure will be even worse. At the same time, the home-building task is slipping away. The National Housing Accord requires an average of 60,000 completed homes every quarter. The latest Australian Bureau of Statistics figures show just 43,816 were completed in the March quarter. The National Housing Supply and Affordability Council expects about 980,000 homes over the accord’s five years under its early-2026 outlook, 220,000 below the target.



We often discuss the housing shortage as a problem of planning approvals, land or finance. All matter. But Australia also has a capacity problem. Homes and megaprojects are not built in separate economies. They draw, to varying degrees, on the same project managers, engineers, surveyors, electricians, plant operators and labourers. They need concrete, steel, timber, cranes, trucks and earth-moving equipment. The overlap is not perfect – a tunnel engineer cannot simply become a house framer – but neither is it imaginary. The infrastructure workforce is already short about 141,000 people and that the gap could exceed 300,000 by mid-2027. Infrastructure Australia’s report notes limited evidence that infrastructure work is currently pulling labour directly from residential construction, and further research is under way. That uncertainty is precisely why governments should measure the effect before committing billions of dollars, not discover it later through higher tender prices and delayed homes. The pressure will not be evenly spread. The energy transition is taking construction deep into regional Australia. Infrastructure Australia forecasts the regional infrastructure workforce gap could grow from about 38,000 jobs in late 2025 to 181,000 in 2027, largely because of energy and utilities projects.



These projects are essential. Yet when a large temporary workforce arrives in a town with few vacant rentals, the pressure does not stop at the project fence. Workers compete for rooms and homes with nurses, teachers, families and people already struggling with rent. Without planned accommodation, a project that strengthens the electricity grid can weaken the community expected to host it. The same collision is emerging in Queensland. Infrastructure Australia warned last October that the state would need almost 98,500 construction workers by March 2026 to deliver its infrastructure pipeline, against a forecast supply of only 43,800, as Olympic construction prepared to accelerate. Queensland still needs homes, hospitals and ordinary transport upgrades. A fixed Games deadline makes sequencing even more important. An artist’s impression of the planned Brisbane Stadium for the 2032 Olympics. More construction workers are needed to meet demands for Games infrastructure. Queensland government The answer is not to stop building infrastructure. Transport and energy networks are often what make new housing possible. The answer is to stop pretending every project can be delivered at once without consequences. Every major publicly funded project should therefore include a housing delivery impact statement. Just as governments examine environmental, financial and traffic effects, they should publish how a project may affect housing construction and nearby rental markets.



Project business cases may consider market capacity, but the public rarely sees a simple account of what a new project means for the government’s housing promise. Nor is there a consistent national method for tracing the effect from a project timetable to local building costs and rents. This should not become another 500-page report. It should be a clear, standard assessment showing the workers and materials required, when and where they will be needed, likely effects on construction prices, pressure on rentals and any expected delay to public or private housing programs. Most importantly, it should examine the combined impact of all projects in the region, not assess each one in isolation. Homes and megaprojects are not built in separate economies. They draw, to varying degrees, on the same project managers, engineers, surveyors, electricians, plant operators and labourers. The statement should also set out practical responses. Governments could shift tender dates to avoid the same peak, coordinate purchasing across agencies, fund apprenticeships before construction begins and use more locally manufactured and prefabricated components. Temporary modular worker accommodation could be designed for later conversion into key-worker, social or community housing. Major contracts could also require real training and local-supplier commitments, so public spending expands capacity instead of merely bidding up its price.



Related Article Opinion

Housing crisis To fix housing, we must try something radical. Here are three ideas to shift the dial Tone Wheeler Australian Architecture Association president None of this is anti-development. It is what serious development policy looks like. Australia’s housing, energy and transport goals are not separate promises. They are one national construction program sharing a limited pool of people, materials and time. A megaproject should not proceed on the fiction that these resources will appear from nowhere. Before governments celebrate the next big announcement, they should answer one simple question: will this project help Australia build more, or make the homes we urgently need even harder to deliver? Dr Ehsan Noroozinejad is an associate professor at Western Sydney University, coordinator of the NSW Affordable Housing Network and secretary of the WSROC Housing Taskforce. World.title: ‘Unacceptable’ Sydney airport reliability expected for weeks at least
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesAviation ‘Unacceptable’ Sydney airport reliability expected for weeks at least Chris Zappone and Matt O'Sullivan Updated August 10, 2026 — 3:27pm ,first published August 10, 2026 — 9:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two airport workers have been stood down and the chief of Australia’s air traffic control agency has been warned that delays at Sydney Airport have become “unacceptable” as investigators probe the second near-collision between planes on the tarmac in the past two weeks. But passengers, who have had to deal with the delays caused by a shortage of air traffic controllers, will have to wait weeks before a new roster comes into effect in September that Airservices Australia hopes will improve reliability. A Jetstar plane and a Qatar Airways plane on the runway at Sydney Airport on Sunday morning. Nine News An air traffic controller and a ground worker involved in an incident on Sunday have been stood down under their employers’ policies while authorities determine how a Jetstar plane got within metres of striking a Qatar jet. The stand downs, which are common after an incident, come as Transport Minister Catherine King criticised the delays and disruptions after meeting with Airservices Australia CEO Rob Sharp.



“The delays and disruptions we have seen at Sydney Airport over the last three days have been unacceptable and have caused significant disruption to passengers, staff and airlines,” King said. Related Article Aviation Dozens of flights out of Sydney delayed up to 80 minutes Airservices committed to implementing “improved rostering practices” for Sydney’s air traffic controllers that will be in place from early September, King said. “I have made my expectations clear that Airservices must carefully manage the situation at Sydney for the rest of August,” she said. Airservices’ Sharp apologised for the impact “on flight delays” and the impact it has on people’s travel plans.



“I want to assure the public that safety is not compromised when issues with staffing levels occur,” he said, who noted the safety measures can lead to flight delays. The Sunday near miss came just weeks after a similar incident in which planes had been given contradictory instructions by controllers at Sydney Airport. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau is now investigating. Its chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said the incident occurred at low speed but still had the potential to be “very significant”. “Those two aircraft should not have come as close as they did,” he said on Seven’s Sunrise. He would not prejudge his organisation’s investigation, but flagged that the traffic control system had been under significant stress. Airservices has repeatedly reduced flight frequencies at Sydney Airport over the past week due to shortages of air-traffic controllers, leading to major delays. Adding to the difficulty, it can take about 18 months to train a new controller to manage a specific piece of airspace or part of the airport. Airservices has been dogged by capacity since a mass retirement of controllers in 2021 as COVID shut down the aviation sector. Additionally, questions have lingered about the work culture.



Aviation safety specialist Geoff Dell said a shortage of air-traffic controllers risked reducing “redundancy” in the system to deal with incidents. Loading “The reality is that if they are short people, it puts stress on the service, and it puts stress on the individuals,” said Dell, a former airport operations safety manager for Qantas. “If you have a lot of aircraft on the ground because of delays, it becomes a chessboard trying to shuffle them around so you don’t have them conflicting where one aircraft is closer than it should be.” Sydney Airport has about 70 aircraft coming and going every hour during morning and evening peak periods, putting it near the cap of 80 an hour. A further five movements are permitted to help the airport recover from cascading delays caused by bad weather or other disruptions.



NSW Premier Chris Minns expressed concern that the major disruptions at the airport could potentially affect Sydney’s reputation as a global city. Related Article Exclusive

Aviation VietJet to offer international flights from Western Sydney “The onus is on everybody associated with the airport to get it done [to resolve the situation] ASAP,” he said. The airlines’ peak body said it had repeatedly raised the performance issues with Airservices. “Airservices Australia management needs to provide greater transparency about the causes of these ongoing disruptions and, importantly, set out a credible plan to immediately resolve them,” Airlines for Australia and New Zealand CEO Stephen Beckett.



“These operational disruptions are now occurring multiple times a week.” Australian Travel Industry Association chief executive Dean Long said the number of delays caused by Airservices had jumped compared with before the COVID pandemic. Long said that the rest of the travel sector had restored performance since the pandemic but “Airservices, for whatever reason, does seem to be really struggling to get their performance where it needs to be”. World.title: Dalaroo set for first drilling of three key Côte d’Ivoire gold targets
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Dalaroo set for first drilling of three key Côte d’Ivoire gold targets Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright August 10, 2026 — 3:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dalaroo Metals has cleared the final hurdles in its preparation to kick-start a major maiden drilling campaign at its Bondoukou Gold Ridge project in Côte d’Ivoire, with all drill pads and access routes now complete. Following a recent 2.5 million capital raise, the company has expanded the planned reverse circulation, or “RC”, drilling program to 12,000 metres from 10,000m, allowing for a more systematic test of three priority gold targets dubbed Mag, Wilfred and Ali. The three targets are evenly arrayed along a more than 5.25 kilometre stretch of a 7km-long northwest-southeast anomalous gold trend. Dalaroo Metals has completed initial drill pads and access routes ahead of its first drilling campaign at the Bondoukou Gold Ridge project in Côte d’Ivoire. The move comes as the West African nation continues to attract exploration capital, with investors favouring the region’s near-surface, structural gold systems in underexplored belts. Côte d’Ivoire has cemented its reputation as one of Africa’s most active gold jurisdictions, with a pipeline of discoveries ensuring new drill programs remain on the market’s radar. The numbers are hard to ignore. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence’s World Exploration Trends’ 2026 report, Côte d’Ivoire attracted $186 million in mineral exploration investment in 2025, the single largest increase anywhere on the African continent. That figure is up from $102 million in 2024, an 82 per cent hike in a single year.



‘The success of our recent capital raising has allowed us to expand Phase 1 from 10,000 metres to 12,000 metres.’ Dalaroo Metals chief executive officer John Morgan Dalaroo’s campaign is designed as a phased, geology-led strategy to unlock the potential of the Bondoukou project in the demonstrably prospective Birimian Greenstone Belt which extends across five West African nations. The company’s exploration work to date has included soil sampling which uncovered a compelling result of 23.26 grams per tonne (g/t) gold along the 7-kilometre-long gold corridor. The 12,000m Phase 1 program, poised to swing into action within a week, will be the opening stage of a more extensive 20,000m drilling strategy, with initial work to consist of 24 orientation holes for 4200m, averaging 175m deep. The company will use a “scissor-drilling” approach which uses opposing angles to cross-examine the target zone from two directions. This strategy mitigates the risk of drilling parallel to the geology, which can distort results. By cutting across the structure from both sides, Dalaroo can more accurately determine the true width, orientation, and continuity of the mineralisation, delivering a markedly more reliable geological model. Dalaroo Metals chief executive officer John Morgan said: “Completion of the initial drill pads and access routes is a significant milestone for Dalaroo, positioning the Company to commence its maiden drilling campaign at Gold Ridge. This will be the first time the extensive surface gold anomalies at Mag, Wilfred and Ali are directly tested at depth, representing an important step in determining the discovery potential of the broader Gold Ridge corridor.”



Based on geological observations from the initial holes, Dalaroo plans to launch into a 78-hole follow-up fence drilling program for a further 7800m. In total, the phase one campaign is expected to comprise 102 holes across eleven drill fences. The program is designed to be flexible, allowing holes to be relocated, extended or reoriented as the geological picture becomes clearer. Drilling is slated to begin no later than August 15, with initial assay results expected roughly four to six weeks after the first samples are delivered to the Intertek laboratory. The company plans to deliver samples progressively, on a weekly basis, to ensure a consistent flow of results. The campaign will be the first time the extensive surface gold anomalies at the company’s Mag, Wilfred and Ali targets are tested at depth. Dalaroo is aiming to establish the orientation and geometry of the mineralisation before designing subsequent phases of drilling. The program will integrate data from previous soil and auger geochemistry, geological mapping, magnetic interpretation and the distribution of artisanal workings. Geological logging, structural observations and assay results from the RC drilling will be fed into an evolving 3D geological model to guide future work. With the program fully funded and the drill rigs about to mobilise, Dalaroo appears to be on the cusp of a defining period of exploration. As the rods start to turn in one of West Africa’s premier gold belts, all eyes will be on the assay results to see if the high-grade surface anomalies translate into a significant discovery at depth. World.title: ‘Difficult to reconcile’: The Australian council moving to ban data centres
World.content:
NationalWAData centres ‘Difficult to reconcile’: The Australian council moving to ban data centres Indigo Lemay-Conway August 10, 2026 — 2:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Perth’s biggest metropolitan council could soon be among the first in the nation to ban data centres in a bid to preserve its residential amenity. The City of Stirling – Perth’s most populous local government area – will consider a notice of motion from councillor Suzanne Migdale on Tuesday night, urging the council to look into amending a local planning policy and reclassify data centres as being “a prohibited use”. The City of Stirling could be the first local council in Australia to ban data centres. iStock It could make Stirling the first local government in the country to take a hard stance against the data centre boom. Migdale said the motion would benefit both the community and environment.



“The council should consider data centres as an ‘X’ use under LPS4 because they can create impacts that are difficult to reconcile with residential amenity, local environmental management, and sustainable planning outcomes,” she said in the report to council. “Data centres are widely identified as energy-intensive facilities with significant environmental footprints, including large electricity demand, water use, and backup generator emissions.” Stirling councillor’s reasons why data centres should not be allowed in the city Data centres require substantial electricity, and their power demand can increase indirect greenhouse gas emissions where the grid is fossil-fuel dependent.

Many data centres use large volumes of water for cooling, which can place pressure on local water supplies.

Cooling systems, fans, and backup diesel generators can create continuous or intermittent noise that affects nearby residents and businesses.

Back-up generators and associated energy production can contribute to air pollutant emissions, including particulates and other combustion by-products.

Security lighting and 24/7 operational requirements can add to light spill and reduce local amenity.

Data centres can generate substantial waste heat and create an industrial character that is often incompatible with surrounding uses.

Large facilities may increase demands on local roads, utilities, and power infrastructure, with costs and disruptions potentially falling on the community.

Research has linked large data centres to community concerns around air quality, noise, water stress, and broader public health impacts. If approved, Tuesday’s notice of motion would see the council request its chief executive to prepare a report for council’s consideration before an official vote would be made. Stirling is a sprawling local government area that is largely residential, however it does include the industrial and business precinct of Osborne Park, which is home to the headquarters of WA iron ore miner Mineral Resources.



Data centres have been a contentious issue across WA this year. Related Article AI Mike Cannon-Brookes’ fortune jumps $2.6 billion in just hours In May, residents in the neighbouring City of Swan claimed victory after plans for a controversial data centre neighbouring the Helena River were withdrawn following significant community pushback. Sydney-based data company GreenSquareDC applied to build the $600 million, three-storey facility next to the Helena River Waldorf School, on two Aboriginal heritage sites and approximately 40 metres from the Helena River channel. Public outcry against the proposal planned for lots 14 and 15 on Stirling Crescent was aired at several Swan council meetings, with concerns around environmental impacts, noise pollution and cultural insensitivity.



The city received a total of 1890 submissions regarding the proposal, with 1829 opposing the project. In the end the company formally withdrew its application. Related Article AI Rogue AI fakes identities, switches languages to trick humans There are currently 15 data centres across WA, 13 of which are in the Perth metropolitan area. In July, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed plans for legislation around the expectations for large AI data centres, which would be introduced to parliament early next year. “Our Australian standards will also set clear rules for large data centres: where they are built – and the power and water they use,” he said during a speech at the University of Sydney.



“We have a continent to ourselves, one of our big advantages. We have more than enough room for new data centres, without them competing with new housing. And we will work with every level of government to see common sense prevail.” Albanese said the government would also create a legal obligation for the next generation of large-scale data centres to underwrite new power supply. “To pay their full share of grid connection, so no costs are passed on to homes or businesses. And to put at least as much energy into our grid as they take out of it,” he said. Other councils across the country have also faced issues with new data centre builds. In NSW, councils including Penrith in Sydney’s west and Ryde – where the Macquarie Park cluster of data centres live – called on the government to hit pause on approvals of new data centres as part of a parliamentary inquiry into the impact they have on communities.



The councils requested the government freeze approvals until it sets rules to guarantee their power and water usage will have no effect on local communities. Related Article Data centres ‘Significant win’: Helena Valley residents cheer power-down of $600m data centre plans Meanwhile, Melbourne’s current data centre power draw could double if plans for a $1.1 billion campus on the former Ford car factory site get the state government’s go-ahead. The Campbellfield proposal by developer Zerra DC has raised concerns with the community about noise, pollution and fuel storage. Plans submitted directly to Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny under special state planning provisions for big projects would mean that residents wouldn’t be eligible to oppose the development at a state administrative tribunal.



The “Project Dune” proposal would consume 336 megawatts of power once fully operational across six stages, matching the cumulative energy of the 55 data centres currently operating in Melbourne. City of Stirling councillors will vote on the notice of motion at the ordinary council meeting on Tuesday night.

World.title: Kaiser digs deep at historic Victorian Maldon goldfield in Victoria
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Kaiser digs deep at historic Victorian Maldon goldfield in Victoria Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 10, 2026 — 2:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Profitable gold producer Kaiser Reef has fired up the underground developmentat its historic Maldon gold project in Victoria, taking the first cut of a new drill drive in what marks the first development on-site in nearly eight years. The work at the project’s Union Hill gold mine will establish a new underground platform to allow for drill testing of several highly prospective, underexplored reef systems. The company says it has already been stripping some narrow sections at the top of the decline with a view to future ore haulage. Kaiser Reef’s jumbo drill rig breaking new ground at the Union Hill gold mine within the Maldon gold project in Victoria. The new Northern drill drive is designed to give Kaiser its first proper look at the territory north of Maldon’s existing workings. The company is aiming its drill rigs at the interpreted extensions of the Eaglehawk and Linscott’s Reefs, in addition to the parallel Ladies and Sailor’s Reefs. Kaiser Reef is already sitting on a 187,000-ounce gold resource at its Union Hill deposit within the project and operates its own 200,000 tonne per annum processing facility at the Porcupine Flat plant nearby. This latest underground development at Maldon represents a significant milestone for the company as it looks to breathe new life into one of the Victorian Golden Triangle’s richest historical goldfields, which churned out 1.75 million ounces of gold at an outstanding average grade of 28 grams per tonne.



‘It’s a milestone for both the Maldon gold project and Kaiser to have jumbo development underway beneath Union Hill.’ Kaiser Reef managing director Brad Valiukas Kaiser Reef managing director Brad Valiukas said: “Maldon represents a district-scale gold opportunity for Kaiser, with numerous historical mines and lines of working that remain substantially underexplored, despite having produced an enviable 1.75Moz at 28g/t. Crucially, Maldon offers more than just historical pedigree and exploration upside. It is supported by a fully permitted and operating processing plant, a fully permitted mining lease and an existing decline that will allow both access for exploration and potential future production.” While the company has been active with a surface drilling campaign that began in June, with 4350 metres to test its Quill target, and refurbishment works to prepare for underground activities, this latest move marks the first time new ground has been broken in the Maldon underground in the better part of a decade. Kaiser is a multi-asset producer, also operating its flagship Henty gold mine in Tasmania. During the recent June quarter, Henty produced 5563 ounces of gold, while Maldon contributed a more modest 437 ounces. The company has reaffirmed its production guidance of a total of 32,000 ounces across both operations for the 2027 financial year. Featuring a healthy cash balance of $37.2 million at the end of the quarter, Kaiser Reef looks to be well-funded to pursue its growth ambitions at both operations. The move to aggressively explore Maldon follows a change in leadership late last year, with former Northern Star Resources operational boss Brad Valiukas taking the helm as managing director.Valiukas topped up his holding in the company with on-market purchases of shares just last month.



Maldon sits within the central Victorian goldfields, a region that hosts world-class deposits such as Agnico Eagle’s legendary 4.6-million-ounce Fosterville gold mine and has seen a resurgence of exploration interest from players including Southern Cross Gold and Catalyst Metals. With a fully permitted 200,000-tonne-per-annum processing facility and established underground access already in place, any exploration success at Maldon could potentially be fast-tracked into production. The old-timers pulled an incredible amount of high-grade gold from Maldon using little more than picks, shovels and sheer grit. Now with a healthy war chest, modern exploration smarts and the drill rods about to spin, Kaiser Reef is getting ready to find out just how much they may have left behind. World.title: Teens ‘armed themselves’ before attending party where 21yo died, police say
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandCrime Teens ‘armed themselves’ before attending party where 21yo died, police say William Davis and Cloe Read Updated August 10, 2026 — 2:18pm ,first published August 10, 2026 — 7:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Four teenagers charged over the bashing murder of a 21-year-old man were part of a group who went to an Airbnb house party armed with weapons and a plan to harm people, police allege. Detectives from Queensland’s Organised Crime Gangs Group are now part of the investigation into the death of Jongkuch Achiew, who was found lying severely injured in a suburban street by police after they were called to the out-of-control house party. Achiew died at Princess Alexandra Hospital after succumbing to head injuries he suffered at the gathering at Bahrs Scrub, a suburb in Logan south of Brisbane, in the early hours of Sunday, July 26. Loading Four male teenagers, aged 18 and 19 years old, were arrested and charged on August 6 following investigations by homicide detectives.



On Sunday evening, four more teenagers aged 17 and 18 were arrested and charged with murder. A video game was playing on the TV and gaming controllers lay on the floor, as the teenagers were arrested at a Morayfield house about 5pm. The teenagers reside in Acacia Ridge, Sunnybank, Inala and Doolandella. Speaking on Monday morning, Detective Inspector Ian Galpin said police would allege the group had a plan to harm people and armed themselves with various weapons, before attending the party. “What the police will allege is that this group attended this location with a common purpose of causing harm to people at that address,” he said.



He would not elaborate on the types of weapons allegedly carried by the group. When asked whether the alleged murder was gang-related, Galpin confirmed the Organised Crime Gangs Group had joined the police investigation. However, he said police liaison officers had been working closely with community leaders to address any concerns. Jongkuch Achiew, 21, died in hospital less than a week after he was found with significant head injuries on a suburban Logan street. Nine “Together they have done an amazing job at addressing any suggestion or tension within the community,” Galpin said.



“I can tell you that everyone that we have spoken to, they want nothing but peace within their community and that’s why I’m confident there won’t be any further retaliation.” Three 18-year-old men charged on Sunday – Morad George, Jason Marik, and Benito Bikanye – had their charges briefly mentioned in Brisbane Magistrates Court on Monday. Their cases were adjourned to August 24. The case of the 17-year-old boy, who cannot be named under Queensland law, was heard in the Childrens Court. Police were called to reports of an out-of-control party at an Airbnb property in Bahrs Scrub, Logan, just after 2am on July 26. Nine News Police have carried out 14 search warrants across Logan, South Brisbane, and Ipswich as part of the murder investigation. Galpin said it was possible more charges could be laid.



When asked about Achiew’s family, Galpin said it had been a very emotional and difficult time for them. A message attributed to Achiew’s family, and posted to a social media group representing members of the Biong community from South Sudan, thanked police and other first responders for their efforts. “This is a life cut far too short, and a loss felt profoundly by all who knew and loved him,” it said. Loading Police were called to the house party on Discovery Boulevard just after 2am following reports of a large disturbance.



They found significant damage at a house and vehicles along the street. People allegedly fled the scene as soon as officers arrived, and Achiew was found with significant head injuries on a nearby street. He was rushed to Princess Alexandra Hospital in a critical condition but died after his life support was switched off six days later. A 22-year-old Heathwood man has also been charged with one count of contravening an order about information necessary to access information stored electronically.
