World.title: Ohakune businesses hurting as water restoration still another 24 hours away
World.content:
Ohakune without tap water for at least another day Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Ohakune water supply expected to return to normal on Tuesday evening, a day later than hoped

Schools and eateries closed on Monday, and one motel reported losing a substantial booking

District councillor labels outage an embarrassment

Mayor says they'll be an investigation.

Ohakune will be without tap water until Tuesday evening, after the district council confirmed the outage affecting the central North Island town would last longer than first feared.

It was originally expected the supply would resume as normal on Monday evening, but a fix had proven more complicated than expected.

This meant eateries and schools would spend another day with their doors closed.

One motel manager told RNZ, the outage was hitting businesses in the pocket.

"[The] council had earlier been confident that water would be restored by 5pm today," Ruapehu District Council chief executive Clive Manley said in a statement on Monday afternoon.

One of many businesses closed in Ohakune on Monday. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

"However, further technical analysis found that repressurising the raw water pipeline too quickly could damage it and cause even longer delays."

He said resuming full flow through the pipeline into town too quickly could risk fracturing it, so a slower, more controlled approach was needed.

"[The] council's water services contractor, Veolia, has confirmed that the airlock affecting the raw water pipeline has been resolved.

"Additional water tankers have also been brought in to help speed up the process as much as safely possible."

Eatery doors stay shut, motel out of pocket

Ohakune town. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

On the streets on Monday portaloos replaced paying patrons, and a water tank parked outside the council office for people to get their supplies. It's estimated more than 5500 water containers were brought to the town for its 1400 residents.

At The Peaks Motor Inn, manager Remi Butler was hauling water around the rooms on Monday morning.

"We've been bucketing water from the cold spa for flushing the toilets, but we got bottled water from the council for washing the dishes," she said.

"We need to do that. We can't use the spa water for cleaning the dishes."

She's hoping the water supply would return as expected, especially as the outage had cost the business.

"The holiday makers from the weekend have left, which is normal, but we actually had a big group that was supposed to come tonight - a full house, for two nights, but they cancelled.

"I don't think insurance will cover anything like that. We'll just have to wear it. It's a big loss, but what can you do?"

At the water tank Angelina Reyes was filling up three five-litre containers for use in the kitchen at her work, the Alpine Motel.

Angelina Reyes filled up water bottles from the council-supplied tank in Ohakune. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

There, she first heard there was a problem with the water on Friday, when warnings to conserve were issued.

"I thought maybe it was a normal glitch but, no, it's for real.

"Yesterday, I had guests in my Airbnb and they said, 'We don't have water.' I had a look on the council Facebook page and they said there's an emergency alert."

Despite that, the town's New World supermarket had remained open, and owner Samuel Fletcher said it was mostly business as usual.

"We follow food safety procedures for something like this. We've got that as part of our food control plan.

"We'll just cut out any non-essential tasks until we get back into normal operations with running water."

Fletcher said those tasks were to do with deep cleaning.

A water truck in Ohakune supplying drinking water. RNZ / Kate Pereyra

Ruapehu College's 250 students spent the day away from class, and principal Kris Vine said he was keeping an hour-by-hour watch on the situation.

"Ideally, we would be open for business and having our students here.

"Health and safety has to come first, so despite the disruption it's a learning curve for our kids about the importance of water and emergency. I guess there's some different learnings our kids can take from an experience like this."

He said students always had work to do online, so could concentrate on that. He was at school catching up on administration tasks.

Investigation confirmed

Ruapehu mayor Weston Kirton told Morning Report the outage could extend into Tuesday, but after a meeting with officials this morning the news was better.

Ruapehu mayor Weston Kirton. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

However, by 3pm, Manley's statement confirmed it was a false dawn.

The outage was due to damage to the pipe into town, caused by an earthquake two weeks ago.

"The line itself is about 70 years old. It's up in terrain by the mountain - about 5 kilometres of line that's had it's issues at times, but this is fairly new to us that it's broken.

"We'll be having an investigation into what happened."

Many locals RNZ spoke to were understanding, but district councillor John Chapman was less so, telling Checkpoint he was embarrassed and appalled this had happened, especially during ski season.

Kirton acknowledged there would be unhappiness.

"Some people are quite angry at the fact it's happened at this time. It always happens on a weekend, of course.

Local Clive Young fills a water bottle. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

"The people who I've being seeing over the past 24 hours have been very co-operative...

"We really apologise to them for the inconvenience."

For now, the town's 1400 residents, such as Evie Story and her 18-month-old daughter Thea, are making do as best they can.

"We've got a little baby bath at home, so she just goes in the baby bath. The drinking water they've given us is really good, so she just has that for her water.

"It's not really affecting us that much."

World.title: Razor in the NRL? Orcas target Scott Robertson for head coach
World.content:
After his unceremonious exit from the All Blacks, Scott Robertson may be set for a shock code switch.

The Southern Orcas - a proposed South Island rugby league club vying for entry into the NRL - has confirmed it is offering Robertson a four-year contract to coach the side, should its license be granted.

Based out of Christchurch and chaired by Sir Graham Lowe, the Orcas are hopeful of becoming the 20th franchise in the NRL from 2029.

Lowe confirmed the club had approached Robertson with a contract, an offer that came as a shock to the man they call 'Razor'.

"There's no doubt that he was surprised when we approached him about it, but also he was excited. It's a very big call for him to make, but it's also been a very big call for us to make as well. We're just excited and hopeful and you know, that, that he will be able to accept," Lowe told RNZ.

Lowe said chasing Robertson was not just about his coaching credentials.

"The very special thing also is Razor's a really good bloke and those who've had the opportunity to meet him would agree with me and if you can match that with being a great leader of men and a great coach, I think you're on a great combination."

Robertson was appointed All Blacks coach in 2024 at the conclusion of the 2023 Rugby World Cup, succeeding Ian Foster.

He lasted just two years in the role before being asked to step aside, replaced by Dave Rennie.

"I'm sure it must have been really difficult for him when he had that call, you know, with the New Zealand Rugby Union, but that's water under the bridge now. It's gone. And what we've done is provide him with an opportunity to move forward."

Lowe said Robertson still had plenty to offer as a coach.

The move would represent a significant change for Robertson, who has spent his entire coaching career in rugby, but Lowe believed Robertson's leadership and understanding of the game would allow him to make the transition.

"He's displayed over a long period of time a leadership quality, a confidence, and can obviously get the best out of those around him.

"While he hasn't coached rugby league, we don't see that as a problem. He understands rugby league, he studied rugby league and certainly he will have the opportunity."

The Orcas' NRL bid has been officially submitted, with the franchise awaiting a decision from Australian Rugby League Commission chairman Peter V'landys.

"All we know is we've had to put our best foot forward, which I'm confident that we have done. So we're just, sitting and waiting with our fingers crossed."

But Lowe believed the time was right for the South Island to join the party.

"Sitting from where we are over here, it looks easy but there's a lot I know for the NRL to consider, I'm not sure what other options they've got over there but I'm certainly confident that another team such as the Orcas based out of Christchurch will actually thrive.

World.title: Convicted insider trader Peter Huljich banned from being company director
World.content:
Businessman Peter Huljich has been banned from becoming a company director for seven years, nearly three years after his conviction for insider trading.

Huljich was convicted on a charge of insider conduct relating to the sale of shares in former NZX-listed company Pushpay Holdings.

After the Supreme Court declined his application for leave to appeal, the Financial Markets Authority applied to the High Court in Auckland for a banning order against Huljich, which he did not oppose.

Huljich is banned from being a director, promoter, or manager of a financial markets participant, or a company intending to become one, for seven years from his conviction on 3 November 2023, unless the High Court gives permission.

"Everyone trading in our markets is entitled to do so on the same footing, without others acting while holding information the market doesn't have," FMA head of enforcement Margot Gatland said.

"Mr Huljich had such information and encouraged others to trade when that information was not generally available to the market trading on it."

Gatland said it marked the end of proceedings relating to the Pushpay insider trading case.

Huljich is part of the Auckland richlister Huljich family, and is the son of Christopher Huljich.

He and his father founded Huljich Wealth Management, which was later sold to Fisher Funds.

The FMA said it also accepted an enforceable undertaking from Peter Huljich's partner Sarah Huljich (née Elder), who was Pushpay's head of investor relations at the time.

She admitted she should have known the information was material, and that she helped to facilitate, and thereby encouraged trading in Pushpay shares while she held that information.

World.title: Council pushes Ohakune's water restoration another 24 hours
World.content:
The Ruapehu District Council is now saying another 24 hours will be needed before Ohakune's water network is safely back online.

The council had earlier been confident supply would be restored around 5pm on Monday.

But it says if the pipeline that carries water from its source to the treatment plant is repressurised too quickly, it could fracture, and cause even longer delays.

Water supplies to the central North Island town were turned off after last month's earthquake near Taumarunui likely damaged a major water pipeline. The town's water reservoir is down to 12 percent.

RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Earlier on Monday morning the district's mayor had said the problem was more serious than originally thought and could not confirm when the town will have water again.

But Ruapehu District Mayor Weston Kirton later told Midday Report that there had been a reassessment of the conditions and water would be back on by 5pm, with experts coming in from all around the country.

Ruapehu Mayor Weston Kirton discusses Ohakune water issues Midday Report Download MP3 4m

'Extremely technical and challenging situation'

Earlier on Monday afternoon the council's chief executive Clive Manley said it was still aiming to get water back by 5pm on Monday.

He said at the time service contractor Veolia was able to locate hidden valves and was installing new ones to help release trapped air from the system.

"Restoring the supply has been complicated by sections of the raw water pipeline being buried and located in heavy bush, making valves difficult to find.

"Veolia has developed a plan for recharging the water network that includes introducing water from the treatment plant end of the system."

One of many closure notices in Ohakune today. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Additional staff and resources were brought in from Whanganui, Auckland and Central Hawke's Bay to help with the repairs, he said.

However later on Monday afternoon Manley said another 24 hours would be needed and water was expected to be back around 5pm Tuesday.

He said if the pipeline that carried water from its source to the treatment plant was repressurised too quickly, it could fracture, and cause even longer delays.

"A slower, controlled approach is therefore needed to protect the repaired infrastructure and safely restore the town's water supply."

"This has been an extremely technical and challenging situation. We have been working to keep the community fully informed as new information becomes available, but the situation and expected restoration time have continued to evolve as work has progressed."

Council's water services contractor, Veolia, had confirmed that the airlock affecting the raw water pipeline had been resolved.

Evie Story says she's been bathing 18-month-old Thea by using bottled water during Ohakune's outage. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

The council said emergency water supplies were available from Ruapehu District Council's office at 37 Ayr St and people could reuse water bottles at this same location.

It said port-a-loos were located at the council's office; Thames Street opposite the Powderhorn; Goldfinch Street / Shannon Street; and the rear carpark of the Ohakune i-SITE.

"We are contacting schools to let them know about this situation. We expect schools will make the decision to close, but that is their decision to make."

Residents were asked to keep all taps inside their properties turned off while network restorations where ongoing.

A water truck in Ohakune supplying drinking water. RNZ / Kate Pereyra

Mayor had been unsure when water would be back

Kirton had first told Morning Report it had been more difficult to fix the piping than had been initially thought.

"We've found the leak, we've actually fixed the leak, we've then tried to flush the system out and it's not working that well... and so we're obviously working hard to overcome that problem."

Kirton had said there was about 5km of concrete piping that was about 70 years old and may have been affected by the earthquake.

But it was in difficult-to-access terrain which was hard to flush out, he said.

Angelina Reyes has filled up water bottles from the council-supplied tank in Ohakune. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

"As soon as we get on top of the airlocks then we'll be able to manufacture the water and then open the systems up for the town, but it's certainly concerning."

The water had previously been expected to be back on by Monday afternoon, but Kirton told Morning Report that was no longer the case, and he did not want to speculate on when it would be back on.

Weston Kirton says it will take longer than initially expected to get the town's regular water system fixed. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

The water plant was brand new and the issue was actually getting the water to the plant, he said.

The emergency situation was worsening and they would be dealing with that this morning, Kirton said.

"It could well be that we have an emergency situation to actually get water from elsewhere, through tankers or the like."

It would take longer than expected to get the existing plant up and running, he said.

Colin Young fills a water bottle. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

It may be necessary to put an emergency water system in place before Ohakune's regular system can be fixed, he said.

"So I can't speculate whether it's a state of emergency yet, but that's one of the considerations you know whether we call on the government for help to actually overcome the issue with our town."

There was an influx of people in Ohakune at this time of year and there were businesses that wanted to be open and operating, he said.

World.title: Voters' digest: Election 2026 by the numbers
World.content:
The Electoral Commission has launched its enrolment campaign ahead of the November election - and with it, a hefty serving of the latest stats.

RNZ has pulled some of them together in an easy-to-digest list:

Timeline

4 October: The cut-off date for being included on the printed roll. Voting is easiest if you are enrolled before this date, and it also ensures you will get an EasyVote card. This follows the dissolution of Parliament set down for 1 October.

25 October: The cut-off date for enrolments. Unlike previous years, voters must be enrolled before this date or their vote will be thrown out.

26 October: The day advance voting begins.

7 November: Election day. Voting closes 7pm. Political advertising ends, and signs and hoardings must be taken down. Adverts posted to social media can remain there if they were posted before this date, with some provisos.

Facts and figures

About 3.6 million: The estimated number of people enrolled, about 89 percent of eligible voters. Electoral Commission chair Simon Moore says it's "not bad, but we don't think it's good enough". Each enrolled person will have an election pack sent to them between 17 and 22 August - if you think you're enrolled and don't receive one, something's gone wrong. You can check your enrolment status at vote.nz,

About 440,000: The number of eligible people estimated to not be on the roll.

53 percent: The enrolment rate for people aged between 18 and 25. About 200,000 people in this age bracket are not enrolled, accounting for about 45 percent of the unenrolled voter base.

About 2 million: The number of emails the commission expects to also be sent out to remind people to enrol and about the new rules for when you can vote. "If you've got a second contact address, we'll use that. If you've given your email, we'll try that. If you've given a mobile number, we'll try that," le Quesne says.

27,000: The rough number of extra people the Electoral Commission needs to employ for the election. "That makes us the single largest employer in the country at that time by some very considerable margin," chief electoral officer Karl le Quesne says.

2300: Roughly how many voting places will be available.

850: Roughly how many advance voting places will be available.

460: The number of events the commission has run this year alone to encourage enrolment and boost voter numbers.

160: The number of schools that have taken part in events like the above.

10: The number of 'enrolment hubs' set up in places with high populations through September and October to encourage enrolment and make the process easy for people.

17: The number of political parties registered for the election.

700,000: The number of special votes the commission still expects to process this election.

55,000: The number of special votes the commission expects will still be disallowed. The total number of disallowed votes will be recorded and reported with the final election result, but the number of people turned away because their enrolment is incorrect or because they missed the 25 October deadline will not be. Le Quesne says a special vote will be taken if there is uncertainty but would be discarded if it does not meet requirements. The post-election survey - which also polls non-voters - may estimate the number of people turned away.

20: The number of days the commission expects a full vote count to take. This puts the estimated date for the official results for the election at 27 November.

Three: The number of days of counting the commission expects to save this election by no longer counting votes made by people enrolling on the day. However, it's expected to take the same time as the last election due to increasing enrolment numbers.

61: The total number of seats (electorate or list) a party or group of parties need to have a majority in Parliament and form a government - presuming there is no overhang.

100,000: The number of enrolled New Zealanders believed to be living overseas. Some in Australia will be able to vote at a voting place, otherwise they can lodge a special vote through the local New Zealand Embassy or download the forms online (if enrolled).

$36,000: The spending limit for electorate candidates to spend on advertising during the three-month regulated period (from 7 August to midnight 6 November).

$1.503m: The baseline spending limit for political parties, with an extra $36,000 per contested electorate for a maximum $4.059m.

$17,000: The amount someone can spend on election-related advertising without having to register with the Electoral Commission. Groups that are not campaigning to enter Parliament can register as 'third parties' and can spend up to $424,000.

$40,000: The fine for failing to include a promoter statement on political advertising.

$179.2m: Rough cost to the Electoral Commission for running the previous 2023 election (not including the additional $1.2m cost of the 2023 Port Waikato by-election or the total $3.6m provided to parties for advertising). That's up from the $135.9m spent in 2020, which included a $36m topup to ensure things ran smoothly despite the Covid-19 pandemic.

Three square metres: The maximum size for election signs.

100 metres: The closest you can be to a voting place while still providing free food, drink (other than water) or entertainment, unless you are an "entity that in its ordinary course of business provides free food, drink or entertainment".

-1: The number of electorates compared to the 2020 election. There are 16 general electorates in the South Island, as required under legislation. The numbers of Māori electorates across the country (seven) and general electorates in the North Island (48, last election there were 49) are adjusted automatically by the Representation Commission based on population levels.

0800 36 76 56: The freephone number for the commission, who can help check if you are enrolled.

3676: The phone number you can text your name and address to, for free, to have an enrolment form sent to you.

World.title: Children as young as 7 seeking help as Youthline calls reach record high
World.content:
One of the country's main crisis helplines says more children than ever before are seeking help - some as young as seven years old.

Youthline says it's reached record levels, connecting an average of four young people every day with emergency services because they were at immediate risk of harm over the past six months.

Just a few years ago, that figure was closer to one a week.

Youthline runs free services including a helpline, face-to-face counselling, mentoring, and programmes in schools.

RNZ reported in March one in ten of its callers was now under the age of 12.

Chief executive Shae Ronald told Checkpoint the age reduction had been a global trend, with similar news emerging in the UK about three years ago.

Young people were reporting experiencing increased pressure, stress and expectations from family, peers and schools - in some cases, exacerbated by social media.

"The situations they're facing are becoming increasingly serious. Every day our team supports young people experiencing anxiety, loneliness, self-harm, suicidal thoughts, family conflict and abuse, often all at once rather than as isolated issues."

New Zealand ranks last among OECD countries for youth mental health and has one of the highest youth suicide rates in the developed world, highlighting the growing need for accessible support services.

Ronald said despite funding from government, they needed public support to keep the hotline open.

"We still need to fundraise over a million dollars every year to keep the helpline going," Ronald said.

This September, it would be running a campaign called Walk the Talk, calling on New Zealanders to commit to walking or moving every day of the month to raise money, with all funding going towards the helpline.

World.title: Chris Hipkins officially rules out working with New Zealand First in any government he leads
World.content:
Labour leader Chris Hipkins has finally and officially ruled out working with New Zealand First in any government he leads.

The announcement had long been expected, with the relationship between the former coalition partners seemingly beyond repair.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters had already ruled out working with Labour

Hipkins had previously said it was "highly unlikely" his party would work with New Zealand First again, and had already ruled out working with Peters as foreign affairs minister.

But on Monday afternoon, he confirmed there had been further internal conversations with his caucus, and he was finally ruling the party out altogether.

"Winston Peters has ruled us out. I'm happy to rule him out. It's clearly not going to happen."

Asked why he could not have said so sooner, Hipkins said New Zealand First's "pattern of behaviour" had escalated.

"I'm not going to put up with overt racism in any government that I lead, as that's the sort of behaviour that Winston Peters and New Zealand First are indulging in. They won't have any role in a government that I lead."

Hipkins said there was "not a single person" in Labour who thought the party should be open to working with New Zealand First.

"I think everybody has been, I guess, wanting to just see how things shake down. But clearly, Winston Peters' recent behaviour has now made that completely unacceptable."

In a post on X, Peters said Hipkins had "severe learning difficulties."

"Why the media aren't lambasting him for "ruling NZFirst out" after we ruled him out four years ago, then again twelve months ago, and repeatedly done so every month when answering the same stupid questions, is beyond a joke."

The definitive rule-out comes off the back of a poll which showed a 3.7 point slump for Labour, and a more difficult path back to power.

The Taxpayers Union-Curia poll, released last Friday, had Labour on 27.8 percent.

The poll had the current coalition parties able to form a government, on 61 seats if the poll was replicated on election day.

The opposition - including the Opportunity Party, which National has already ruled out working with - would have just 59 seats - not enough to govern.

Hipkins, who had previously described the poll as "rogue", was sticking to his guns, saying Labour's polling had otherwise been steadily increasing since the election.

World.title: Head aims to maintain opening spot ahead of busy 12 months
World.content:
Travis Head can envisage himself continuing to open the batting for Australia at the end of next year's Ashes.

The positive mindset of the back-to-back Allan Border Medal winner is no surprise.

Head was a revelation in home conditions in last year's Ashes series with three centuries after moving up from the middle order.

Ahead of the opening Test against Bangladesh in Darwin, the 32-year-old was asked if his order switch was short-term or whether it could work across the 20 or more Tests Australia will play in the next 12 months.

There was a sense that Head's move up the order against England was intended to counter their ultra-aggressive "Bazball".

It worked so well that the term "Travball" was coined.

Prior to the home Ashes, his stints as an opener had been short-lived.

Travis Head scored three centuries as an opener in the last Ashes series. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

Head was unstoppable on home tracks in the Ashes series, but he will face a variety of surfaces in Australia, South Africa, England and India in the next 12 months.

He says he is not worried about playing in different conditions.

"I feel like I have been adaptable in the places that I have played," Head said.

"In India and England I have opened the batting, which is a slightly different to Australia.

"Everything is going to be different, but what I have been able to do over my career is problem solve the best that I can and work through challenges — whether they are green wickets or flat wickets.

"It will look different in every Test match or every series. I am trying to be as calm and consistent as I can."

Whether Head stays an opener will depend largely on how he performs and also on the displays of the middle order.

Tweaks may be made but right now Head plans to be opening in the final Test of next year's away Ashes series.

"I think it will work," he said.

"If I have done it for [another] 20 Tests and I am sitting there in a few years and I have opened the batting the whole time … I would have done an OK job and been consistent, contributed and had a good partnership with Jake [Weatherald].

"It is a new challenge coming here and a new challenge in South Africa in a month's time and I am looking forward to the challenge."

International cricket coach Joe Gatting has posted videos of how Head plans for a variety of scenarios and surfaces and he is expected to continue to find the best approach in all conditions.

"We have a lot of footage and we couldn't be more resourced in that space. I'll continue to do that," Head said.

AAP

World.title: Geelong Cats board holds crisis meeting over concussion deal
World.content:
Geelong is about to reply to the AFL's "please explain" as the Cats brace for a potential massive penalty over the secret concussion deal with Jake Kolodjashnij.

Amid speculation over the futures of Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and AFL chairman Craig Drummond, the club board held a crisis meeting on Monday to work out its response to the league.

Also on Monday, Geelong captain Patrick Dangerfield said the club had "buggered up", but strongly defended Hocking.

Pressure has been mounting on Geelong and the AFL since it emerged last Thursday that the Cats struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij, who had a history of concussion.

Drummond apologises AFL chair Craig Drummond issues a statement apologising for his part in the Jake Kolodjashnij concussion contract saga.

"We acknowledge this has been a challenging time for Jake, our club and Geelong supporters," Cats president Grant McCabe said in a statement on Monday.

"The board has met this morning to discuss our response to the AFL's letter. That will be submitted by end of day Tuesday, 11 August.

"This will provide the club with the chance to detail the actions it took in navigating this complex matter. We welcome this opportunity.

"The club remains committed to providing our players with the highest standard of care and support."

Hocking was Cats chief executive and Drummond was the club president when the deal was struck two years ago with Koladjashnij.

The Geelong defender signed a waiver that meant he effectively took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to indemnify the club and its medical staff from potential court action.

On the weekend Hocking defended the club in a radio interview and argued there was not a lot they would do differently.

"As a leader it's really important to take ownership and just lead through this. It's not easy to do, but I wouldn't change too much — we are a really good football club," he said.

"I know there are people out there who say culturally we are maybe not as strong as we have been, but we do so much right and occasionally there might be one or two per cent we don't get right.

"In this case that will be proven, I would suggest, that will be proven with the 'please explain'. We don't get everything right."

Drummond also released a statement in which he apologised over the deal. He added he would not be involved in the AFL's assessment and deliberation of the Kolodjashnij situation.

On Monday, Dangerfield told Fox Footy that Hocking was one of the most "placid" people he had met and gave him his full support.

"He's a man of the highest integrity … we're lucky to have him," Dangerfield said.

But he acknowledged mistakes had been made.

"Clearly there were some parts that we buggered up as a club. We can be better," he said.

AAP

World.title: WNBA player claims 'white privilege' saw her ejected after foul
World.content:
DiJonai Carrington of the Chicago Sky has been ejected after being called for a Flagrant 2 foul on Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever.

Minutes after the eviction on Saturday (local time), Carrington posted on social media the words "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever.

Cunningham, who is white, was shooting a fast-break lay-up in the first quarter when Carrington, who is black, came from behind and hit her in the head and neck, knocking her to the court as the shot went in.

Cunningham said she thought the foul in the 90–86 Indiana win was "absolutely" intentional.

"Clearly I think it was unnecessary," Cunningham said.

"I've never really spoken to her and I have no beef with her, but I guess she has some pent-up stuff."

DiJonai Carrington had little to complain about, most suggested. (Getty Images: Michael Reaves)

Fever coach Stephanie White had a different view of the play.

"It was a hard foul," White said.

"I don't think that DiJonai intentionally came out to get her across the neck like she did, but it did happen, and I thought it was the right call."

Cunningham got up immediately, charged toward Carrington and pushed her as she was held back by a teammate.

"I popped up," Cunningham said.

"I'm not going to let anyone just do that to me. I think everyone knows that. I think that's why she did it, because she wants attention."

Sophie Cunningham had to be held back after popping up after the foul. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/Melissa Tamez)

The play was reviewed and upgraded to a Flagrant 2 after the referee said there was wind-up, impact and follow-through on the foul.

Sky coach Tyler Marsh said he had not seen a replay of the play, but that seeing it live, he thought Carrington was making a play on the ball and that he did not believe it warranted a Flagrant 2 foul.

"I haven't looked at that play since, so I really don't know if it was justified or not," he said.

"But, that's what I thought in the moment."

Marsh was then asked about Carrington's social media post.

"I have to get back to you on that because I'm just now hearing about that," he said.

"So yeah, we'll handle that."

But Cunningham had plenty to say about the post.

"I think the league is taking care of that," she said.

"This has nothing to do with race. Last year, I did the same thing and I got kicked out. And I deserved to be kicked out. There's no reason even to play that card."

In the third quarter, Fever star Caitlin Clark was assessed a technical foul after she made contact with a referee when she was forced out of bounds.

WNBA champs rubbish claims of Clark jealousy The outsized spotlight on Caitlin Clark has prompted some to suggest others in the WNBA are jealous of her, but two champions of the league say that is nonsense.

The technical was Clark's eighth of the season, triggering a one-game suspension for Indiana's next game if not rescinded by the league.

"She said I ran into her," Clark said in a post-game television interview.

"I've already watched it on the tape, so we'll let the league decide. But it wasn't intentional or anything, so I'm hoping it's getting rescinded,"

A few hours after the game, Clark got her way. The WNBA rescinded the technical foul.

Cunningham has frequently come to Clark's defence after physical play by opponents and has become one of the higher-profile players in the league this season.

AP

World.title: Brazilian footballer falls in tunnel after scoring disallowed goal
World.content:
Brazilian footballer Jacy Maranhão was rushing to meet a sea of his supporters, ball in hand and jumping with joy, before he fell down a dark tunnel.

The Corbita defender had just put his club 2-0 up against Chapecoense in the first half of a game in the Brazilian Serie A.

But just as he found his footing again and dusted himself off from the fall, the referee halted the game.

On review, the Video Assistant Referee (VAR) found the 29-year-old's goal was offside.

Jacy managed to continue playing into the first few minutes of the second half before being substituted with an injury.

The incident was not the first time a footballer had fallen foul of the tunnel at the Estádio Major Antônio Couto Pereira.

Loading...

Almost a decade earlier, Cameroonian forward Diederrick Joel Tagueu-Tadjo ran to the same end of the pitch, jumping over the same advertising hoardings before falling into the now-infamous Corbita tunnel.

But unlike Jacy, his goal was not ruled out, and he managed to finish the game against São Paulo.

But according to Brazilian journalist Leonardo Mendes Jr, there was a striking similarity to the two incidents.

"There's one detail that makes it even more unbelievable," he posted on social media.

World.title: Chiefs sign premiership winger To'o away from Panthers
World.content:
Four-time premiership-winning winger Brian To'o has become the sixth player to sign with the PNG Chiefs for their inaugural NRL season in 2028.

The signing of the Penrith Panthers flyer, who has represented NSW in State of Origin and Samoa in Test matches, was announced by the Chiefs on Monday.

To'o has signed a three-year deal to join the Chiefs, with 2027 to be his final year with the Panthers.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"Brian is an exceptional rugby league player, but this signing is about much more than football," PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said.

"The PNG Chiefs will be a club proudly built in Papua New Guinea but with a strong Pacific identity.

"Across our region, family, culture, community and rugby league are deeply connected, and Brian represents those values every time he takes the field.

"He is fiercely proud of his Samoan heritage, incredibly close to his family and understands what it means to represent something bigger than yourself.

"That is exactly the kind of person we want wearing the Chiefs jersey."

To'o has been a key component of the Penrith Panthers dynasty, which won four consecutive premierships from 2021–2024, were grand finalists in 2020 and made last year's preliminary final.

The Panthers are on top of the NRL ladder in 2026, seeking a fifth title in six years.

To'o has played 151 matches for the Panthers since making his debut in 2019, scoring 99 tries to date.

He has played 17 Origins for the Blues, and 11 Tests for Samoa.

"Brian is an exceptional player, but he's an even better person. He's a great teammate, a devoted family man and someone who brings so much energy and positivity to our club every day," Penrith coach Ivan Cleary said.

"He's been a huge part of what we've built here and we're looking forward to sharing one more season with him before he begins his next chapter."

The Chiefs have now signed six players to its maiden roster, but have already secured key talent.

Former Penrith five-eighth Jarome Luai, who won four premierships with To'o, was the club's marquee signing earlier this year.

Alex Johnston, the all-time leading try scorer in Australian premiership rugby league, was a key outside back signed along with NSW Origin representative Zac Lomax.

Sydney Roosters utility Connor Watson and Englishman Matty Lees have also been signed.

World.title: Yeo learns fate on pec in seismic moment for Panthers
World.content:
Penrith's premiership charge has received a massive boost, with Isaah Yeo a chance to play again this year after avoiding surgery on his pectoral injury.

Yeo had been at risk of missing the rest of the NRL season after he left the field in Friday's loss to the Warriors, in what shaped as a major blow for the Panthers.

But Penrith medical staff confirmed on Monday the club's co-captain would not go under the knife following scans, and could begin rehabilitation in a bid to play again in 2026.

The news will also likely come as a relief to Australia coach Kevin Walters, with Yeo expected to again lead the Kangaroos at the World Cup if he avoids later surgery.

Former Panther Apisai Koroisau missed just one week with a pectoral injury early this year, as opposed to the 10 weeks usually out if surgery is required.

Penrith has made a habit of having players play through injury to be part of premiership wins throughout their dynasty.

Almost half of their squad were walking wounded through the first title of their four-peat in 2021, which the club compared to climbing Mount Everest.

Halves Jarome Luai and Nathan Cleary both played through persistent shoulder issues in 2023 and 2024 respectively, with both requiring surgery afterwards.

Had Yeo been sidelined, it would have been a monumental blow to the first-placed Panthers, given the role he plays in both attack and defence at lock.

Ex-Panther Spencer Leniu described Yeo as the "heartbeat" of Penrith's team over the weekend, declaring his injury would be a "massive loss" for the club.

Penrith faces Leniu's Sydney Roosters in a blockbuster top-of-the-table clash on Thursday night, which Yeo would not be expected to play in.

AAP

World.title: Walker announces retirement after one last shot at AFL premiership
World.content:
Adelaide Crows great Taylor Walker has announced the 2026 AFL season will be his last, saying he hopes to end his career as a premiership winner.

The Crows today announced the veteran of 316 games would bring an end to his playing career, where he has kicked a club-record 706 goals to date.

Affectionately known as Tex, the 36-year-old told media after the announcement that the decision to step away had been "probably the hardest one of my life".

"I knew it was the right time for me and the football club that I retire at the end of the year, hopefully with a premiership cup or a medallion around my neck," he said.

"I don't want to be that player that goes that extra year or probably outstays their welcome.

"The closer I've got to the end, it's probably become a little bit more evident that it might be this year, but I've sort of treated it like my last year for the past six years."

Walker was drafted by the Crows in 2007 and made his AFL debut during the 2009 season.

He captained the club from 2015-2019, where he was twice named the AFL Players Association Best Captain in 2016 and 2017. He also led the Crows to the 2017 grand final, the club's most recent appearance in the sport's biggest game.

Today Walker was asked about one of the low points in his career — when he was fined and suspended for using a racial slur in 2021.

The Crows great described the incident as the "one thing I wish never happened".

"That was an incredibly difficult time for my family and I, and I suppose the biggest thing I learnt was that words don't just hurt one person, they can hurt so many different people, and I feel like I'm a better person for that mistake that I made," he said.

While Walker's sights remain firmly fixed on the remainder of the season, he said his hometown of Broken Hill had been very much in his thoughts as he looked both back and forward.

"I grew up barracking for the Adelaide footy club. It was my dream. I had Crows posters all through my room as a little kid," he said.

"I've said to my two best mates that are still playing back in Broken Hill that I want to go and try and win a premiership back there, so we'll try and do that next year."

The Crows currently sit fifth on the AFL ladder, level on points with fourth-placed Brisbane on percentage.

Adelaide travels to Perth for a Friday night blockbuster against ladder-leaders Fremantle, then hosts GWS in the final round of the home and away season at Adelaide Oval.

World.title: Aussie high jumper wins gold at under-20 world titles
World.content:
Australian high jumper Izobelle Louison-Roe has won gold at the World Athletics U20 Championships.

The 19-year-old came into the championships in Eugene, Oregon as the leading under-20 jumper this year, twice hitting a personal best of 1.95 metres.

She would not need a personal best to win gold on Sunday (local time), with a jump of 1.92m enough to be crowned champion, adding to the silver she won at Lima during the 2024 championships.

Hungary's Lilianna Bátori claimed silver and Spaniard Aitana Alonso won bronze, both jumping 1.90 metres.

"It was such an exciting competition, one of the moments of my life," Louison-Roe said.

"It was an incredible feeling when I won.

"I was crying so much I couldn't keep it together, it was amazing."

Louison-Roe was not the only Australian to medal on Sunday, with the 4x400m relay team securing a silver.

The Aussie quartet of Shari Hurdman, Xanthee Watts, Charlotte McAuliffe and Alice Hill ran a 3:31.39 to finish second behind the United States.

"Honestly, it's surreal to just go out there and get the job done," McAuliffe said post-race.

"I think we knew coming into this what we were all capable of, and we knew a medal was definitely possible.

" To go out and do the job is just amazing. "

Australia's men's 4x400m relay team — Seth Kennedy, Fred Hamblin, Dylan Hall and Chase Grant — came agonisingly close to also winning a medal, missing out on the podium by four-hundredths of a second.

Grant produced a brilliant final leg of 44.85 seconds, but was just pipped at the line by the French runner.

The women's 4x100m team — Thewbelle Philp, Zara Hagan, Grace Crowe and Emilia Reed — were also pipped at the line and placed fourth.

Kieran Shepherd ran a personal best of 3:42.25 to place eighth in the men's 1,500m, while Milla Roberts overcame a mid-race fall to be 14th in the women's 1,500m.

Elijah Wilson placed 13th in the men's discus final with a best throw of 56.47m.

Tech.title: No Dogs in Space is a music history podcast for true obsessives
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Sadly, there hasn’t been a new episode of No Dogs in Space since July of 2024. Part four of the podcast’s series on Can wrapped up an abbreviated season three, which focused on experimental rock. Don’t get me wrong, I loved seasons one and two, but the show seemed to be gearing up for a deep dive into Krautrock, and I was hype. Unfortunately, that episode ended with hosts Marcus Parks (Last Podcast on the Left) and Carolina Hidalgo declaring they were going to do another season on punk (the topic of season one), only for the feed to go quiet.

If you’re a music obsessive, this is a must-listen podcast. Over the course of 73 episodes, the husband-and-wife duo digs into the careers of the Beastie Boys, The Velvet Underground, Joy Division, and more. Even if you think you know everything there is to know about iconic bands like The Stooges, I guarantee there will be new info here.

The show dedicates multiple hours over the course of several episodes to its subjects. Its two-part intro to Krautrock, which heavily focuses on Amon Düül II is over three hours long, and that’s on the shorter side. The Replacements series is nearly nine hours long, and Beastie Boys is even longer still.

Over these exceptionally long series, it never gets dull, though. The two balance scripted info-dense sections with more improvisational sidebars expertly. They also, as you’d expect from a married couple, have great chemistry on mic. They also make sure to share all their sources at the end of the episode in case you want to track down the primary source or do your own fact-checking.

The show isn’t officially over. As recently as a couple of months ago, Carolina was responding to Instagram comments saying she’d love to do more episodes. And the possibility of the show returning has come up multiple times on live streams. But as of this writing, we’re still waiting on that Punk Rock 2.0 series.

Tech.title: Zuckerberg’s yacht was closer, but someone else saved a stranded boat
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Earlier this week, the Alaskan cruise ship Wilderness Legacy rescued a small skiff stranded near Farragut Bay after running out of fuel. But, according to tracking data reviewed by the Alaska Beacon and Halifax Shipping News, the closest vessel was actually Mark Zuckerberg’s super yacht, Launchpad.

Michael Love, a passenger on the Wilderness Legacy, posted on Bluesky that the captain announced the Launchpad was closer, but “repeatedly refused to respond,” which was met with booing from the passengers. The AIS tracking (embedded below) seems to support that the Launchpad was closer to the vessel in trouble, but then stopped near the entrance of the bay. The Wilderness Legacy can be seen passing Launchpad, then turning around and towing the stranded boat back to safety.

The US Coast Guard and the Marine Exchange of Alaska did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But Coast Guard Public Affairs Specialist Shannon Shepard told the Alaska Beacon that “at approximately 9:56 p.m., the Coast Guard determined they were not in distress and issued a marine assistance request broadcast on their behalf.”

Brian Baker, spokesperson for Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan, told The Verge that “Mark and his family were not on board at the time of the incident. As the Coast Guard noted, the boat was not in distress, and by the time the crew reviewed the Coast Guard contact on a different radio channel from the one they were operating on, the assist was already underway. We’re grateful all parties are safe.”

Tech.title: 49ers coach says his Tesla was on Autopilot when he crashed
Tech.content: “I’ve had Autopilot for nine years, so I’m pretty comfortable with it and, you know, who knows what happened when I turned around? Whether it malfunctioned or whether I knocked it off? That’s something I don’t know yet. But regardless, that’s… it is always your fault, whether you’re on Autopilot or not. You can’t take your eyes off the road. It’s a partnership driving, you don’t just turn it over to a computer.”

Tech.title: Dropbox is a PC builder’s best friend
Tech.content:
In 2018 I bet my reputation and self-worth on a huge crowdfunded game design project. It could have been a failure for many reasons, but the one I became most worried about was losing all of the work that was stored locally on my home-built PC — a scenario that would have left a lot of people very upset and placed me in deep trouble. I wasn’t irresponsible, I had local backups, but at some point I found myself in custody of so many important files that it scared me. And no matter how many redundancies I could build at home, they’d all still be in the same place — a risky bet. So I bought a subscription to Dropbox. Years later, it’s still one of the best software subscriptions that I happily renew each year.

It was great to have all that work backed up in the cloud — both for peace of mind and because it made working with collaborators breezier, letting them upload stuff directly to my drive, and letting me transfer files up to 50GB in size. In quick order I had built a trove of incredible artwork and complicated InDesign, Photoshop, and Illustrator files. The original goal for my Dropbox configuration was to make sure I wouldn’t lose any data in a worst-case scenario, so I set it up to mirror everything living on my work partition. Eventually, I ran smack into a worst-case scenario. Not once, but twice.

I’m still not sure why, but my latest home-built PC chewed through two separate 2TB Samsung 970 Evo SSDs. It’s difficult to tell what went wrong with them, but in each case I woke up one morning to find when I tried to boot up that no drive could be detected. I can still feel my stomach trying to sink into the floor when I press that power button these days, never knowing if my drive had died in its sleep.

Fortunately, both times, after some process-of-elimination testing I learned that just the drive had gone bad and everything else in my system was A-OK. Maybe I should have ditched Samsung after the second disaster, but I’m now on an 2TB 990 Evo Plus. Knock on wood, this thing better not fail. That drive now costs almost twice what I originally paid for it thanks to our new outrageously priced world of parts.

My Dropbox bill is about $204 a year for a family plan ($17 a month), which includes up to six members. If you’re just in it for yourself you can get it for $9.99 a month billed yearly (about $120 a year), which comes with 2TB of storage. You can upgrade to 3TB for around $143 a year. That might be a tough sell for people who already have dozens of subscriptions, but I find it to be a decent price for excellent digital insurance.

There are other powerful options out there, especially for professionals working with heavy files or complicated workflows. Backblaze, for example, has a personal backup plan with unlimited data for $99 a year and no restrictions on file size. And, of course, if you live on the Mac, Apple iCloud Plus isn’t a bad option — especially if you’re already paying for an Apple One subscription. Even Adobe offers file backups through Creative Cloud if that’s your jam, but I would not recommend using that clunky software suite for anything other than doing the work you need to do.

I can’t recall a single time the service failed

I prefer Dropbox because the software works consistently well across multiple operating systems and is usually neither seen nor heard. The Windows client is snappy and I’ve found with a fast internet connection that its real-time syncing is efficient and painless. Anytime a file is modified in the partition I have mirrored in the cloud, Dropbox quietly begins uploading it and making changes to my mirrored files in the cloud. After using it for about eight years now I can’t recall a single time the service failed or faltered. It’s so fast and reliable I often forget it’s even there.

Now, for the important caveat: This might not work for you if you have poor internet speeds. It really depends on how much data you’re regularly moving around on your computer and how quickly you make changes to it. This could particularly be a problem for asymmetrical data plans that commonly boast lightning-fast download speeds while offering pathetic upload speeds. I’ve done fine averaging only about 20Mbps upload, but if you’re on something even lower you should try a free trial for a backup plan before committing. You can also find plenty of download time calculators online; at my gigabit download speed it usually takes around two hours to download the 1TB of files I have synced in the cloud.

And one more caveat: Putting everything (or even just many things) on your computer in the cloud isn’t for everyone, and I completely understand why many folks wouldn’t or shouldn’t do that for sensitive files. I once built local RAID drives and even airgapped storage systems to avoid having everything online. These things are still possible but getting more expensive by the day as storage prices spike. You’re the best judge of how and where your data should be protected.

That sinking feeling of potentially losing my whole PC? It was immediately followed each time by the assurance that I’d only lost a computer’s body and not its soul. When I got my PC back up and running with new storage, it ended up taking less time to resync all my files than it did to troubleshoot and install new hardware. I can almost hear Billy Crudup doing a Mastercard commercial in my head: New solid state drive, three hundred eighty-nine dollars. Yearly Dropbox subscription, two hundred and three dollars. Never worrying about losing your data? Priceless.

Tech.title: AI detectors are creating a new era of distrust
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more news about how AI is changing our daily lives, follow Emma Roth. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

Long before ChatGPT became a thing, educators and editors frequently used anti-plagiarism tools to see if writers were being honest about their work. These tools work by comparing a written work against a database filled with content from across the web, scholarly articles, and more to check for matching sentences and phrases. Some, like Turnitin, offer a percentage that claims to illustrate how much of the student’s writing overlaps with other works. Between potential false positives and uncertainty about whether work was duplicated intentionally, some educators have backed away from using that particular tool.

But now, the hunt for copied content is evolving into a war on AI-generated work. As quickly as students have picked up ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, teachers have adopted so-called AI detectors just as fast. A survey from the Center for Democracy and Technology found that 43 percent of sixth to 12th grade teachers in the US regularly used AI detectors between 2024 and 2025. Some universities already using Turnitin in their learning management systems found that the service automatically enabled AI detection when the tool launched in 2023.

Instead of comparing pieces of written content, AI detectors like GPTZero, Pangram, and the one created by Turnitin rely on their own AI models to guess whether something might not be human-written — a process that’s arguably even murkier than matching text on the web. As noted by GPTZero, AI detectors use an algorithm to analyze a text’s wording, rhythm, and structure, as well as to pick up on patterns in length and tone that may be more common in AI-written text. This relatively subjective evaluation isn’t as solid as something you could back up by matching text online, and can get tripped up by writers who speak English as a second language. Despite this, Turnitin has said that its AI detector falsely flags less than 1 percent of human-written content as AI, while Pangram claims its false positive rate is just 1 in 10,000. GPTZero claims it has a similarly low rate of mistaking human content for AI.

How it’s going

People online are already accusing each other of “sounding like AI,” but the ready availability of AI detection tools is only adding fuel to the LLM witch hunt. In some high-profile cases, AI writing accusations have directly impacted people’s livelihoods and reputations. Last month, the publisher Minotaur dropped a $2 million book deal over concerns that its author, Jerry Falade, used AI — something he vehemently denies.

There’s Thierry Rignol, a French national who sued Yale last year after a professor accused him of writing portions of his final exam with AI, resulting in a failing grade and a one-year suspension. The professor used GPTZero to scan Rignol’s writing for signs of AI, but the lawsuit argues that “AI surveillance and detection tools are known to unfairly target non-native English speakers” like Rignol. In February, a student at Adelphi University won a lawsuit against the school after his professor similarly claimed he used AI to write an essay. Though the lawsuit doesn’t say which AI tool the professor used to examine the student’s essay, Adelphi University has a licensing agreement with Turnitin.

As pointed out by the University of California, Los Angeles, AI detection tools are trained to pick up on patterns that could indicate AI use, such as repetitive terms and phrases, text that sounds too formal or informal, and nonsensical phrasing. Some, like QuillBot, also measure the “unpredictability” of text, as “AI tends to make the most ‘obvious’ or most common language choices as compared with human-produced writing,” according to UCLA. They may also look for sentence structure that remains the same throughout as another sign of AI. But these measurements aren’t indicative of AI on their own, as some people may just have a writing style with these qualities.

Even though Turnitin touts low false positive rates, it maintains that its tool “may not always be accurate” and shouldn’t be used to take actions against a student. Grammarly warns that users “should never rely on the results of an AI detector alone,” while GPTZero says “no AI detector can ever truly be 100% perfect.” OpenAI even shut down its own AI writing detector in 2023 due to low accuracy.

But AI writing accusations are still being flung across the web. Last week, in a video broadcast to the more than 3.5 million followers across his social channels, Ozzy Osbourne’s son, Jack, accused journalist and Verge contributor Kat Tenbarge of using AI to write an article for Rolling Stone, while flaunting the results from an AI detector, Getsolved, as “proof” of his claim. Tenbarge has refuted the claim in a video and a post on her website, but Osbourne hasn’t retracted his accusation or deleted the video, leaving Tenbarge to deal with the trolls.

There are numerous examples of false accusations, from writers to students, with many accusers failing to acknowledge the disclaimers that come along with some of these AI detection tools.

What happens next

The uncertainty surrounding AI detectors is enough for some educational institutions to stop using them altogether. Yale University, Johns Hopkins University, Vanderbilt University, Georgetown University, and others have disabled or restricted the use of AI detection tools. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology also warns that “AI detectors don’t work.”

Instead of relying on tools to weed out AI, many schools are encouraging educators to rethink their lessons. The University of Chicago, for example, suggests telling students to slow down their reading, breaking up longer writing assignments, and requiring students to reflect on their work. Stanford University says professors can consider holding assessments in classrooms, while MIT advises professors to leave room for students to disclose whether they used AI for help on an assignment, without penalty.

With AI becoming more prevalent in and outside the classroom, efforts to suss out what’s written by a human or a machine are ramping up as well. Some online platforms are only exacerbating suspicions surrounding AI use. Substack has built Pangram into its app, allowing users to scan blogs for suspected AI-generated content, while LinkedIn added a “seems like AI slop” button on posts. The result is a new era of distrust, where readers constantly question whether what they’re reading is AI and real human writers try their best not to sound like it.
